nodes.name: Colorimetry
nodes.note: A coloured compound absorbs light. The more concentrated, the darker the colour. Using a standard solution of known concentration, an unknown can be estimated by colour matching. Or pass light through both and compare intensities. Requires consistent lighting.

nodes.name: Combustion analysis of organics
nodes.note: A weighed sample is combusted in a hot copper tube with oxygen. Products pass through a drying agent, absorbing water in one bulb, then through base, absorbing CO2 in another. Weighing each gives moles of H and C. Requires a furnace at 800-900 C and precise temperature control.

nodes.name: Complexometric titration
nodes.note: A chelating agent like EDTA binds metal ions very tightly. The metal indicator dye also binds the metal but less tightly, so EDTA displaces it, changing colour. Works for calcium, magnesium, zinc, etc. Requires careful control of pH.

nodes.name: Conductometry
nodes.note: A small AC voltage is applied across two electrodes immersed in the solution. The current depends on the concentration and mobility of ions. Conductivity can titrate; as a precipitate forms, conductivity drops sharply at the endpoint.

nodes.name: Flame photometry
nodes.note: Each metal emits light at a characteristic wavelength when heated in a flame. Sodium is orange, potassium is lilac, lithium is red. The intensity depends on concentration. A diffraction grating or prism isolates each wavelength. Highly selective and sensitive.

nodes.name: Glass pH electrode
nodes.note: A special glass is formulated; thin membrane prevents error from water penetration while allowing ion exchange at the surface. The voltage across the membrane varies linearly with pH. Requires a reference electrode and a high-impedance amplifier to measure the tiny current. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Gravimetric analysis
nodes.note: E.g. to find sulphur in coal, burn it to SO2, absorb in base to form sulphate, precipitate as BaSO4, filter, dry and weigh. The mass of BaSO4 multiplied by the ratio of atomic weights gives the original sulphur. Accuracy depends on pure precipitate.

nodes.name: Acid-base indicators
nodes.note: Methyl orange is red below pH 3.1, yellow above. Methyl red is red below pH 4.4, yellow above. Phenolphthalein is colourless below pH 8.2, pink above. Each substance needs the right indicator; choosing wrong gives an error. The indicator must not react with the analyte.

nodes.name: Kjeldahl nitrogen method
nodes.note: The sample is heated with conc. H2SO4 and copper sulphate. The high temperature carbonises the sample and oxidises nitrogen to NO, which forms (NH4)2SO4. Ammonia is driven off by distillation with base and collected in acid, then back-titrated. Very robust method.

nodes.name: Melting point determination
nodes.note: A sample is placed in a capillary tube and heated slowly in a bath or over a flame. The temperature is recorded when the solid first liquefies. Pure substances have sharp melting points; impurities lower and broaden the melting point. Used as a purity test.

nodes.name: Polarography
nodes.note: A dropping mercury electrode hangs in the solution. As voltage sweeps from negative to positive, each reducible ion accepts electrons at its characteristic voltage, creating a current pulse. A chart records current versus voltage, showing each ion's reduction potential. Quantitative and selective.

nodes.name: Redox titration
nodes.note: Permanganate solution is deep purple; at the endpoint a tiny excess gives a pink colour that does not fade. Dichromate must have an indicator. Works for any species that oxidises or reduces. The reaction must go to completion and must be fast.

nodes.name: Refractometry
nodes.note: Light bends at different angles depending on the refractive index of the medium. Dissolved substances change the refractive index. A refractometer measures the critical angle of total internal reflection. The value depends on temperature and concentration of solutes.

nodes.name: Spectrophotometry
nodes.note: A prism or grating isolates a narrow band of wavelengths. The solution is placed in a cuvette and light is passed through. The transmitted light is measured by a photoelectric cell or photographic plate. The absorbance at each wavelength reveals the identity and concentration.

nodes.name: Titrimetry and burettes
nodes.note: A burette is a long glass tube with a glass stopcock at the bottom, graduated in millilitres. The taper and stopcock must be precise or the burette leaks or sticks. The endpoint must be sharp and visible. Success depends on indicator choice and technique.

nodes.name: Azeotropic distillation
nodes.note: Ethanol and water form an azeotrope at 96 per cent ethanol; cannot be separated by ordinary distillation. Adding benzene shifts the azeotrope and allows anhydrous ethanol to be drawn off. Requires knowing what the azeotrope is for your pair.

nodes.name: Centrifuge
nodes.note: A rotating bucket or rotor creates artificial gravity, accelerating sedimentation a thousand-fold. Particles settle in seconds instead of hours. The tube must be strong; high-speed breakage is dangerous. Design of rotor balance is critical.

nodes.name: Column chromatography
nodes.note: The column is a glass tube packed with finely ground adsorbent. Solvent drips down slowly; compounds emerge at different times. The invention is realising that flow rate, particle size, and solvent polarity are the controlling parameters. Carbon or silica work; choice changes the separation.

nodes.name: Dialysis through parchment
nodes.note: Used to separate salts from proteins, or colloids from small ions. The driving force is diffusion; it is slow. A bag of parchment filled with solution, immersed in water, leaches out the small ions while keeping the colloid inside.

nodes.name: Electrophoresis in gelatin
nodes.note: The gel is gelatin or agar. A steady voltage is applied. Different proteins move at different speeds depending on their net charge and mass. Requires a stable voltage source and knowledge that the gel must be pH-controlled. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Fractional crystallisation
nodes.note: The key is knowing the solubility curve of each substance versus temperature. One compound might dissolve at 20 C but not at 5 C; another the reverse. Cooling in stages, filtering each crop, and recrystallising each fraction purifies both.

nodes.name: Freeze-drying apparatus
nodes.note: The sample is frozen solid, then pressure is reduced to perhaps 10 pascals. Ice sublimes directly to vapour without passing through liquid. Preserves heat-sensitive compounds and yields an airy powder. Requires a condenser to capture the water vapour.

nodes.name: Gas chromatography
nodes.note: The column is filled with an adsorbent or liquid on an inert support, heated to 200 C or more. The sample vaporises and passes through. Each compound sticks and releases at a different temperature, detected as it emerges. Requires precise temperature control.

nodes.name: Ion exchange resin
nodes.note: A resin carries fixed negative or positive charges on its skeleton. Mobile counterions in the pores swap with ions in the solution. Allows softening water, concentrating rare ions, or fully deionising. Capacity is finite; resin is regenerated by reversing the swap.

nodes.name: Paper chromatography
nodes.note: Paper acts as the stationary phase; the solvent is the mobile phase. Compounds separate by their affinity for each. Spot the mixture at the bottom, suspend in a jar with solvent in the bottom, the liquid wicks up. Each compound travels to a different height.

nodes.name: Recrystallisation
nodes.note: Not dissolution plus evaporation, but controlled cooling: the key is knowing exactly when mother liquor will release only the pure crystal. Impurities stay dissolved or crystallise at different temperatures. Each substance needs a different solvent.

nodes.name: Reflux condenser
nodes.note: The discovery is that you can heat a reaction indefinitely without losing solvent. Allows long reactions at controlled temperature. The cooling finger must be of the right dimensions to balance condensation rate with back-pressure.

nodes.name: Liquid-liquid extraction
nodes.note: Water and ether do not mix. If you dissolve a salt in water and shake it with ether, some salts transfer to the ether layer. The degree of transfer depends on solubility in each solvent. Repeat extraction exhausts the aqueous phase.

nodes.name: Soxhlet extractor
nodes.note: The siphon is the invention: gravity triggers emptying at exactly the right moment, so the same solvent portion hits fresh solid repeatedly. Extracts far more than single contact. The glass siphon tube is the critical precision piece.

nodes.name: Steam distillation
nodes.note: Works at boiling point of water, not the boiling point of the oil, so thermally labile compounds survive. The product is an emulsion of oil and water; separation requires decanting or salting out. Standard for essential oils.

nodes.name: Sublimation apparatus
nodes.note: A cold finger condenses the vapour. The apparatus must be absolutely sealed and the heating exact. Used for camphor, naphthalene, iodine. Quality difference: crude apparatus gives degradation, proper cooling finger does not.

nodes.name: Vacuum distillation
nodes.note: A liquid that decomposes at 250 C can be distilled at 100 C under half-bar vacuum. Requires a pump that does not introduce oil vapour, else contamination. The condenser must be cold; ice bath is standard.

nodes.name: Anodising and anodic oxidation
nodes.note: Aluminium is the anode, an inert metal is the cathode, and dilute H2SO4 is the electrolyte. Applying voltage oxidises the aluminium surface to Al2O3. The oxide layer is porous and can be dyed. Anodised aluminium resists corrosion far better than bare metal. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Colligative properties
nodes.note: Adding 1 mole of solute to 1 kg water raises the boiling point by 0.5 C, lowers the freezing point by 1.9 C, and raises osmotic pressure by 22 atm. This allows determining molecular weights or detecting dissociation of ionic compounds. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Electrochemical series
nodes.note: Magnesium is more easily oxidised than iron, which is more easily oxidised than copper. A more easily oxidised metal reduces a less easily oxidised metal salt. Used to predict reactions and design electrochemical cells. Potentials are measured versus a standard hydrogen electrode. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Equilibrium and equilibrium constant
nodes.note: At equilibrium, K = [products]/[reactants]. Changing concentration, temperature, or pressure shifts the equilibrium to re-establish K. The position of equilibrium is independent of how much starting material you use. This is Le Chatelier principle. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Chemical kinetics and rate laws
nodes.note: Rate = k [A]^m [B]^n. The powers m and n are determined experimentally by varying concentrations and measuring initial rates. The rate constant k depends on temperature via the Arrhenius equation. Catalyst lowers activation energy without changing equilibrium. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Le Chatelier's principle
nodes.note: Increasing concentration of a product shifts equilibrium to the left. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles. Understanding this allows controlling yields in large-scale synthesis. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: The mole and Avogadro constant
nodes.note: One mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 litres. One mole of solute dissolved in 1 litre gives a one-molar solution. The concept allows exact stoichiometric calculations. Without the mole, chemistry would remain a craft without quantitative control. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Nernst equation for electrode potential
nodes.note: E = E0 + (RT/nF) ln Q. At 25 C with log instead of ln: E = E0 + 0.06/n log Q. Used to predict cell voltages under non-standard conditions. When Q = 1, E = E0. When Q > 1, the potential decreases, pushing the reaction backwards. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Overpotential and electrode kinetics
nodes.note: Hydrogen evolution on copper has high overpotential; on platinum it is much lower. This allows electroplating copper onto steel without plating hydrogen gas. Overpotential depends on current density, temperature, and electrode surface. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Phase rule and phase diagrams
nodes.note: F = C - P + 2. At a triple point, all three phases coexist and no variable can be changed without losing a phase. Binary phase diagrams show how composition and temperature determine the phases present. Used for design of distillations and crystallisations. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Thermochemistry and Hess's law
nodes.note: Hess's law: the heat change depends only on initial and final states, not the path. A simple calorimeter measures temperature change when a reaction occurs in an insulated container. Knowing specific heats allows computing the enthalpy change. Used to predict unfeasible reactions. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Bakelite thermosetting resin
nodes.note: Phenol and formaldehyde condense under heat and catalyst to form novolac or resole, depending on conditions. The linear polymer is infusible. Adding more formaldehyde and heating crosslinks it into a thermoset. Very hard, good electrical insulator.

nodes.name: Buna synthetic rubber
nodes.note: Butadiene and styrene (about 3:1) are emulsion copolymerised at 5 C. The low temperature gives high yield and longer chains. Vulcanised with sulphur. Slightly harder than natural rubber. Used for tires, belts, and footwear.

nodes.name: Celluloid from nitrocellulose
nodes.note: Nitrocellulose alone is brittle and explosive. Camphor dissolves in it, acting as a plasticiser. The mixture can be molded when warm and hardens on cooling. Used for combs, billiard balls, and early film. Highly flammable.

nodes.name: Cellulose acetate plastic
nodes.note: Cellulose + acetic anhydride + H2SO4 catalyst gives cellulose acetate. The product is plastic without needing camphor. Less flammable than celluloid. Can be molded when warm. Used for safety film, spectacle frames, and cigarette filters.

nodes.name: Neoprene synthetic rubber
nodes.note: Chloroprene (2-chlorobutadiene) is emulsion polymerised at 40 C. The chlorine substituent enhances oil and flame resistance compared to natural rubber. Vulcanised with sulphur like natural rubber. Used for hoses, seals, weatherstripping.

nodes.name: Nylon-66 polyamide fibre
nodes.note: H2N(CH2)6NH2 and HOOC(CH2)4COOH at 270 C condense with loss of water, forming a linear polyamide. Extruding the molten polymer through a spinneret forms fibres. Nylon is strong, elastic, and used for textiles, hosiery, bristles. Moisture uptake can be significant.

nodes.name: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA)
nodes.note: Methyl methacrylate at 50-100 C with peroxide initiator forms clear polymer. Can be injection molded or cast. Much clearer than polystyrene. Used for aircraft windows, signs, sheets. Good chemical resistance.

nodes.name: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) polyester
nodes.note: HOCH2CH2OH and HOOC-C6H4-COOH at 260 C with a tin catalyst condense with loss of water. The linear polyester is extruded and solidified. Fibre has good tenacity and chemical resistance. Films are clear and used for flexible packaging.

nodes.name: Polyethylene
nodes.note: Ethylene at 150-300 C and 1000+ atm with peroxide catalyst forms low-density polyethylene (LDPE). A dense structure forms at lower pressure over a Ziegler catalyst. Used for bags, films, insulation. The branching in LDPE makes it flexible; linear HDPE is stiffer.

nodes.name: Polystyrene
nodes.note: Styrene (C6H5-CH=CH2) is polymerised at 60-100 C with a peroxide initiator. The polymer is glassy and hard. Can be molded by injection or extrusion. Foamed polystyrene is used as insulation and packaging.

nodes.name: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
nodes.note: Vinyl chloride (CH2=CHCl) is polymerised in water at 50 C with a peroxide initiator. The vinyl chloride monomer must be dry; water causes side reactions. The polymer forms as a suspension. Used as pipes, insulation, upholstery.

nodes.name: Silicone polymers
nodes.note: Dimethyldichlorosilane hydrolyzes to form siloxane monomers, which condense into a polymer chain. The Si-O backbone is very stable. Varying the alkyl groups and cross-linking gives oils, rubbers, or resins. Excellent thermal stability and water repellency.

nodes.name: Urea-formaldehyde resin
nodes.note: Urea + formaldehyde + acid catalyst condense to form a linear polymer, then cross-link on further heating. Harder than bakelite, bleached (white), used for electrical fittings, tableware, adhesives for plywood.

nodes.name: Viscose from cellulose
nodes.note: Cellulose + NaOH forms sodium cellulose. Adding CS2 forms sodium cellulose xanthate, which dissolves in dilute alkali to form viscose. Extruding through a spinneret into acid regenerates cellulose fibre. The fibre is strong and used for rayon textiles.

nodes.name: Alkylation of aromatic hydrocarbons
nodes.note: Benzene and ethylene react over AlCl3 to form ethylbenzene. Toluene and methanol react to form xylene. The reaction is fast and exothermic. Product selectivity depends on catalyst choice and operating conditions. Important for synthetic detergents and solvents.

nodes.name: Bayer process for alumina
nodes.note: Bauxite contains silica, iron oxide and alumina. In hot NaOH solution, alumina dissolves as sodium aluminate while silica and iron stay behind. Filtering, cooling and seeding precipitates Al(OH)3, which is filtered and calcined. SiO2 contamination ruins the process; careful ore selection matters.

nodes.name: Bergius coal liquefaction
nodes.note: Coal and oil are mixed into a paste with a hydrogen donor, heated to 450 C at 200 atm with a catalyst. The coal is hydrogenated and liquefied. Produces 100 litres of liquid per kg of coal at 70 per cent yield. Very high pressure and temperature make the apparatus expensive.

nodes.name: Birkeland-Eyde process for NOx
nodes.note: The arc heats air to 3000 C, causing N2 and O2 to combine to form NO. Cooling quenches the equilibrium, preserving product. Less efficient than Ostwald; main advantage is no catalyst needed, so no contamination risk. Now obsolete due to Ostwald superiority.

nodes.name: Castner-Kellner process
nodes.note: Unlike the diaphragm cell, the mercury cathode prevents Cl2 and NaOH from mixing. Sodium dissolves in mercury, forming an amalgam, then is reacted with water in a separate vessel to produce NaOH and H2. Yields high-purity product. Capital cost and mercury loss are high.

nodes.name: Catalytic cracking of oil
nodes.note: A solid catalyst cracks oil at lower temperature than thermal cracking, giving better selectivity. The catalyst is regenerated by burning coke off the surface. Main products are gasoline-boiling-range alkenes and aromatics. Economics are better than thermal cracking.

nodes.name: Claus process for sulphur recovery
nodes.note: Two-thirds of H2S is oxidised to SO2, one-third stays as H2S. They react at 250 C to form elemental sulphur: 2 H2S + SO2 -> 3 S + 2 H2O. A catalyst is not strictly needed but makes the reaction faster. Multiple stages recover 95 per cent of sulphur.

nodes.name: Contact process for H2SO4
nodes.note: The reaction SO2 + O2 -> SO3 is an equilibrium; high temperature drives it backwards. Using a catalyst at 400-450 C allows good conversion without decomposition. Direct absorption of SO3 in water is violent; dilute acid is recycled instead. Cheaper than lead chamber for large scale.

nodes.name: Cyanamide process
nodes.note: CaC2 + N2 at 1200 C yields CaCN2. The cyanamide can be hydrolysed to ammonia. This is a way to fix atmospheric nitrogen without needing the Haber process or electricity-intensive methods. Requires cheap calcium carbide.

nodes.name: Deacon process for Cl2
nodes.note: The reaction 4 HCl + O2 -> 2 Cl2 + 2 H2O is thermodynamically downhill but slow. A copper or iron oxide catalyst at 400-450 C makes it practical. Exhaust gases must be cooled and absorbed in alkali to recover unreacted HCl, else losses are severe.

nodes.name: Fischer-Tropsch synthesis
nodes.note: Syngas is produced from coal or oil. The stoichiometry is CO + 2 H2 -> CH2 + H2O. A chain reaction at 200 C and 20 atmospheres over iron or cobalt gives a mixture of alkanes and alkenes, predominantly C8-C20. Water is removed as it forms. Yield is 80-90 per cent carbon.

nodes.name: Frasch process for sulphur
nodes.note: Sulphur has a melting point of 115 C. Superheated water (160 C) injected through a pipe liquefies it. Compressed air lifts the liquid sulphur to the surface. The trick is the triple concentric pipe: steam goes down the outer annulus, air down the inner tube, liquid sulphur up the middle. Capital is very high.

nodes.name: Kraft pulping of wood
nodes.note: White liquor (NaOH and Na2S) at 170 C and 10 atm dissolves lignin selectively, leaving strong cellulose fibres. Black liquor (the dissolved lignin and spent chemicals) is burned for energy. Recovery of chemicals by crystallisation and calcining closes the cycle. Produces very strong paper.

nodes.name: Ostwald process for HNO3
nodes.note: Ammonia and air are passed over heated platinum at 850 C; ammonia oxidises to NO. NO is cooled and oxidised to NO2 by air. NO2 is absorbed in water, producing HNO3. Platinum is essential; base metals poison the reaction. Yield approaches 95 per cent.

nodes.name: Reforming of naphtha
nodes.note: Straight-chain alkanes are dehydrogenated and cyclised, forming aromatics. Branched alkanes are formed. The octane number jumps from 50 to 90+. Hydrogen is produced as a by-product. Platinum requires regeneration to remove coke, and catalyst poisons must be removed from feed.

nodes.name: Sulphite pulping of wood
nodes.note: SO2 and Ca(OH)2 form calcium bisulphite, which at 150 C breaks C-O bonds in lignin. Cellulose is not attacked. Liquor is not recovered, so chemicals must be replenished. Product is weaker than kraft but easier processing. Pulping liquor can be used for vanillin extraction.

nodes.name: Thermal cracking of oil
nodes.note: Visbreaking cracks long chains into shorter ones, lowering viscosity. Full cracking at 800 C gives gasoline and gas-oil. The products are high in alkenes and aromatics. The selectivity is poor; products are complex. Used to increase yield from the crude.

nodes.name: Acetic acid production
nodes.note: Ethanol is oxidised in two steps: to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid. Air oxidation requires a catalyst like copper or cobalt at 200 C. Permanganate is faster but requires stoichiometric reagent. Old vinegar fermentation is slow but cheap. Used for making acetates and esters.

nodes.name: Acetone production
nodes.note: Isopropanol is oxidised by permanganate or dichromate to acetone. Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised to a hydroperoxide, which rearranges to phenol and acetone. Cumene process is cheaper at large scale. Acetone is a polar solvent and ketone intermediate.

nodes.name: Acetylene from calcium carbide
nodes.note: CaC2 + 2 H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2. The reaction is vigorous and exothermic; water control is important. Acetylene is a gas at STP, used for welding, lighting, and as a chemical intermediate. Production is simple and scalable. Only needs calcium carbide and water.

nodes.name: Aniline synthesis from nitrobenzene
nodes.note: PhNO2 is reduced by Fe/acetic acid. The iron is oxidised to Fe2+ and Fe3+, which reduce the nitro group stepwise. The aniline salt is basified and extracted. Pure aniline is a colourless liquid but oxidises in air to a dark polymer. Used as intermediate for dyes and pharmaceuticals.

nodes.name: Benzene from coal tar
nodes.note: Coal tar distillation yields light oils containing benzene, toluene, xylene. Fractional distillation separates benzene at 80 C. Washing with sulphuric acid removes impurities. Recrystallisation from cold alcohol gives pure benzene. Industrial scale needs many litres of coal tar.

nodes.name: Carbon tetrachloride synthesis
nodes.note: Methane and Cl2 at 250 C form a mixture of chlorinated products. Sequential chlorination: CH4 -> CH3Cl -> CH2Cl2 -> CHCl3 -> CCl4. Selectivity to CCl4 is poor; product separation is needed. Used as solvent for fats and dry cleaning.

nodes.name: Chloroform synthesis
nodes.note: Acetone is treated with Cl2 and base. Chlorine and base form hypochlorous acid, which chlorinates the methyl group. Haloform reaction cleaves the molecule to chloroform and carboxylate. Or: ethanol with Cl2 over heat gives chloroform. Used as anaesthetic and solvent.

nodes.name: Citric acid synthesis and fermentation
nodes.note: A mold ferments glucose, acetate or itaconate to citric acid. Chemical synthesis is complex. Fermentation is practical but requires careful sterile technique and nutrient control. Citric acid is precipitated as the calcium salt, dissolved in H2SO4 to displace Ca2+, and recovered.

nodes.name: Diethyl ether synthesis
nodes.note: Two ethanol molecules condense via their -OH groups: C2H5OH + C2H5OH -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + H2O. The reaction is an equilibrium; boiling off the ether product drives it forward. Conc. H2SO4 absorbs water, aiding equilibrium. Old synthesis, very simple.

nodes.name: Formaldehyde synthesis
nodes.note: Methanol vapour and air over a silver catalyst at 600-700 C form formaldehyde. The reaction is exothermic; heat must be removed. Yield is 90 per cent; unreacted methanol is recycled. Formaldehyde is used for making resins, preservatives, and explosives.

nodes.name: Glycerol as soap byproduct and synthetic
nodes.note: Saponification of fats produces glycerol along with soap. Glycerol is removed by salting out or distillation. Purity is improved by fractional distillation. Also made by reduction of dihydroxyacetone. Used for lubricants, explosives (nitroglycerin), and sweetness.

nodes.name: Methanol synthesis
nodes.note: Syngas (CO + 2 H2) over copper-zinc oxide catalyst at 200-250 C and 50-100 atm yields methanol. The reaction is exothermic and reversible; high pressure and lower temperature favour methanol. Unreacted gas is recycled. Used as solvent and fuel.

nodes.name: Phenol production
nodes.note: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which rearranges in acid to phenol and acetone. Chlorobenzene hydrolyzes with NaOH at 300 C and high pressure. Cumene route is economically better. Phenol is acidic and forms salts with base.

nodes.name: Toluene from coal tar
nodes.note: Toluene boils at 111 C, separate from benzene at 80 C. Fractional distillation yields toluene of 95 per cent purity. Washing and recrystallisation improves it further. Used for TNT synthesis, solvents, and chemical intermediates.

nodes.name: Urea synthesis from ammonia
nodes.note: NH3 and CO2 at 150-200 C and 100-200 atm form ammonium carbamate, which dehydrates to urea at higher temperatures. Water is removed as ammonia and CO2 are recycled. Yield approaches 100 per cent. Urea is used as fertiliser and for making resins.

nodes.name: Xylene from coal tar and synthesis
nodes.note: Coal tar contains ortho-, meta-, and para-xylene in roughly equal amounts. Boiling points are close (137-139 C). Separating the isomers requires many distillations or chemical methods. Or: toluene is dimerised over acid to give xylene. The isomers have different properties.

nodes.name: Addition polymerisation
nodes.note: Ethylene under pressure with a peroxide catalyst at 200 C forms polyethylene. Vinyl chloride forms PVC. Styrene forms polystyrene. The reaction can be free-radical, cationic, or anionic. Temperature and pressure control molecular weight. Molecular weight in the range 5000-100000 is typical.

nodes.name: Aldol condensation
nodes.note: Base deprotonates the alpha carbon, forming an enolate carbanion. It attacks the carbonyl carbon of another molecule. The aldol product has OH and can be dehydrated to an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl. Used to make aromatic aldehydes and complex organic molecules.

nodes.name: Bechamp reduction of nitro compounds
nodes.note: ArNO2 is suspended in acetic acid with iron powder. Water is added slowly. The iron is oxidised to Fe2+ and Fe3+, which reduce the nitro group stepwise to ArNH2. Much cheaper than catalytic hydrogenation. The amine salt is basified and extracted. Very robust process.

nodes.name: Catalytic hydrogenation
nodes.note: Hydrogen and the organic compound are passed over nickel or palladium powder or pellets at 100-200 C. Alkenes add hydrogen to form alkanes. Alkynes give alkenes first, then alkanes. Aromatic rings require higher temperatures and pressure. Catalyst selectivity allows controlling which double bond reacts first.

nodes.name: Condensation polymerisation
nodes.note: Ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid form polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid form nylon-66. Each esterification or amidation releases water. High temperature drives equilibrium forward. Molecular weight can exceed 100000.

nodes.name: Diazotisation and coupling
nodes.note: ArNH2 is treated with nitrous acid (HNO2, generated from NaNO2 and dilute HCl) at 0 C to form ArN2+. This diazonium salt is highly reactive. Coupling with phenol or aniline gives azo compounds, highly coloured. The entire history of synthetic dyes rests on this reaction.

nodes.name: Dichromate oxidation
nodes.note: In conc. H2SO4, dichromate oxidises primary alcohols to aldehydes, then to carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols form ketones. The colour changes from orange to green. Addition of water controls the degree of oxidation. Old, standard method in classical organic chemistry.

nodes.name: Esterification reaction
nodes.note: R-COOH + R'-OH <-> R-COO-R' + H2O. Equilibrium is unfavourable; success requires removing water. A condenser refluxes the mixture; water distils off. Conc. H2SO4 acts as both acid catalyst and dehydrating agent. Esters often smell of fruits and are used for flavour.

nodes.name: Friedel-Crafts acylation and alkylation
nodes.note: AlCl3 activates acyl chlorides to form acylium cations, which attack the aromatic ring. This is how acetophenone and propiophenone are made. Alkylation is similar but uses alkyl halides; requires excess AlCl3 and is harder to control. Acylation is cleaner.

nodes.name: Grignard reaction
nodes.note: RMgX is formed by adding alkyl halide to magnesium in dry ether. The Grignard carbanion attacks carbonyls. Formaldehyde gives primary alcohols, aldehydes give secondary, ketones give tertiary. Esters give ketones. Water quench liberates the alcohol. Requires scrupulous dryness.

nodes.name: Halogenation of aromatics
nodes.note: Chlorine and AlCl3 form the active electrophile. Iodine requires activation by an oxidiser like HNO3. Ortho/para selectivity depends on temperature and substituents. Each halogenation can be followed by another at a different position. Used widely for making intermediates.

nodes.name: Nitration reactions
nodes.note: The nitronium cation NO2+ is generated in-situ and attacks the aromatic ring. Each position can be nitrated; mono, di, tri products are possible. Temperature controls selectivity; hot favours ortho/para, cold favours meta. Strongly exothermic; heat removal is critical.

nodes.name: Permanganate oxidation
nodes.note: Cold dilute permanganate oxidises alkenes to diols and alkynes to dicarbonyls. Hot permanganate oxidises alcohols to carbonyls and carbonylsto carboxylic acids. Aromatic side chains are oxidised to carboxylic acids. The solution decolourises as it reacts; endpoint is visible. Very versatile.

nodes.name: Saponification and soap making
nodes.note: Fats are triglycerides. Hot NaOH breaks the ester bonds, forming glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids. The sodium salts precipitate from the aqueous solution as soap. Yield is quantitative. The byproduct glycerol is valuable. An old industry now with exact chemistry.

nodes.name: Sulfonation reactions
nodes.note: Fuming sulphuric acid contains free SO3. At 80-100 C, SO3 attacks the aromatic ring. Multiple sulfonation can occur. Sulfonated aromatics are water-soluble and useful as intermediates for dyes and detergents. The reaction is reversible; dilution with water drives formation.

nodes.name: Vulcanisation of rubber
nodes.note: Raw rubber is soft and sticky. Heating with sulphur causes the sulphur to react with the double bonds in the polymer chains, forming crosslinks. More sulphur creates more crosslinks, making the rubber harder. Over-vulcanisation embrittles it. Temperature control is critical.

nodes.name: Coppiced charcoal at industrial scale
nodes.note: Charcoal supply, not ore, is the real ceiling on pre-coke iron output, and it deforests regions. Coppice rotation of 15-20 years on dedicated land is the answer. Budget the land or your furnace will starve. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Activated carbon production and use
nodes.note: Charcoal is heated with steam at 900 C. Water reacts with carbon, gasifying the interior and creating a porous structure with enormous surface area, up to 3000 m2/g. Activated carbon adsorbs colour, odour and trace contaminants. It is used for water treatment and gas purification. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Alizarin synthesis: oxidation of anthraquinone
nodes.note: Anthraquinone is easily extracted from coal tar. Oxidation with air and catalysts yields alizarin. Before synthesis, alizarin dye came from madder root cultivation in fields, so synthetic alizarin crashed the price by 99%, destroying the madder industry. This is the first wholly synthetic industrial organic dye and set the pattern for the twentieth century.

nodes.name: Leblanc process waste: calcium carbide and the alkali waste problem
nodes.note: One tonne of soda ash from Leblanc produces three tonnes of toxic sulfide waste. Dumping it into rivers creates hydrogen sulfide gas and kills fisheries. Britain's Alkali Act of 1863 was the first environmental regulation in history, requiring soda makers to absorb 95% of the acid mist. This made Leblanc uneconomical where Solvay could operate.

nodes.name: Ammonia recovery and regeneration in soda plants
nodes.note: The Solvay cycle is only better than Leblanc if you actually recover the ammonia. This requires distilling the mother liquor under controlled heat and condensing the vapour in a coil condenser. Without ammonia recycling, Solvay is just another expensive acid-soda process.

nodes.name: Aniline from benzene via nitrobenzene
nodes.note: Oleum nitrates benzene to nitrobenzene in minutes. Reduction with iron powder in dilute acid yields aniline. Aniline is a colourless liquid, bp 184 C, that polymerises in air to a black tar unless kept dry. It is the keystone of synthetic dyes and must be kept under nitrogen or mineral oil. [FIXED after independent audit: nitration of benzene needs nitric acid, which was missing. The Bechamp reduction uses iron in dilute acid, not hydrogen, so the industrial_gases prerequisite was not load-bearing and has been removed.]

nodes.name: Anthracene extraction and oxidation
nodes.note: Anthracene is the highest boiling component of coal tar. It crystallises readily and is extremely pure after recrystallisation. Oxidation of anthracene yields anthraquinone, which is further oxidised to alizarin. Anthracene is also photosensitive and used in photochemistry. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Aspirin synthesis from salicylic acid
nodes.note: Salicylic acid tastes bitter and upsets the stomach. Acetylation to aspirin does not reduce the anti-inflammatory effect but eliminates most gastrointestinal irritation. Aspirin revolutionises medicine; mass manufacture becomes possible after the synthesis chain is optimised.

nodes.name: Azo dyes: diazotisation and azo coupling
nodes.note: Aniline plus nitrous acid yields ArN2+ diazonium salt. This is weakly stable in acid at 0 C and couples to nucleophilic aromatics yielding azo dyes with colours from bright red to deep black. Azo dyes are wash-fast because the ArN=NAr group is chemically stable. Millions of tonnes are made industrially each year.

nodes.name: Bakelite: phenol-formaldehyde plastic
nodes.note: Phenol and formaldehyde condense at 150-180 C in the presence of acid catalyst. The resin is thermoset: once cured, it cannot be remelted. Bakelite is hard, brittle, and heat-resistant. It is used for electrical insulation, radio bodies, and industrial equipment. It was the first fully synthetic plastic and dominated the 1920s. [FIXED after independent audit: the note said phenol and formaldehyde condense, but formaldehyde appeared in neither the prerequisites nor the materials.]

nodes.name: Benzene extraction from coal tar
nodes.note: Benzene boils at 80 C, well separated from toluene at 111 C. A fractionating column with 20-30 trays yields benzene at 99% purity. Benzene vapour is intensely toxic; chronic exposure causes aplastic anaemia. Early workers in benzene manufacturing died of leukaemia within a few years of exposure.

nodes.name: Black powder: gunpowder production
nodes.note: Rome already has gunpowder. This node exists to prevent anachronism: Rome does NOT have potassium nitrate or saltpetre. The nitrum of Roman texts is sodium carbonate natron, entirely different.

nodes.name: Blasting cap and fulminate detonator
nodes.note: A blasting cap is useless without an initiator: a tiny shock-sensitive charge inside. Mercury fulminate explodes from spark, friction or impact. The detonator shock wave initiates the main explosive charge. Without the detonator, TNT and dynamite are inert. The detonator is what makes high explosives strategically useful.

nodes.name: Bleaching powder: mixed calcium hypochlorite
nodes.note: Chlorine dissolves directly into lime slurry. The product is a mixture of Ca(OCl)2, CaCl2, and excess lime that is chemically stable and safe to handle dry. It became the standard bleach for cloth and later drinking water because chlorine gas is too corrosive and dangerous to transport.

nodes.name: Casein plastics from milk protein
nodes.note: Milk is acidified to precipitate casein protein. The wet casein is dried and mixed with formaldehyde, then heated and moulded. The product is hard, waterproof, and can be dyed. Casein plastic was used for buttons, fountain pens, and jewellery until phenolic plastics displaced it.

nodes.name: Catalysis and catalyst theory
nodes.note: The kernel: some substances accelerate reaction without participating in it. This explains why platinum speeds many reactions and why heated iron catalyses ammonia decomposition. You cannot build a contact process or ammonia synthesis without understanding this.

nodes.name: Caustic soda: concentration and purification
nodes.note: Caustic soda boils above 100 C, so direct heating to dryness would decompose it. Vacuum evaporation keeps temperature below 100 C while removing water. The product is chemically pure but must be handled in glass or lead; iron is attacked immediately and dissolved. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Celluloid: nitrocellulose plastics
nodes.note: Nitrocellulose becomes plastic when mixed with camphor. Sheet is then made by rolling between heated cylinders. Celluloid revolutionises photography by replacing glass plates, enables flexible film stock, and is used for combs, buttons, piano keys. The material is flammable and degrades over time to become increasingly brittle. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Industrial centrifuge for separation
nodes.note: A scroll inside a spinning cylinder conveys sediment toward the outlet while supernatant overflows a weir. Centrifugal force is 1000 times gravity, so settling that would take hours happens in minutes. Bearing wear from the immense centrifugal force is the main maintenance burden.

nodes.name: Chlor-alkali process: asbestos diaphragm cell
nodes.note: Asbestos diaphragm avoids mercury entirely. Chlorine is produced at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode. The diaphragm prevents mixing while allowing ions to pass. Caustic product is dilute (5-10%) so requires concentration by evaporation. Eventually diaphragm cells replace mercury because the health cost of mercury is unsustainable, but asbestos dust also kills workers decades later.

nodes.name: Chlor-alkali process: mercury cathode cell
nodes.note: Mercury wets the cathode, preventing hydrogen evolution and protecting sodium metal that would otherwise form. Sodium amalgamates into the mercury, is drawn off and reacted with water to yield NaOH. This yields caustic soda of exceptional purity, but mercury is volatile and extremely toxic. Worker exposure to mercury vapour causes tremor, gingivitis and permanent neurological damage. The process dominates industry for fifty years but is eventually abandoned because of environmental and health costs.

nodes.name: Chromatography: column and paper methods
nodes.note: A solution of mixed compounds is percolated through a column of silica gel or charcoal. Compounds with different affinities for the stationary phase elute separately. Paper chromatography using capillary action works in smaller scales and requires only filter paper and solvent.

nodes.name: Coal tar fractionation and distillation
nodes.note: Coal tar boiling below 300 C contains benzene, toluene, phenol. Above 300 C come naphthalene and anthracene. Fractional distillation with bubble-cap trays gives cuts of surprising purity if reflux is high. The vapour pressure differences are only a factor of two, so reflux ratio must exceed 10:1 to separate them properly.

nodes.name: Contact process for sulfuric acid using platinum catalyst
nodes.note: Platinum refuses to poison and remains active indefinitely. The trick: SO2 feed purity above 99.5% or the catalyst silts up. Temperature control to 400-450 C is critical - too hot and equilibrium shifts wrong, too cool and kinetics stall. This yields acid with 98% sulfur recovery, halving the cost versus lead chamber.

nodes.name: Vanadium pentoxide catalyst for contact sulfuric acid
nodes.note: Vanadium catalyst poisons slowly from trace impurities in SO2 feed, requiring periodic regeneration, but costs one-twentieth of platinum. The silica support geometry matters: small pellets expose more surface but choke flow; large pellets flow freely but starve for area. Industrial practice settles on 3-5mm rings.

nodes.name: Continuous versus batch processing decision
nodes.note: Continuous reactors have lower capital cost per tonne when scale is large and products are stable. Batch processes suit pharmaceutical work where recipes change frequently and product shelf-life is measured in months. Continuous operation demands process control; any upset propagates downstream. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Glass-lined steel vessels
nodes.note: Glass fuses to steel at 1400 C. The thermal expansion mismatch between glass and steel causes peeling if temperature gradients are steep. Industrial practice uses special borosilicate glasses and slow heating and cooling. Glass-lined vessels combine steel strength with glass's chemical resistance.

nodes.name: Corrosion-resistant plant: lead and lead-lined vessels
nodes.note: Sulfuric acid dissolves iron instantly but is nearly inert to lead. The acid tank is lined with lead sheet, joined by soft-solder, and sealed with a lead gasket. Lead is soft, so it is cast thick to resist rupture from external mechanical stress. This was the standard until stainless steel displaced it in the 1950s.

nodes.name: Stainless steel vessels for corrosive service
nodes.note: Chromium above 13% in steel passivates the surface, preventing corrosion. Nickel is added for chloride resistance. 304 stainless is austenitic and weldable. Costs three times as much as carbon steel but outlasts it by an order of magnitude in corrosive service. Stainless steel eventually became the material of choice for all chemical plant.

nodes.name: Corrosion-resistant vessels: acid-resistant stoneware
nodes.note: High-fired stoneware has sufficient mechanical strength for small vessels and is inert to all acids. The glaze must be ash-based or lead-based and fully matured. Stoneware is cheaper than lead but brittle, so it is used for containers and small reaction vessels up to ten litres. Industrial-scale acid storage still required lead-lined iron.

nodes.name: Crystallisation and crystal separation
nodes.note: Cooling a saturated solution nucleates crystals that grow if undisturbed. Temperature control to within 1 C is essential. Impurities prefer to stay dissolved, so crystals are purer than the starting solution. This is the principal method of refining all salts. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Cyanamide process: nitrogen fixation by carbide
nodes.note: Calcium carbide is made by arc furnace: limestone and coke to 3000 C in one step. The carbide then reacts with nitrogen gas at 1000 C to yield calcium cyanamide, which hydrolyses to ammonia. This route predates Haber-Bosch and requires less pressure, but yields fewer tonnes per unit energy. Arc furnace demands kilowatts of electric power. [FIXED after independent audit: the cyanamide route runs through calcium carbide, which needs the electric arc furnace.]

nodes.name: Deacon process: oxidation of hydrogen chloride to chlorine
nodes.note: Converts otherwise-waste HCl from nitrification into chlorine gas. The copper chloride catalyst cycles between Cu(II) oxide and Cu(I) chloride. Temperature above 1600 C is critical; below that, conversion drops sharply. Heat recovery from the exothermic reaction is essential to the economics.

nodes.name: Synthetic detergent from petroleum sulfonic acid
nodes.note: Synthetic detergents are made by sulfonation of alkenes from cracking petroleum fractions. The sulfonic acid is neutralised with soda ash. Detergent molecules have a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail that dissolves in grease and a polar sulfonate head that dissolves in water. Synthetic detergents work better in cold water than soap and do not leave scum. nodes.name: Indigo synthesis from N-phenylglycine

When synthetic indigo was commercialised in 1897, indigo-dyeing agriculture in India and West Indies collapsed. Millions of farmers lost their livelihood. nodes.name: Nitroglycerin synthesis and stabilisation
nodes.note: Nitroglycerin is prepared by adding glycerol dropwise to a mixture of nitric and sulfuric acid at 10 C or below. nodes.name: Nylon 6,6 synthesis and polymerisation
nodes.note: Adipic acid is made by oxidising cyclohexane with HNO3. Hexamethylenediamine comes from adiponitrile and ammonia. These are condensed at 250 C under controlled pressure, forming long polyamide chains. Nylon has a melting point of 265 C and can be drawn to strong fibres. Nylon is the first fully synthetic fibre and is used for everything from stockings to parachutes.

nodes.name: Oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) production
nodes.note: Oleum contains free SO3 dissolved in H2SO4. It is phenomenally corrosive and must be stored in glass-lined steel or lead, never iron. Used for nitration of aromatics where ordinary sulfuric acid is too dilute. The hazard is water contact - violently exothermic absorption of moisture releases heat that can vaporize the whole batch.

nodes.name: Ostwald process: oxidation of ammonia to nitric acid
nodes.note: Platinum gauze at 800-900 C oxidises ammonia to nitrogen oxides in seconds. The nitrogen oxides are then absorbed in water to yield nitric acid. This is cheaper than the saltpetre-based or lead chamber methods and yields pure dilute acid. Platinum is essential; iron corrodes instantly under these conditions.

nodes.name: Phenol extraction from coal tar and synthesis
nodes.note: Coal tar contains phenol in the middle boiling fraction. Early sources used distillation. Later, benzene is sulfonated and the sulfonate is fused with molten alkali at 300 C to yield phenol. Phenol is corrosive to skin, denatures proteins and was the first antiseptic used by Lister.

nodes.name: White phosphorus extraction from bone ash
nodes.note: Bone ash is calcined phosphate. Heating with carbon in a closed retort at 1300 C reduces it to phosphorus vapour. The vapour is condensed under water to white phosphorus. This method dates to 1669 and predates the identification of phosphorus as an element by 100 years.

nodes.name: Silver halide photographic chemistry
nodes.note: Silver halide crystals are formed by mixing silver nitrate and sodium halide. Gelatin is added as a binder. Development is performed with reducing agents like hydroquinone or metol in alkaline conditions. Each step requires strict control of temperature, pH and oxidising impurities. Photographic film is the foundation of cinema and still photography. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_measure_temp added by a reviewer working node by node. nodes.name: Picric acid: trinitrophenol synthesis
nodes.note: Phenol is nitrated to yield a yellow acid that is surprisingly stable. Picric acid is used as a dye and in photoflash powder. Its use as a military explosive faded when TNT became available because TNT is more powerful and much less hygroscopic.

nodes.name: Polyethylene synthesis under high pressure
nodes.note: Ethylene is exposed to 1000 atmospheres and 150 C in the presence of an organic peroxide free-radical initiator. Polymer chains grow and link randomly. The product is low-density branched polyethylene. A later low-pressure process using a Ziegler catalyst yields linear high-density polyethylene, which is stronger and more useful.

nodes.name: Potash mining and refining
nodes.note: Potash salts like sylvinite are mined like any mineral ore. The mined rock is then dissolved in water, filtered to remove insoluble matter, and crystallised. Potassium is essential to agriculture: wheat and potatoes are heavy exporters of K2O, depleting soils rapidly without replenishment. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Bourdon tube pressure gauge and safety relief valve
nodes.note: The Bourdon tube uncurls proportionally to pressure, moving a needle on a dial. The relief valve must crack at exactly the safe pressure or the autoclave becomes a bomb. Precision here saves lives.

nodes.name: High-pressure autoclave and steam digester
nodes.note: High pressure demands absolute rigidity and control. The drum must withstand internal stress while keeping temperature uniform. Failures are catastrophic. The riveted seams are the critical weak point; you need sub-millimetre alignment and reliable riveting technique.

nodes.name: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) synthesis
nodes.note: Vinyl chloride is made by acetylene plus HCl or ethylene dichloride cracking. Polymerisation in aqueous emulsion yields PVC plastic. Plasticisers are added to make flexible sheet; unplasticised PVC is rigid and chemical-resistant. PVC is the most widely used plastic on Earth. Thermal decomposition releases hydrogen chloride, making fires extremely dangerous.

nodes.name: Ammonia as refrigerant in compression cycles
nodes.note: Ammonia has a high latent heat and boils at -33 C. Liquid ammonia evaporates in the cold box and is compressed back to liquid, rejecting heat in the condenser. Ammonia is toxic and requires sealed copper tubing, but it is non-reactive with copper and iron. Industrial food freezing and ice manufacturing rely on ammonia refrigeration.

nodes.name: Saccharin synthesis
nodes.note: Toluene is sulfonated with oleum, giving toluenesulfonic acid. Oxidation with permanganate to toluic acid, then reaction with ammonia and loss of water yields saccharin. Saccharin is 500 times sweeter than sugar by mass and costs one-tenth as much at scale. Food preservation becomes possible without cane sugar.

nodes.name: Salicylic acid: hydroxylation of benzenesulfonic acid
nodes.note: Benzene is sulfonated to benzenesulfonic acid. Molten alkali at 300 C causes Ar-SO3H to be replaced by Ar-OH, yielding phenol. Phenol is then converted to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid is acetylated to yield aspirin, the world's most widely used pharmaceutical.

nodes.name: Smokeless powder: nitrocellulose ballistic propellant
nodes.note: Nitrocellulose particles are stabilised with diphenylamine or similar hindered amine to suppress autocatalytic decomposition. Grain size and shape control burn rate. Smokeless powder has three times the energy density of black powder, enabling lighter rifles, higher velocities, and longer effective ranges.

nodes.name: Superphosphate: acidulation of rock phosphate

nodes.name: Toluene extraction from coal tar

nodes.name: Chlorination of drinking water for disinfection
nodes.note: Chlorine kills bacteria within seconds at concentrations above 0.2 ppm. Residual chlorine must be maintained to prevent recontamination in pipes. Chlorination remains the standard method for microbiological control of water supplies.

nodes.name: Water treatment by coagulation and settling
nodes.note: Fine clay and organic particles remain suspended in water as colloids. Alum or ferric sulfate ions hydrolyse to form hydroxide gelatine that neutralises colloid charges. Particles flocculate and settle quickly. This is the first step in modern water purification.

nodes.name: Sand filtration and multimedia filter beds
nodes.note: After coagulation, water passes through a filter bed of coarse gravel, sand, and sometimes anthracite coal. The bed removes particles down to 10 microns. The filter must be backwashed periodically when pressure drop becomes excessive.

nodes.name: Weldon process: regeneration of manganese dioxide from manganous chloride
nodes.note: In bleach production, MnO2 is reduced to MnCl2. Weldon's trick: oxidise the manganese back with hypochlorite, then filter and recycle the MnO2. This more than halves manganese consumption. Lime is needed to adjust pH so precipitation is quantitative.

nodes.name: Roman citizenship by grant
nodes.note: Gives provocatio, the right of appeal, which is the difference between a governor executing you and Rome hearing you. Buy it with a public benefaction.

nodes.name: Amphitheatre with tiered seating
nodes.note: Concentric ovals of arched vaults and seating on filled earth. The Colosseum seated 50,000. Ruins of amphitheatres across the empire show that Romans mastered the geometry and structure of large public spaces long before the modern stadium.

nodes.name: Roman aqueduct with inverted siphons
nodes.note: Gravity-fed water under precise gradient over vast distances. At valleys, inverted siphons (pipes under pressure) carried water below ground, then up the other side. Rome's engineering was not obvious; this was clever and stable.

nodes.name: Roman masonry arch
nodes.note: The wedge-shaped stone voussoir locked under compression. Rome perfected this; the arch remains the fundamental load-bearing form through the Middle Ages and beyond. Spans cannot be thrown long without collapse or immense depth, but the principle is unbreakable.

nodes.name: Bending moment and shear diagrams
nodes.note: A beam under load is bent. Shear forces and bending moments vary along its length; calculus (the derivative of shear is load, the derivative of moment is shear) gives the full distribution. Maximum moment indicates the critical section; this is what a designer must check.

nodes.name: Box girder beam
nodes.note: A hollow rectangular tube of steel or concrete. Material is placed far from the neutral axis (the walls), giving maximum rigidity with minimum weight. Bridges and long-span buildings use box girders. Torsional stiffness is also high; useful when spans are asymmetric.

nodes.name: Roman fired brick and tile
nodes.note: Fired clay in standard sizes, facings for concrete, tiles for roofs. Uniform sizing was a Roman innovation; mass production of standard parts. The tiles lock together with ribs and survive centuries of weather.

nodes.name: Cantilever bridge
nodes.note: Pairs of cantilevers extend from towers toward each other, meeting or nearly meeting. Forth Bridge (1890) is a cantilever; it has massive rigidity. Requires deep towers and strong base connections. Spans to 400m. Rivals suspension in elegance.

nodes.name: Cast iron bridge
nodes.note: Cast iron is brittle and strong in compression, weak in tension. Arched cast iron bridges (like the 1779 Ironbridge in Shropshire) mimic the arch form to keep the material in compression. Cast iron does not corrode like wrought iron but is prone to sudden brittle fracture.

nodes.name: Steel arch bridge
nodes.note: An arch of steel riveted or welded. Steel can be made into arched members with joints. Span to 500m. Requires calculation of arch stresses and support reactions. Sydney Harbour Bridge (1932) is a steel arch; it carries road, rail, and pedestrians.

nodes.name: Suspension bridge with wire cables
nodes.note: Cables slung over towers and anchored at the ends, with vertical hangers supporting the deck. The cable takes the shape of a catenary under load (not a parabola). Long spans (1000m+) require understanding catenary geometry and high tensile wire. The first major suspension bridge was Brooklyn (1883).

nodes.name: Timber trussed bridge
nodes.note: Timber trusses on stone piers. Spans to 80 metres were built. Timber is strong in tension and compression but rots; maintenance is perpetual. Covered bridges survive longer (dryness is the enemy of rot).

nodes.name: Wrought iron truss bridge
nodes.note: Wrought iron does not have the span of cast iron arches, but can carry tension. Wrought iron truss bridges (using the method of joints to proportion members) enable spans to 150 metres with light weight. Riveted wrought iron held up until the 1960s.

nodes.name: Building code and regulatory standards

nodes.name: Cofferdam and underwater concrete
nodes.note: Wooden piling in rings, the interior pumped or bailed dry, filled with pozzolanic concrete that sets underwater. Roman harbour piers used this. The concrete set faster in water than in air; not accident but observed principle.

nodes.name: Treadwheel crane
nodes.note: Large wooden drum turned by men inside a hamster wheel. Could lift tens of tonnes. Documented in Vitruvius; used to build the aqueducts and temples. Survives in medieval and Renaissance construction accounts.

nodes.name: Curtain wall (non-load-bearing facade)

nodes.name: Arch dam in concrete

nodes.name: Roman concrete dome
nodes.note: The Pantheon dome (126 AD) measures 43.3 metres and is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built. Pozzolanic concrete actually strengthens in seawater. Modern Portland cement does not; Pantheon beats it on durability.

nodes.name: Dredging for channel maintenance
nodes.note: Sediment fills harbours and channels; dredges scoop it up. Early dredges were buckets on a chain driven by water power. Suction dredges (pump-driven) are later but far more powerful. Maintenance dredging is expensive and continuous. The removed material can be sold or used for land reclamation.

nodes.name: Theory of elasticity
nodes.note: Stress-strain relationship for materials. Young's modulus relates stress to strain; Poisson's ratio the transverse to axial strain. Allows prediction of deformation, not just failure. Requires testing to find material constants; without it, design is guesswork.

nodes.name: Elevator with safety brake (Otis)
nodes.note: A steam-powered cab on a rope. If the rope breaks, mechanical wedges jam against the guide rails and lock the cab. Otis (1853) demonstrated this at a fair by cutting the rope; the cab held. Without the brake, nobody will ride it. The brake is the actual invention; vertical transport scales only after people trust their lives.

nodes.name: Euler buckling of slender columns
nodes.note: A slender column under axial load will suddenly buckle sideways at a critical load, not from material failure but from geometric instability. Euler's formula shows the critical load depends on length squared and moment of inertia; long thin columns buckle easily. Calculation replaces guessing.

nodes.name: Factor of safety concept
nodes.note: Design load times a safety factor (typically 2 to 5) must not exceed the material strength. A codification of caution. Different factors for different risks; this is risk management, not ignorance. Without it, every overload is a surprise failure.

nodes.name: Fireproofing and fire-resistant structure
nodes.note: Steel loses strength at high temperature (500 C is critical). Concrete or ceramic encasement keeps the steel cool. Compartmentation (fire walls, fire doors) stops spread. The triangle: materials (incombustible), structure (load paths survive local fire), and exits (life safety). All three matter.

nodes.name: Foundation piles and pile driving
nodes.note: Drive long timber posts into soft ground to reach firm strata. The pile takes vertical load and transfers it down. Rome used piles under the Theatre of Pompey; medieval builders drove thousands for cathedrals. Bearing capacity is guessed; soil testing came much later.

nodes.name: Spread footing on compacted soil
nodes.note: A wide stone or brick base distributes the wall load over a larger footprint. Soft clay will compress under load; settlement cracks the building. Soil testing (boring and observation) tells you what depth to go. Without it, you guess and hope.

nodes.name: Sluice gate for water control
nodes.note: A wooden or iron gate that slides vertically in a groove, controlling the flow of water. Water pressure increases with depth (the force is immense at the base). The gate must be strong; friction resistance must be manageable. Used for mills, docks, and irrigation.

nodes.name: Plate glass for windows and storefronts
nodes.note: Large flat panes of clear glass. Cast plate glass (poured onto a flat table, then ground and polished) allows sizes to 3-4 metres. Transforms storefronts and windows. Sheet glass (drawn from a bath) is cheaper but smaller. Large panes are fragile but stunning. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.] [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: grinding and polishing flat glass requires 0.1mm surface accuracy]

nodes.name: Glass panes for windows
nodes.note: By 100 AD Roman glassblowers produced clear soda-lime panes, often small. A luxury in Rome, it was still cheaper than oiled linen or mica. Roman houses with glass windows survive; the material itself is durable.

nodes.name: Harbour and dock with breakwaters
nodes.note: A protected basin with stone or wooden walls. Breakwaters outside reduce waves. Quays allow cargo loading and unloading. Docks with gates can maintain constant water level despite tides. Venice was the model; modern container ports are different in scale only. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Insula: Roman apartment block
nodes.note: Multi-storey blocks of small rented rooms around a courtyard, using brick and timber joists. Rome housed its poor in dense urban clusters; the form remains standard. Fire risk was immense (hence frequent collapse in literature).

nodes.name: Wrought iron working and riveting
nodes.note: Wrought iron from bloomery furnace is ductile, tough, and resistant to corrosion. Smith heating and hand-forging creates toughness. Rivets are driven hot; the cooled rivet locks parts together. Roman and medieval smiths knew this; it is not high art, but skilled work. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_heat_0700 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: riveting and forging require heating wrought iron to cherry red approximately 750 C]

nodes.name: Lightning conductor and grounding
nodes.note: A copper or iron rod running from the roof to ground rod(s) in moist earth. Captures lightning and shunts it safely into the ground. Franklin (1752) invented this; it saved many buildings. Reduces fire and injury. Requires good earth contact; a dry ground rod does nothing. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Marble veneer and ashlar facing
nodes.note: Thin slabs of marble or stone cut to dimension and affixed to concrete, creating facade and surface. Aesthetic, durable, and separates structure (concrete) from facing, a principle unchanged to this day.

nodes.name: Materials testing and calibration
nodes.note: Pull samples to failure and measure the load. Cast a batch and test it; the material constants you need (tensile strength, Young's modulus, elongation to failure) come from experiment. No two batches are identical; testing catches the weakest.

nodes.name: Method of joints for truss analysis
nodes.note: At each joint of a truss, forces are in equilibrium. By solving joint by joint (starting from known loads), the tension or compression in each member can be calculated. This displaced rule-of-thumb proportioning; calculation is faster and correct.

nodes.name: Neutral axis in bending
nodes.note: When a beam bends, the top fibres go into compression, the bottom into tension, and there is a neutral surface in the middle with no stress. The stress magnitude increases linearly with distance from the neutral axis. This is why deep beams (I-beams) are efficient: material far from the axis is stronger.

nodes.name: Precise levelling and level network
nodes.note: A telescope on a spirit level, with a graduated rod. From one point, sights the rod at a distant point and reads the height difference. Chain many such sightings and you have a network of height reference points. Modern mapping uses electronic total stations; the principle is 200 years old.

nodes.name: Prestressed concrete
nodes.note: Steel cables under high tension are embedded in concrete, then the tension is released. The concrete is compressed throughout. This pre-compression means the concrete can resist higher loads before cracking. Beams can span further. Freyssinet (1928) pioneered this.

nodes.name: Pumping station and mechanical lift
nodes.note: A water-powered pump (or steam-powered later) lifts water uphill against gravity. The Archimedean screw predates Rome; centrifugal pumps came later. Lifting water to a tower gives pressure for distribution. Without lift, you must be lower than the source.

nodes.name: Reinforced concrete construction
nodes.note: Steel bars embedded in concrete take tension; concrete takes compression. Their thermal expansion coefficients happen to match (both expand at roughly 10-12 ppm/K). Steel does not rust in the alkaline environment of concrete. This works; Coignet patented it (1891). Allows thin slabs and long spans.

nodes.name: Roman paved road with surveying
nodes.note: Multilayered stone and gravel bed, crowned for drainage, aligned by groma (X-staff with plumb bobs). Roman roads lasted centuries. The technique is durable and maintainable; paving without surveying is wasteful.

nodes.name: King post roof truss
nodes.note: Two sloped rafters meeting at a peak, with a vertical king post from peak to tie-beam, and a horizontal tie keeping the rafters from thrusting outward. The tie is in tension, the post in compression. Simple and elegant; medieval roofs used this.

nodes.name: Queen post roof truss
nodes.note: Two vertical posts between tie and rafters, with a horizontal strut between them. Allows longer spans than king post without intermediate supports. The posts are in compression, the tie in tension, the struts shared the vertical load.

nodes.name: Sewage treatment works and activated sludge
nodes.note: Sewage (biological waste) requires aerobic decomposition. Activated sludge is bacteria and protozoa that eat organic matter when aerated. Germ theory explains why pathogens die in treatment; without it, the mechanism is invisible. Treated effluent is safe to discharge. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Roman sewer with gravity flow
nodes.note: The Cloaca Maxima in Rome still functions after 2400 years. Gravity-fed, arched, with gradient for scouring. Medieval towns often rebuilt sewers on Roman alignment; the Romans had solved the problem.

nodes.name: Separate foul and storm sewers
nodes.note: Two pipes: foul (sewage) and storm (rain). Storm sewers are large but infrequent flow; foul sewers are constant. Combined sewers overflow during heavy rain, contaminating rivers. Separation is expensive but hygienic; Victorian engineers standardised it. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Soil mechanics and bearing capacity
nodes.note: Terzaghi (1920s) developed the theory of effective stress and bearing capacity formulas. Before this, foundation depth was guess-work. Soil is not a simple material; water content, grain size, cementation all matter. Boring and sampling are the tools.

nodes.name: Spillway and flood management
nodes.note: A controlled overflow weir at a set height. If the dam fills above that level, water goes over the spillway, not over the dam. The spillway must carry high velocity water without erosion. Most dam failures are hydraulic: overtopping erodes the downstream slope.

nodes.name: Statics and equilibrium of forces
nodes.note: Force balance: sum of forces and moments at each point must be zero. Archimedes knew this; the formalism of vectors and moment arms is Renaissance work (Leonardo). Essential to size any structural member without collapse.

nodes.name: Steel frame building
nodes.note: A skeleton of steel beams and columns carries all loads; the exterior walls are non-load-bearing curtain walls. This is the essence of the skyscraper. Bulk steel (converter) and riveted or bolted connections. London's Great Exhibition building (1851) was a proto-steel frame; Chicago's Home Insurance building (1885) was the first true one.

nodes.name: Street lighting with electricity
nodes.note: Gas lamps (post-1800) were bright but hot. Arc lamps (post-1850) were bright and stable. Incandescent bulbs (post-1880) were safer. Electric grid power (post-1900) made street lighting universal. Crime dropped; nightlife boomed. The cost was perpetual maintenance of wiring and poles. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Paved street and sidewalk
nodes.note: Concrete or stone surface, crowned for drainage. Sidewalks segregate pedestrians from vehicles. Paving is expensive but lasts decades. Brick or stone is traditional; concrete (post-1900) is cheaper. Proper drainage prevents flooding and freezing damage.

nodes.name: Groma: Roman X-staff surveying tool
nodes.note: Four plumb bobs hanging from the four arms of a cross allow rapid sighting of right angles and straight lines. Crude and ingenious. Used to lay out Roman towns and roads across the empire.

nodes.name: Theodolite for surveying angles
nodes.note: A telescope on a graduated circle; turns to measure angles to two objects. From a point, you can sight two distant landmarks and calculate their angle. Repeated sightings from multiple points give positions by triangulation. Accuracy to seconds of arc changes the scale of surveying from sight to hundreds of kilometres.

nodes.name: Town planning and street layout
nodes.note: Systematic design of streets, squares, and districts rather than organic growth. Rome's colonial towns used a grid (the orthogonal plan). Haussmann (Paris, 1850s) imposed radial avenues and parks. Planning is contentious (disrupts existing patterns), but saves lives (fire lanes, flood avoidance, sanitation) and improves efficiency. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted.
