nodes.name: Triangulated truss frame
nodes.note: A truss is fundamentally different from an arch: it carries load by rigid tension and compression in its members, not by geometric compression of wedges. A triangle cannot be deformed without changing member length. This is not intuitive; it requires understanding materials can pull apart.

nodes.name: Rock drilling and tunnelling
nodes.note: Percussion drills (hitting, not rotation) cut rock slowly. Blasting with dynamite (nitroglycerin) broke larger rock faster (1867 onwards). Timbering the walls prevents collapse. Tunnels need gradient and drainage; straight-line surveying through a mountain is hard.

nodes.name: Tunnelling shield and incremental advance
nodes.note: A large cylindrical shield advances meter by meter through soft ground (clay, silt). Men dig at the face inside; segments are assembled behind; the shield is jacked forward. London Underground used this (1863 onwards). Prevents cave-ins but is slow and heavy.

nodes.name: Barrel vault
nodes.note: An arch extruded in the third dimension: a continuous stone tunnel. Massive, permanent, and the ceiling form for the Basilica of Maxentius. Rome pushed vaults to extremes; Renaissance architects still marvelled at them.

nodes.name: Water tower and pressure system
nodes.note: Water stored in an elevated tank. Pressure at the base is proportional to height (0.1 kg/cm2 per metre). Sufficient pressure to feed a city from a single tower. Replaces the Roman need for gentle gradients in aqueducts; now you can serve hilly ground.

nodes.name: Water treatment works and coagulation
nodes.note: Alum added to water causes clay particles to coagulate and settle. Sand filters then remove fine particles and some bacteria. Boiling kills most pathogens. Chlorine (post-1900) kills the rest. Water treatment makes urban life possible; sewage in the water kills you fast.

nodes.name: Drawn wire and wire rope
nodes.note: Fine wire drawn through successive dies, twisted into strands, twisted again into rope. Wire rope has the tensile strength of steel and flexibility of rope. Essential for suspension bridges. High quality drawplates are needed; brittle dies fail.

nodes.name: Pendulum clock and later the balance spring
nodes.note: The Antikythera mechanism proves Roman-era gear-cutting is already good enough; what is missing is the escapement and the pendulum's isochronism. Accurate time gives navigation, longitude, physics, and later electrical measurement. Also a superb luxury product. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: escapement and clock wheels require 0.1mm tolerance work]

nodes.name: Masonry aqueduct arch bridge
nodes.kb: Series of tall arches carrying water channel across valley
nodes.note: Water pressure is constant, not dynamic. Channel must be nearly level to maintain flow. Multiple arches share the load; failure of one makes the bridge catastrophically unstable.

nodes.name: Steel arch bridge
nodes.kb: Two-hinged or fixed arch of steel, carrying load in compression to abutments
nodes.note: Arch must be hinged or buckling becomes a problem. Fixed arch is indeterminate; temperature change and settlement cause internal stress, not reactions.

nodes.name: Arch dam curved structure
nodes.kb: Curved arch carries water load horizontally to valley walls
nodes.note: Arch curve reduces mass needed compared to gravity dam. Abutments must be strong and rock; bad foundations cause catastrophic failure.

nodes.name: Artificial cast stone
nodes.kb: Lime mortar cast in wooden moulds to create facing stones
nodes.note: Eliminates quarrying and stone shaping work. Moulds are reusable but casting and curing is slower than laying natural stone. Works only where artificial facing can pass as masonry.

nodes.name: Asphalt roll roofing and shingles
nodes.kb: Bitumen-impregnated felt, laid in overlapping layers with hot tar
nodes.note: Installation temperature is critical. Too cold, bitumen cracks; too hot, it flows away. Laps must overlap correctly to shed water downslope, not trap it.

nodes.name: Bascule drawbridge
nodes.kb: Counterweighted leaf pivoting up on hinge to allow ship passage
nodes.note: Counterweight must balance leaf exactly. Load moves as bridge opens, changing balance. Seals and guides must not jam under any circumstance.

nodes.name: Block and tackle with rope
nodes.kb: Fixed and movable pulleys multiply force by rope arrangement
nodes.note: Mechanical advantage equals number of rope parts under load. Rope must not slip on sheaves. Friction in blocks reduces actual advantage by 10-20 percent.

nodes.name: Bolted connection with nut
nodes.kb: Threaded bolt through plates, tightened with wrench and nut
nodes.note: Bolt threads must be accurate and consistent. Tightness is limited by thread strength and tool torque. Joints can loosen under vibration unless locked.

nodes.name: Box girder or tubular section
nodes.kb: Closed hollow section with four sides, resisting torsion effectively
nodes.note: Box resists torsion in proportion to enclosed area. Open section (I beam) has no torsional stiffness. Welding the box closed is expensive but essential.

nodes.name: Cable anchorage block
nodes.kb: Massive concrete or steel block anchoring cable at tension, preventing pull-out
nodes.note: Cable is wedged and stressed into the block. Cone of stress must stay within mass. If block is too small, wedge pulls free, catapulting cable.

nodes.name: Caisson cofferdam box
nodes.kb: Watertight box sunk to bedrock, filled with air, allowing work underwater
nodes.note: Box is heavy, sinks under its own weight. Must be sealed at corners and joints. Explosive decompression if air is lost. Caisson disease kills workers who decompress too fast.

nodes.name: Cantilever beam or slab
nodes.kb: Beam fixed at one end, projecting unsupported
nodes.note: Fixed end experiences very high moment. Deflection is cubic in length, so small overhang looks fine but is actually close to failure.

nodes.name: Cast iron beam
nodes.kb: I-shaped or hollow-section beam cast in one piece
nodes.note: Cast iron is much weaker in tension than compression. Bottom fibre is under tension in bending. Beams crack unpredictably. Wrought iron or steel is superior but slower to install.

nodes.name: Cavity wall with air space
nodes.kb: Two separate leaves of masonry with air gap, stopping moisture penetration
nodes.note: Outer leaf weathers, inner leaf stays dry. Ties hold leaves together but create thermal bridges. Cavity must be kept clean or moisture settles.

nodes.name: Cement clinker mill grinding
nodes.kb: Ball mill or roller mill grinds clinker to fine powder for cement
nodes.note: Grinding heats cement. If overheated, early hydration begins in the mill, weakening final product. Cooling is essential. Ball mill creates abrasive dust that wears liners.

nodes.name: Central heating hot water system
nodes.kb: Boiler heats water circulated through pipes to radiators
nodes.note: Boiler must be kept filled and bleed of air. Expansion tank absorbs water expanding as it heats. Radiators must drain when not in use or freeze.

nodes.name: Cofferdam temporary barrier
nodes.kb: Temporary enclosure of sheet pile or timber, pumped dry for work
nodes.note: Simple dike around the work area, then pump it empty. Leakage increases as water pressure builds. Backup pump must run continuously.

nodes.name: Rotary concrete mixer drum
nodes.kb: Rotating drum tumbles concrete ingredients to uniform mix
nodes.note: Drum must rotate at optimum speed. Too slow, materials segregate; too fast, centrifugal force throws concrete outward. Discharge gate must not jam with set material.

nodes.name: Derrick crane with guy lines
nodes.kb: Tall mast held by cables and guy ropes, hook suspended from peak
nodes.note: Stays on the mast must be tight or it whips in wind. Mast is weak against side load. Guy cables must be tensioned equally or mast bends.

nodes.name: Tower crane on fixed base
nodes.kb: Steel tower with rotating jib and hoist, electrically driven
nodes.note: Jib and load are cantilevered. Base must be heavy to resist overturning moment. Wind creates side load; bracing must hold or tower tilts.

nodes.name: Treadwheel crane
nodes.kb: Large wooden wheel driven by workers walking inside it
nodes.note: Mechanical advantage comes from wheel radius. Internal braking is essential; if rope breaks, load and cage slam down, killing occupants.

nodes.name: Curtain wall non-structural facade
nodes.kb: Lightweight panel hung from floor slab, carrying no structural load
nodes.note: Panels are supported only at top, not at sills. Wind load is transmitted through fasteners to the frame. Sealing is critical; no redundancy if one panel fails.

nodes.name: Damp proof course barrier layer
nodes.kb: Impermeable layer in wall preventing capillary rise of moisture
nodes.note: Capillary rise can be metres high in masonry. Moisture triggers rot and salt crystallisation. Damp proof course breaks the capillary chain.

nodes.name: Deformed reinforcing bar
nodes.kb: Steel rod with ribs or deformations for better concrete bond
nodes.note: Ribs cut into the surface create mechanical bond better than friction. Bond failure is difficult to detect until beam collapses. Testing requires destructive sampling.

nodes.name: Dewatering system with pumps
nodes.kb: Pumps remove groundwater from foundation excavation
nodes.note: Lowering water table causes settlement of nearby buildings. Particles clog pumps and seals. Two pumps must run simultaneously; if one fails, site floods in minutes.

nodes.name: Diaphragm wall with slurry
nodes.kb: Slurry-filled trench with concrete wall cast in place
nodes.note: Bentonite slurry supports trench walls without temporary shoring. Concrete is heavier than slurry, so it sinks and replaces it. Requires careful placement and tremie.

nodes.name: Drill and blast tunnel
nodes.kb: Holes drilled in rock face, filled with explosives, detonated in sequence
nodes.note: Blast timing is critical. Wrong sequence creates large boulders and poor fragmentation. Too much explosive wastes powder and damages rock walls.

nodes.name: Earth dam with clay core
nodes.kb: Compacted earth with impermeable clay core, gravel and filter zones
nodes.note: Core must be more impermeable than surrounding zones or seepage concentrates. Piping failure (internal erosion) is sudden and catastrophic. Requires continuous monitoring.

nodes.name: Elevator with safety brake
nodes.kb: Counterweighted cage with mechanical brake that grips guide rails if rope breaks
nodes.note: Brake works only if jaws are pre-tensioned by cable tension. As rope breaks, tension drops, triggering brake. Wedge angle must be perfect or brake slips.

nodes.name: Expansion joint control system
nodes.kb: Gaps and filler materials allowing concrete movement from temperature change
nodes.note: Concrete expands 10-15 mm per 100 metres with 50 degree temperature change. Filler must compress, not extrude. Spacing closer than 20 metres is normal.

nodes.name: Fire escape stairs and landings
nodes.kb: External metal stairway providing emergency exit route
nodes.note: Stairs must not be obstructed or lockable. Pivot hinge ladder can trap people if hinge seizes. Many fire escape deaths were from mechanism failure, not fire.

nodes.name: Flying buttress in stone
nodes.kb: External arched support transferring vault load outboard to distant pier
nodes.note: Takes vault thrust outboard without disrupting interior space. Enables tall nave walls unsupported from inside. The arch does not pass through the wall, it connects at one point.

nodes.name: Forced ventilation mechanical system
nodes.kb: Fan driven by motor or steam engine pushes air through ducts
nodes.note: Ducting must be sized to prevent noise and vibration. Fan noise increases as speed increases. Dampers must adjust flow without complete closure or stall.

nodes.name: Formwork and shuttering system
nodes.kb: Temporary wooden or steel mould supporting concrete until cured
nodes.note: Formwork must be strong enough to hold wet concrete without deflection. Deflection continues after striking, permanently distorting the concrete surface.

nodes.name: Gang saw for stone
nodes.kb: Multiple parallel blades driven by water power to cut stone simultaneously
nodes.note: Parallel saws cut multiple blocks simultaneously from one stone blank. The synchronisation problem: slipping and binding destroy either the work or the machine. Requires heavy bearings and careful clearance.

nodes.name: Gravity dam masonry structure
nodes.kb: Massive triangular dam wall where weight resists water pressure
nodes.note: Must not slide on foundation. Foundation must be rock; soil underneath cannot support the load. Uplift pressure under base can lift dam like a balloon.

nodes.name: Groin vault in stone
nodes.kb: Two barrel vaults intersected at right angles, creating four curved triangular surfaces
nodes.note: Two arches cross at right angles. The groin curves are the geometry problem. Vault is self-supporting once completed but extremely delicate during construction.

nodes.name: Gusset plate reinforcement
nodes.kb: Diagonal or triangular plates added at joints to carry shear
nodes.note: Riveted joints are weak under shear. Gusset plates redirect force along stiffer paths. Excessive riveting in gussets causes stress concentration.

nodes.name: Gypsum plaster finish
nodes.kb: Calcined gypsum mixed with water for quick-setting finish plaster
nodes.note: Gypsum plaster sets in minutes, unlike lime which takes weeks. The speed forces different working methods and cannot be slowed down.

nodes.name: Building insulation materials
nodes.kb: Fibrous or cellular materials filling cavities and reducing heat transfer
nodes.note: Insulation works by trapping air in cells. Compression destroys it. Vapour barrier is needed or condensation saturates insulation in cold climates.

nodes.name: Cast iron column
nodes.kb: Hollow cast iron shaft for vertical load bearing
nodes.note: Iron is much stronger than timber in compression. Hollow section is economical. Cast iron is brittle; sudden shock loads can snap columns.

nodes.name: King post roof truss
nodes.kb: Single vertical post from apex to tie beam, supporting ridge under tension
nodes.note: Central post is in compression. Ties spread the apex, pulling down on beam ends. Very old form, but only works for narrow spans.

nodes.name: Lattice truss for beams
nodes.kb: Timber ribs in criss-cross pattern to create deep beam with minimal weight
nodes.note: Removes weight from the centre while keeping depth. Works if all diagonals are tied properly. Joint failures are catastrophic and not obvious until collapse.

nodes.name: Lime mortar
nodes.kb: Slaked lime mixed with sand, water and sometimes tallow or blood to bind masonry
nodes.note: Lime carbonates slowly in air over years. The binder is the product of a chemical reaction you cannot control, only manage with thickness and porosity.

nodes.name: Pile driving by drop hammer
nodes.kb: Heavy weight dropped onto pile to drive it into soft ground
nodes.note: Weight and drop height determine driving force. Pile compresses ground, packing it. As ground gets denser, driving becomes harder; each drop achieves less penetration.

nodes.name: Steel plate girder assembly
nodes.kb: Steel plates and angles welded or riveted into deep box girder
nodes.note: Stiffness comes from geometric depth, not just material. Web must be braced to prevent buckling. Flanges carry bending, web carries shear.

nodes.name: Plate glass large pane
nodes.kb: Polished sheet glass cast and ground flat, large transparent panes
nodes.note: Casting is slow and expensive. Annealing must be carefully controlled or internal stress cracks glass months later. Each large pane is handmade and unique.

nodes.name: Plumbing vertical stack system
nodes.kb: Lead or iron pipe stacks for water supply and waste drainage
nodes.note: Waste must slope correctly or it backs up. Soil pipe must be large to prevent siphoning. Supply lines must be sloped so air cannot trap high points.

nodes.name: Pneumatic caisson with air pressure
nodes.kb: Compressed air pumped into caisson keeps water out at depth
nodes.note: Air pressure must equal water pressure at working depth. Divers descend and work in high pressure. Sand boils unexpectedly when pressure drops, sucking water under walls.

nodes.name: Pontoon floating bridge
nodes.kb: Floating barges or floats lashed together, connected by chains, with deck on top
nodes.note: Bridge sinks and rises with water level. Approach ramps must adjust. Pontoons can be removed in winter or when passage is needed.

nodes.name: Portland cement powder
nodes.kb: Calcined limestone and clay ground to powder, hydrates with water
nodes.note: Clinkering temperature is 1450 C. Clinker is the active phase; grinding it fine increases early strength but consumes energy. Raw materials must be fed as slurry.

nodes.name: Post and lintel structure
nodes.kb: Vertical posts with horizontal beam spanning between them
nodes.note: Beam strength and span are limited by its cross-section. Stone and timber beam bending is the constraint that architects worked around for millennia.

nodes.name: Post tensioning with stressing jacks
nodes.kb: Cables stressed after concrete hardens using large hydraulic jacks
nodes.note: Jacks apply huge force; hydraulic failure kills workers. Ducts for cables must be placed accurately or stressing is uneven, causing internal damage.

nodes.name: Pozzolana hydraulic concrete
nodes.kb: Lime and volcanic ash create a binder that sets underwater
nodes.note: Pozzolanic reaction between silica and lime happens slowly and imperceptibly. The concrete is weak for months then becomes very hard. No chemical knowledge, only empirical observation of ash quality and mixing ratio.

nodes.name: Pratt truss
nodes.kb: Diagonals slope inward from panel ends, verticals carry shear
nodes.note: Diagonals in tension, verticals in compression. Longer diagonals mean shorter verticals. Compression members must not buckle, so they must be heavy or braced.

nodes.name: Precast concrete panel
nodes.kb: Concrete element cast off-site in controlled conditions, transported and erected
nodes.note: Factory control improves quality and speed. Transport is expensive; distance limits economy. Connections between panels are weak points; connection design is critical.

nodes.name: Prestressed concrete element
nodes.kb: Steel cables stressed before concrete sets, then released, creating internal compression
nodes.note: Stressing imparts compression that cancels tensile stress from bending. Longer spans and thinner sections are possible. Stress loss over time requires careful design margins.

nodes.name: Stone quarrying with wedge
nodes.kb: Drive wedges into natural fissures to break stone blocks
nodes.note: Wedges are inserted along planes of weakness, then tapped in sequence to split stone cleanly. Without this, stone quarrying is random fracture, not construction.

nodes.name: Queen post roof truss
nodes.kb: Two posts set back from apex, with central strut and spreading collar tie
nodes.note: Two posts working inward reduce the tie-beam span compared to king post, enabling longer roof slopes. Geometry is trickier to lay out.

nodes.name: Cast iron radiator
nodes.kb: Cast iron section carrying hot water, radiating heat to room
nodes.note: Fins increase surface area for heat transfer. Scaling inside radiators reduces heat flow; circulation must be clean. Thermostat valve controls flow independently.

nodes.name: Reinforced concrete slab and beam
nodes.kb: Steel bars in tension zones of concrete element counteract concrete cracking
nodes.note: Steel and concrete have nearly identical thermal expansion; if not, the bond breaks every summer and they separate. This accidental match made reinforced concrete possible.

nodes.name: Retaining wall gravity structure
nodes.kb: Massive masonry wall holding back soil pressure
nodes.note: Wall must be heavy enough that soil pressure cannot overturn it. Base angle and drainage affect stability. Passive pressure of soil in front of toe adds resistance.

nodes.name: Ribbed vault in stone
nodes.kb: Arched stone ribs bear the load, with lighter web filling in between
nodes.note: Heavy ribs carry load. Web is incidental, can be thin or even omitted. Ribs can be built first as temporary trusses, supporting the web. Load path becomes clear and traceable.

nodes.name: Riveted bolted connection
nodes.kb: Hot rivets upset through overlapping plates to create permanent joint
nodes.note: Hot rivet is upset under the hammer, growing to fill the hole. Force comes from thermal contraction after cooling. Each rivet must be hand-hammered; no way to speed it up.

nodes.name: Rolled iron or steel I beam
nodes.kb: I-shaped section hot rolled from solid billet in one pass
nodes.note: Heating steel to rolling temperature is energy-intensive. Section must be designed to flow evenly through rolls. Dies wear quickly. Economy comes from not riveting.

nodes.name: Roof truss with corrugated iron
nodes.kb: Wooden or steel truss supporting corrugated sheet metal roof
nodes.note: Corrugations are structural; corrugated iron is much stiffer than flat. Fastening through corrugations creates stress concentration. Expansion and contraction create noise.

nodes.name: Rotary cement kiln
nodes.kb: Large rotating drum maintaining clinkering temperature for continuous production
nodes.note: Kiln rotates 1-3 rpm. Material must not stick to walls or discharge will jam. Flame temperature at inlet must reach 1800 C. Insulation must survive 1450 C inside.

nodes.name: Sash window with cord and weight
nodes.kb: Two glass panes slide vertically in wooden frame, balanced by counterweights
nodes.note: Cord wears and breaks; rope must be threaded through pulleys. Weights must exactly balance panes or window stays open or slams shut.

nodes.name: Timber scaffolding system
nodes.kb: Temporary timber framework lashed together with rope and planks for worker access
nodes.note: Lashing discipline is critical. A single untied rope can unravel the whole frame. Deflection under load is visible and causes worker fear.

nodes.name: Screw pile with helical blade
nodes.kb: Spiral blade on shaft screws into ground like a corkscrew
nodes.note: Eliminates the hammer and drop. Helix must have correct pitch and angle or pile spins in place without driving. Torque must be balanced; twisted piles lose capacity.

nodes.name: Sewer gravity drainage network
nodes.kb: Underground pipes collecting and transporting waste to treatment or discharge
nodes.note: Network effect: one house benefits little; system must serve whole city. Slopes must be precise or sediment settles. Cleanouts must be spaced to allow maintenance.

nodes.name: Sheet piling wall
nodes.kb: Interlocked steel or timber sheets driven side by side to create waterproof wall
nodes.note: Interlock must be tight or water seeps between sheets. Each new sheet is pushed down by the ones already driven; last sheets are hardest to drive.

nodes.name: Sprayed concrete shotcrete
nodes.kb: Concrete sprayed at high velocity onto surface, compacted in flight
nodes.note: Rebound of aggregate on vertical surfaces wastes material. Air pressure and nozzle angle control placement. Curing must be slow to prevent drying shrinkage cracks.

nodes.name: Inverted siphon pipe
nodes.kb: Pipe drops below required level then rises, allowing water to cross obstacles
nodes.note: Siphon works by gravity and atmospheric pressure. Air locks destroy the flow. Pipe must be primed and remain full. Sediment accumulates at the low point.

nodes.name: Slipform creeping formwork
nodes.kb: Formwork slowly rises as concrete cures, allowing continuous pour
nodes.note: Creep rate must be controlled so concrete sets enough to hold form weight. Too fast, concrete breaks; too slow, set concrete cracks from form friction.

nodes.name: Soil compaction by roller
nodes.kb: Heavy roller or rammer compacts soil in lifts, increasing bearing capacity
nodes.note: Soil density increases with each pass, but benefit decreases. Optimal moisture content exists; too wet or too dry, soil resists compaction.

nodes.name: Space frame three-dimensional truss
nodes.kb: Pyramidal cells of tetrahedral trusses creating deep beam in three dimensions
nodes.note: Stiffness comes from three-dimensional triangulation, not from depth. Very light for span, but joints are complex and must carry loads in many directions. Assembly is intricate.

nodes.name: Spillway overflow structure
nodes.kb: Controlled overflow channel protecting dam from overtopping
nodes.note: High-velocity water in spillway can erode concrete. Stilling basin dissipates energy. Spillway must never be overtopped; if crest elevation is wrong, whole dam fails.

nodes.name: Automatic fire sprinkler
nodes.kb: Heat-triggered valve on water pipe, spraying room when temperature rises
nodes.note: Thermal element must melt reliably at set temperature. Solder plug can fail if handled. Water pressure must be adequate to drive flow at all nozzles.

nodes.name: Steel frame skeleton building
nodes.kb: Multi-storey frame of rolled columns and beams, with non-structural walls
nodes.note: Load flows down the steel grid, not through walls. Walls need not be structural, only weathertight. Foundations must carry all load through frame, not spread it.

nodes.name: Stiffening truss for deck
nodes.kb: Deep truss runs along deck, resisting wind and dynamic loads
nodes.note: Light decks oscillate in wind. Stiffening truss adds weight and damping. Tuned mass dampers do the same job with less weight, but are harder to design.

nodes.name: Stone polishing and smoothing
nodes.kb: Rubbing stone surfaces with abrasive blocks to achieve smoothness
nodes.note: Emery or other hard stone grinds softer stone flat. Requires rhythm and feel. Machine polishing comes much later.

nodes.name: Stone saw with abrasive
nodes.kb: Frame saw with abrasive sand to cut stone into dressed blocks
nodes.note: Stone is harder than tools. Abrasive (usually sand) embedded in the saw does the cutting, not the blade. The saw itself serves as a guide.

nodes.name: Suspension bridge system
nodes.kb: Flexible cable hung from towers suspends deck via vertical hangers
nodes.note: Main cable carries all load in tension. Hangers support deck from cable, like a string pulled upward at midspan. Towers must resist enormous horizontal thrust.

nodes.name: Swing bridge on central pivot
nodes.kb: Bridge rotates on central post, aligning with river or opening for traffic
nodes.note: Pivot must be perfectly centred and smooth. Friction from bridge weight is enormous. Rail must guide bridge smoothly without binding on approach.

nodes.name: Terrazzo floor finish
nodes.kb: Lime mortar with stone chips and marble dust, polished smooth
nodes.note: Aggregate size and porosity must be matched to allow polishing down to stone-wide sheen. Under-fired mortar remains soft and yields to the stone dust. Over-fired mortar tears the chips.

nodes.name: Timber roof truss
nodes.kb: Triangulated timber frame with tension ties and compression struts
nodes.note: Wood is weak in tension. Truss geometry converts bending into pure tension and compression. Ties must not slip, so joints are critical.

nodes.name: Trap with water seal
nodes.kb: U-bend under sink that holds water to block sewer gas and pests
nodes.note: Water seal is only 5-10cm. Siphoning or evaporation breaks it. Every fixture must have a trap or smell is unbearable.

nodes.name: True arch in stone
nodes.kb: Wedge-shaped stones arranged radially, transmitting load laterally to supports
nodes.note: Load flows through the curve to the supports, not down through the span. Each stone is under compression only, never tension. Geometry, not material strength, is the constraint.

nodes.name: Trussed arch
nodes.kb: Arch ribs braced by interior timber trusses to prevent spreading
nodes.note: Arch wants to spread. Timber bracing, if properly located and strong, resists the spreading force. Requires coordination of load paths between materials.

nodes.name: Tunnel by cut and cover
nodes.kb: Open trench with roof beam and arch or vault cover, then backfill
nodes.note: Roof must support all overburden load plus live load above. Shallow tunnels this way. Deep tunnels need shield method.

nodes.name: Tunnel permanent lining
nodes.kb: Cast concrete rings bolted together inside tunnel to support walls
nodes.note: Segments are cast and cured before installation. Installation is quick, 1-2 rings per day. Joints must be tight; water ingress rots concrete.

nodes.name: Tunnel shield method
nodes.kb: Steel cylinder pushed forward, excavating at front, lining installed behind
nodes.note: Shield is pushed forward by jacks. Face is pressurised or shielded to prevent collapse. Rings are bolted together as shield advances. Grout fills void behind.

nodes.name: Underpinning of existing structure
nodes.kb: Installing new foundation beneath existing building without damage
nodes.note: Building must be supported while old foundation is removed and new one installed. Settlement of even 1mm can crack walls. Shoring must be adjustable and carefully monitored.

nodes.name: Ventilation shaft and duct
nodes.kb: Secondary shaft for air circulation in long tunnels
nodes.note: Shaft is usually shallower than main tunnel. Ventilation depends on natural stack effect or mechanical fans. Pressure difference drives flow.

nodes.name: Vibratory compaction of concrete
nodes.kb: Electric or pneumatic vibrators eliminate air pockets in fresh concrete
nodes.note: Over-vibration segregates aggregate from paste. Under-vibration leaves voids and weak zones. Duration is only 5-10 seconds per area.

nodes.name: Warren truss
nodes.kb: Diagonal members at 45 degrees with no vertical struts, all triangles pointing same way
nodes.note: 45-degree angles mean each member carries load efficiently in pure tension or compression. No shear in diagonals, no verticals needed. Requires precise geometry.

nodes.name: Water main distribution pipe
nodes.kb: Underground pipeline supplying water to district
nodes.note: Pipe must be buried below frost line or it freezes. Corrosion creates holes; no way to inspect or repair without excavation. Pressure rating must be adequate.

nodes.name: Electric arc welded joint
nodes.kb: Electric arc melts base steel and electrode, creating homogeneous joint
nodes.note: Weld is as strong as or stronger than base steel if cooled slowly. Rapid cooling creates brittle martensite. Technique matters enormously: speed, angle, heat input all affect final strength.

nodes.name: Steel wire rope and spinning
nodes.kb: Twisted steel wires bundled into large-diameter rope under tension
nodes.note: Twisting individual wires increases axial stiffness. Rotation of the bundle during spinning must be controlled, otherwise the rope twists itself apart.

nodes.name: Wrought iron plate girder
nodes.kb: Flat plates riveted together to form deep I-shaped beam
nodes.note: Riveted plate girders are flexible, not stiff. Many rivets must hold against vibration and stress concentration at holes. Riveting skill is critical.

nodes.name: Coal, and coking it
nodes.note: Romans burn coal in Britain but never coke it. Raw coal ruins iron through sulfur; coking drives off sulfur and volatiles and leaves a strong porous fuel that will bear the burden in a tall furnace. Breaks the charcoal ceiling permanently. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: coking coal to 900-1000 C to remove sulfur and volatiles]

nodes.name: Licensed collegium of physicians and teachers
nodes.note: Unlicensed associations are illegal; Trajan refuses Pliny even a fire brigade at Nicomedia (Ep. 10.34) for fear of factions. Get the licence or your school is a conspiracy.

nodes.name: Accumulator - arithmetic work register
nodes.note: A register connected to an adder circuit (carries propagate left through carry-look-ahead or similar). A number can be added to the accumulator in one clock cycle. Repeated additions multiply (accumulate a number N times), division by repeated subtraction. The accumulator is the primary work register in early computers, used for nearly all arithmetic. Later CPUs generalize this to multiple general-purpose registers. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Amplitude modulation (AM) - encoding audio on radio
nodes.note: A microphone signal (audio, 0-10 kHz) is added to the RF oscillator output, varying its amplitude. The modulated wave is transmitted; a receiver detects the envelope (the modulation) using a rectifier, recovering audio. The trick: a 1 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio produces sidebands at 999 kHz and 1001 kHz. Radio stations are spaced 10 kHz apart (AM broadcast). The bandwidth is about 2x the audio frequency. Simple and robust.

nodes.name: Analytical engine - programmable mechanical computer
nodes.note: Babbage's design for a universal mechanical computer: a large mill (arithmetic unit) and store (memory), programmed by punched cards like Jacquard looms. It could perform any sequence of arithmetic operations, conditional on intermediate results. The killer insight: a general-purpose machine can solve many problems if programmed differently. Ada Lovelace sketched an algorithm for it (1843). It was never built (same tolerance problems as the Difference Engine), but it was the conceptual foundation of the stored-program computer. [FIXED after independent audit: the note itself said Babbage failed on tolerance, and the node listed no tolerance prerequisite at all.]

nodes.name: Antenna and ground system for radio
nodes.note: An antenna is just a wire at a height or length that couples to the air (transmitting) or the air couples to it (receiving). A ground is a connection to earth (literally a copper plate or rod buried 2 metres). Radio waves need an antenna and a return path (ground) to form a closed loop. The antenna length determines efficiency at a given frequency. This was not obvious: early radio pioneers accidentally discovered that tall antennas worked better. Design theory came later. nodes.name: Arithmometer - mass-produced mechanical calculator
nodes.note: The first calculator to reach mass production (thousands made, not just hundreds). Uses standardized parts, precision jigs, and assembly-line methods. Reduced price from 500 denarii to 100 denarii. The Arithmometer (1851 onward) was the accountant's standard tool until electric calculators appeared (1960s). The innovation was not mechanical (same as Pascal's design) but manufacturing: making them cheaply and reliably.

nodes.name: Baudot code - 5-bit telegraph encoding
nodes.note: Each character is encoded as 5 binary digits (bits): mark (current) or space (no current). Letters, numbers, and symbols each have a 5-bit code. A teleprinter has 5 solenoids, one per bit. All 5 are energized simultaneously on reception, positioning the 5 levers correctly, and a mechanical stroke fires the type. This is the first digital telegraph code and the ancestor of modern binary encoding (ASCII, etc.). Standardized by the ITU in 1874.

nodes.name: Binary arithmetic - base-2 number system
nodes.note: Binary: digits 0 and 1 only. Addition, multiplication, and logic are all simpler in binary than decimal. A two-state device (relay on/off, transistor on/off) represents 0 or 1 directly. Decimal requires devices with 10 states (complex and error-prone). All electronic computers use binary for this reason. The conceptual link: binary numbers are data, Boolean logic is control, they use the same substrates (switches). [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Boolean algebra - logic and switching equivalence
nodes.note: Boolean algebra: true/false, AND, OR, NOT. Claude Shannon's insight (1938): switching circuits are Boolean algebras. A series switch is AND (both must be closed), parallel is OR. This is the single most important conceptual link in computing: abstract logic is isomorphic to physical electronics. Once realized, designing computers becomes designing logic circuits, which become routine engineering. No breakthrough in physics or chemistry needed, just the right mathematical language. nodes.name: Broadcasting as an institution - scheduled transmission and profit model
nodes.note: Not a technical innovation but an economic and political one. Broadcast stations transmit on fixed schedules so listeners know when to tune in. Content (music, news, drama) is produced by local staff. Revenue comes from advertising (selling commercial time). This is a radical model: entertainment and information are free to the listener, paid for by advertisers. By 1930, broadcasting is the dominant communication medium and has shaped politics, culture, and commerce.

nodes.name: Cathode ray tube (CRT) - electron beam display
nodes.note: An evacuated glass tube with a heated cathode that emits electrons, accelerated by 10,000 V towards a phosphor-coated anode. The electron beam is steered by magnetic coils (X and Y deflection). Where the beam hits the screen, the phosphor glows. Varying the beam current modulates the brightness. This is the display technology that made electronic television possible. The key: the beam is fast (MHz), allowing full-screen raster scanning at video rate. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: evacuated tube for electron beam display requires high vacuum]

nodes.name: Coherer - primitive radio detector
nodes.note: A tube of glass filled with iron filings between two metal plugs. When RF current (from a radio signal) passes through, the filings cohere (stick together), dropping resistance from 1 megohm to 1000 ohms. A relay responds to this current change, signalling the received dot or dash. After each signal, a tapper mechanically shakes the tube to decohere the filings. Unreliable and slow (tapping delay), but it was the only radio detector before solid-state rectifiers.

nodes.name: Compiler and high-level programming language
nodes.note: A language like FORTRAN or ALGOL (not machine code) that expresses computations in human terms. A compiler translates source code to machine code. The breakthrough: programmers no longer need to think in bits and registers. They write mathematics and logic directly. Compilers handle optimization, memory allocation, and code generation. FORTRAN (1957) became the standard for scientific computing. This raised the abstraction level from machines to problems. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Comptometer - key-driven calculator
nodes.note: Instead of a crank (one operation per second), the Comptometer (1887 onward) uses keys (one per digit). Pressing a key lever multiple times increments that digit, accumulating the sum. Touch typists could use Comptometers almost as fast as they thought of numbers. Faster than Arithmometer. The innovation is that the operator interface is ergonomic and intuitive (press 5 five times to add 5), not just mechanical optimization.

nodes.name: Continuous wave (CW) generation with triode
nodes.note: A triode acts as an amplifier: a small signal on the grid amplifies a large signal in the anode. Fed back to the grid through a tuned circuit, this creates sustained oscillation (feedback), generating continuous RF at the resonant frequency. The generator is stable, efficient, and clean (no spark noise). Morse code is sent by turning the oscillator on/off with a telegraph key. Continuous wave replaced spark transmitters by 1920. nodes.name: Substitution and polyalphabetic ciphers
nodes.note: Caesar cipher (shift alphabet by N) was known to Rome. Vigenere cipher (shift depends on a repeating key) was stronger (1553 onward). Both are vulnerable to frequency analysis (common letters are obvious). The Vigenere cipher remained unbroken until the 19th century (Kasiski examination), making it militarily useful for 300 years. Encryption was the luxury of armies and empires; telegraph traffic required it, making cryptography a core technology. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Crystal set receiver - galena rectifier radio
nodes.note: A tuned coil and capacitor select one radio station, a galena rectifier converts the RF signal to audio (crystal detects, headphones reproduce). No power source needed (rectified signal drives headphones directly). Range is short (5 km), quality is poor (strong local station only), but the cost is near zero. Crystal sets were toys in 1910, but mass-produced for every youth by 1920. They taught radio to the world, but they are obsolete once vacuum tube amplifiers exist. nodes.name: Difference engine - mechanical polynomial solver
nodes.note: A mechanism that uses the method of differences to evaluate polynomials and tabulate mathematical functions. Babbage built a working prototype in 1832, but the complete engine was never finished. Reason: tolerances. Brass expands and contracts with temperature (5 metres of machinery spans 0.5 mm over 10 degrees Celsius), cams wear, precision degrades. 19th century machine tools could hold 0.1 mm tolerances; the engine needed 0.01 mm consistency. It was engineering overreach, not a bad idea.

nodes.name: Duplex telegraphy - simultaneous two-way transmission
nodes.note: A simple telegraph line is half-duplex: one side transmits while the other listens. Duplex uses a bridge circuit (Wheatstone bridge) to cancel your own transmitted signal at your receiver, so you hear only the far end. The trick: send your signal balanced (symmetrical) through two wires to ground so your receiver sees it as zero, but the asymmetrical current flowing through the line carries the signal. Doubles line capacity.

nodes.name: Error detecting and correcting codes
nodes.note: Parity bit (odd/even) detects single-bit errors. Hamming codes detect and correct single-bit errors. More powerful codes (Reed-Solomon, convolutional) can correct multiple errors. Used in memory (cosmic ray bit flips), transmission (noise corruption), and storage (magnetic media decay). The principle: add redundancy (extra bits) that encodes a checksum. On reception, recompute the checksum; if it mismatches, an error occurred and can be located/corrected. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Flip-flop circuit - one-bit memory
nodes.note: Two relays (or vacuum tube stages) cross-coupled: output of one feeds input of the other. The system has two stable states: relay A on and B off, or vice versa. A pulse on 'Set' line (via a contact closure) fires relay A, which holds itself on. A pulse on 'Reset' line fires relay B, which forces A off. This is a one-bit storage element: it 'remembers' whether it was last set or reset. The flip-flop is the foundation of all memory and state machines. nodes.name: Frequency modulation (FM) - superior radio broadcast
nodes.note: Audio signal varies the frequency of the RF carrier instead of the amplitude. A 100 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio swings ±75 kHz. FM is immune to amplitude noise (static, ignition noise), so reception is much quieter. Bandwidth is about 10x wider than AM (200 kHz for 15 kHz audio), requiring wider channel spacing. Requires sophisticated receivers (discriminators, limiters). Adopted late (1940s in consumer radio) due to infrastructure cost, but ultimately superior.

nodes.name: Heliograph - sun mirror telegraph
nodes.note: A polished mirror reflects sunlight to encode Morse dots and dashes. Works in daylight at range up to 50 km. Lighter and cheaper than optical towers. Cannot work at night or in cloud. The constraint is weather: an overcast day stops all communication, but the apparatus itself is simpler and more portable. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Hollerith tabulation - punched card data processing
nodes.note: Punched cards record data (census: age, occupation, birthplace, etc., each in a column). A machine reads the holes and closes electromagnetic switches, incrementing counters. The 1890 U.S. Census was tallied in months instead of years. This created data processing as an industry: IBM emerged from tabulating machines. The insight: data can be stored and processed mechanically, and this is faster than manual accounting. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Information theory - entropy and the bit
nodes.note: Shannon's theory (1948): information is measured in bits (binary digits). Entropy quantifies the average number of bits needed to encode a message. A channel's capacity (bits per second) sets the maximum transmission rate. Compression algorithms reduce redundancy (entropy coding). This theory unified communication, storage, and computation under one mathematical framework. Every modern system (networks, storage, codes) is designed using information theory. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Integrated circuit - many transistors on one chip
nodes.note: A single silicon chip (1 cm square) with thousands of transistors and resistors, interconnected by metal lines. The Small Scale Integration (SSI, 1960s) level put 10-100 components on a chip. Later: LSI (1000-10000), VLSI (millions), and beyond. The innovation is not a single transistor but the entire ecosystem: design tools, fabrication processes, testing, and assembly. One chip replaces a circuit board full of discrete components. Cost per transistor drops exponentially.

nodes.name: Jacquard loom - punched card control
nodes.note: A loom with thousands of vertical threads (warp). A deck of punched cards controls which threads are lifted on each pass of the shuttle. Complex patterns (brocade, damask) can be woven automatically. This was the first programmable machine: change the cards and the output changes. The innovation is separating control (the cards) from mechanism (the loom). This idea was revolutionary and inspired Babbage's Analytical Engine. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Loading coil - range extension for telegraph lines
nodes.note: A coil of wire inserted periodically into a long telegraph or telephone line. Wire acts as a capacitor that stores charge; the coil inductance smooths it out. This compensates for cable distortion and allows signals to travel further before attenuation kills them. A loading coil every 2 km extends range from 50 km to 500 km on a submarine cable. The physics is: inductance and capacitance in series form a filter that attenuates high frequencies (noise) less than the signal distortion. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: coil winding requires file and gauge precision to achieve specified inductance]

nodes.name: Logic gate - elementary switching circuit
nodes.note: A circuit that implements Boolean logic: AND (output high if all inputs high), OR, NOT, NAND, NOR. Diodes and resistors suffice for simple gates. Transistors give active amplification (necessary for cascading gates). By the 1960s, logic gates were the design vocabulary for digital systems. A computer is built by combining gates into larger functions (adder, multiplier, controller). The innovation is recognizing that Boolean algebra and circuits are the same thing. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Magnetic core memory - fast addressable RAM
nodes.note: Toroidal ferrite cores (0.5 mm) arranged in a 2D grid (64x64 cores = 4096 bits). Each core stores 1 bit (magnetized clockwise or counter-clockwise). Access time is 1 microsecond (1000x faster than tape). Each core is addressed by X and Y wires (select row and column), read and write wires complete the circuit. Core memory was the standard for mainframe computers (1960s-1970s) until semiconductor RAM replaced it. Handwiring a core array took weeks. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: 0.5 mm ferrite cores need precise size consistency]

nodes.name: Magnetic drum storage - early rotating memory
nodes.note: A cylinder coated with iron oxide, rotating at 3600 RPM. Read/write heads are stationary, positioned around the drum. Average access time is half a rotation (8 ms). Faster than tape, but requires synchronization with the rotating medium. Used as main memory in early computers (1950s) and later as auxiliary storage. Eventually replaced by moving-head disk drives (faster, fewer mechanical issues). [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: rotating cylinder storage needs precise cylindrical geometry and head spacing]

nodes.name: Magnetic tape storage - bulk archival memory
nodes.note: Paper or plastic tape coated with iron oxide, wound on reels. Data is stored sequentially (cannot directly access the middle). Cheap storage for large datasets (gigabytes on a compact reel). Speed is slow (minutes to locate a record). Used for daily backups, program storage, and archival data. IBM's System/360 (1965) relied on tape for I/O. Magnetic tape remained standard until optical media and solid-state storage arrived.

nodes.name: Magnetic wire storage - first practical memory
nodes.note: Steel wire wound on a reel, magnetized by a coil (1 bit = magnetized forward or backward). Access time is slow (wait for the right section of wire to pass the read/write head, like tape), but storage is cheap and non-volatile (data survives power loss). Used for audio recording and computer memory (1940s-1950s). Superseded by magnetic tape (cheaper) and later by core memory (faster). The innovation: ferromagnetism stores data, not mechanical position.

nodes.name: Mechanical calculator - Pascal and Leibniz designs
nodes.note: A desktop mechanism with gears and stepped drums that performs addition, subtraction, and multiplication by repeated addition. Operator cranks and manipulates dials. Precision is critical: gears must mesh smoothly, and carries must propagate correctly through multiple decades. Hand-made calculators were expensive (200+ hours labor) and slow (1 operation per minute). But they were used by accountants for payroll and bookkeeping.

nodes.name: Morse code - dot, dash, space encoding
nodes.note: Morse code is not a hardware innovation; it is a language for the telegraph. Dots and dashes match the sounder's 'click' and 'hold', encoded by hand at the key. The genius is that it is rhythmic and acoustic: a skilled operator hears the message, not reading visual symbols. Fast hands can send 30 words per minute.

nodes.name: Morse register - recording apparatus
nodes.note: An electromagnetic solenoid pulls a stylus down onto a paper tape moving past it. When current flows, the dot or dash is recorded as a mark. The register was the original telegraph receiver: it married mechanical motion to electrical signal. A human operator then reads the tape and transcribes the message. The key limitation: without a sounder (sound output), it was slow to read and error-prone.

nodes.name: Morse sounder - audio telegraph receiver
nodes.note: A solenoid pulls an armature down onto a metal block (click), springs push it back (click). Morse is designed to be heard: a short current = dot sound, long current = dash sound. This was the killer innovation: skilled operators hear the message directly instead of squinting at paper tape. It increased speed tenfold. The sounder, not the relay, is the human interface to telegraphy.

nodes.name: Multiplexing - combining multiple signals on one line
nodes.note: Time-division multiplexing: 4 calls take turns using the same trunk line, each getting 1/4 of the time (switching at 1000 Hz, fast enough that voice sounds continuous). Frequency-division: use different frequency bands on the same line. Both require precision filters and were impractical until vacuum tube amplifiers. The principle: more calls per cable = more revenue per infrastructure dollar. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Napier's bones - calculating rods
nodes.note: Rods with multiplication tables engraved in rows (one rod for each digit 0-9). To multiply 45*67, lay out the 4 and 5 rods, read the rows for 6 and 7, add diagonally. Reduces multiplication to table-lookup and addition. Slow compared to memorized multiplication, but eliminates error. Used by merchants and accountants. Fell out of use by 1700 as slide rules became popular, but conceptually important (separation of the multiplication table into components that can be recombined). nodes.name: One-time pad - information-theoretically secure cipher
nodes.note: A random key, used once, added to plaintext bit-by-bit (XOR). No amount of codebreaking can recover the plaintext without the key (Shannon's proof, 1945). The catch: you must generate, securely transmit, and store a key as long as the message. For millions of messages, this is impractical (key logistics). Used for highest-security traffic (Red Phone, diplomatic cables). The OTP is the gold standard, but its key distribution is a nightmare.

nodes.name: Codebook for optical signal tower
nodes.note: Not the tower itself, but the agreed language it speaks. Without a standardised codebook (a government document), each tower operator invents his own alphabet. The innovation is making it systematic: three-position arms encode 8 letters per second in groups (like Morse). Requires coordination across the empire.

nodes.name: Optical semaphore tower
nodes.note: Tall wooden or brick tower with rotating wooden arms on three axes (shutter positions: open, half, closed). Operator turns cranks to set position, next tower sees it through telescope, relays instantly. No power needed. Can send 20 words per minute across 100 km chain. The killer innovation: a message travels the length of France in hours instead of weeks. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Photolithography - precision pattern transfer
nodes.note: UV light exposes a photoresist layer (thin polymer) through a mask. Exposed regions polymerize, unexposed regions dissolve. The pattern is then etched into the silicon with acid, creating trenches and ridges. This process repeats dozens of times (layers of metal, oxide, silicon). Feature size starts at 10 micrometers (1970), shrinks to 1 micrometer (1980), 0.1 micrometer (1995), and continues. Photolithography is the core of all semiconductor manufacturing.

nodes.name: Public-key cryptography - RSA and successors
nodes.note: A key pair: public key (known to all) encrypts, private key (secret) decrypts. Asymmetric encryption (different keys for encode/decode) solves key distribution: no need to send a shared secret. RSA (1977) bases security on integer factorization (hard for large numbers). Each party publishes their public key; anyone can encrypt for them, only they can decrypt. This invented secure communication without pre-shared keys: revolutionary for email, web, and digital signatures.

nodes.name: Quadruplex telegraphy - four signals on one wire
nodes.note: Quadruplex uses two independent duplex channels on the same wire: one at high current (positive), one at low current (negative). Requires precise impedance matching and filtering. The circuit is fragile (crosstalk is constant enemy), but it quadruples capacity. Thomas Edison's major telegraphy innovation. Marginal returns made it uneconomical by the 1900s, but it did prove the principle: multiplex the line, not the wire.

nodes.name: Magnetron - compact high-power microwave generator
nodes.note: A thermionic tube with a hot cathode that emits electrons, a strong axial magnetic field that curves them into a circular path, and resonant cavities around the periphery. Electrons oscillate between cavities, exchanging energy with the RF field. The result: very high power (kilowatts) at very high frequency (microwave, 9 GHz). Compact because the wavelength is tiny. Invented in 1939, it was classified as a weapon; it made radar practical for aircraft detection. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Spark transmitter - radio broadcast generator
nodes.note: A high-voltage battery (5000 V) charged a capacitor that discharged across an air gap, creating a spark. The spark radiates radio waves across a broad spectrum. A telegraph key interrupts the spark stream, encoding Morse code. Inefficient (most energy is heat and light), unreliable (spark gap is erratic), and creates tons of radio interference across all frequencies. But it works and requires no vacuum tubes. Replaced by continuous wave (CW) generation after 1915. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Register - multi-bit storage and transfer
nodes.note: Multiple flip-flops (one per bit) cascaded: an 8-bit register holds 8 bits. A control pulse transfers data into the register (latch), or shifts the data left/right (shift register). Registers are the basic building blocks of CPU architecture: accumulator (for arithmetic), memory buffer (for I/O), instruction register (for control). Every arithmetic operation reads from registers and writes back to them. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Relay - current amplification for long lines
nodes.note: A weak current (from the distant telegraph key) flows through a solenoid, pulling a switch that closes a local circuit with a strong battery. This solves the fundamental problem: telegraph wire has resistance; after 100 km, the signal is too weak to operate the sounder. A relay at each station regenerates the signal at full strength. Without relays, the telegraph network stops at about 50 km. With relays, it can span continents.

nodes.name: Relay computer - automated logic and arithmetic
nodes.note: A computer built entirely from relays (Zuse Z1-Z3, 1930s-1940s). Thousands of relays form registers, accumulators, and adders. A paper tape feeds instructions, step by step. The computer executes addition and subtraction in one second per operation. Multiply takes 20 seconds. The machine works, but it is slow, loud, and unreliable (relays stick, wear out). Replaced by vacuum tube computers (1000x faster) by 1950. The relay computer proved the principle: automation of calculation is feasible.

nodes.name: Ring counter - timing and sequencing circuit
nodes.note: A shift register with the output of the last stage fed back to the input. A single 1-bit propagates around the ring. On each clock pulse, the 1 moves to the next position. This generates a sequence of pulses on N different output lines, one line active at a time. Used for timing and sequencing in computers: generating control signals for memory access, ALU operations, etc. Simple and reliable, particularly in relay computers. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Rotor cipher machine - Enigma and successors
nodes.note: A rotor (circular disk) with internal wiring that implements a substitution. As you type, each rotor rotates one position (like an odometer), changing the substitution. Three to five rotors in sequence give enormous key space (26^N combinations). The Enigma machine (1923 onward) was adopted by German military and was believed unbreakable until codebreakers (Turing, Rejewski) found flaws. The rotor machine was the standard for military encryption until electronics arrived. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: rotor with internal wiring needs precise electrical contact and alignment]

nodes.name: Semiconductor diode - p-n junction rectifier
nodes.note: A junction between p-type (hole-doped) and n-type (electron-doped) semiconductor. Forward bias allows current flow (low resistance), reverse bias blocks it (high resistance). Used as rectifier (AC to DC), detector, and digital switch. Silicon and germanium diodes were reliable by 1952. In logic, diodes replace vacuum tubes: smaller, cooler, longer-lived. The key is that the diode's threshold voltage sets the logic swing (0-5V typical). [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.] [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_pure_6N added by a reviewer working node by node. nodes.name: Signal flags for maritime communication
nodes.note: Flags of different colours and patterns, read at distance. First step beyond simple smoke: it is quick, daylight-reliable, and needs no line-of-sight relay network. A ship can read flags from another ship miles away. Codebook is implicit in sailor tradition.

nodes.name: Slide rule - mechanical multiplier
nodes.note: Two wooden rules with logarithmic scales, aligned by hand and compared visually. To multiply 5*7, you find 5 on one scale and 7 on the other, align them, and read 35 off the fixed scale. Uses the log identity: log(a*b)=log(a)+log(b). Accuracy is 3 digits, good enough for engineering work. Ubiquitous by 1900, slide rules were the dominant calculation tool until electronic calculators (1970s). Simple, cheap, and fast enough for design iteration. nodes.name: Stepped drum - mechanical counter and incrementor
nodes.note: A drum with 10 pins at different radial distances (0 to 9 steps). A rotating arm engages the appropriate pin and lifts a counter register once per turn. Used in Pascal's and Leibniz's calculators to perform addition and carry-over (successive addition is multiplication). The stepped drum was a brilliant mechanical innovation, but hand-cranked operation was tedious. Every mechanical calculator from 1600 onward used this principle or something similar. nodes.name: Stock ticker - financial telegraph terminal
nodes.note: A telegraph receiver modified to print stock prices and ticker symbols on a paper tape instead of requiring manual transcription. A ticker in each brokerage receives the same broadcast telegraph signal from the exchange, all printing simultaneously. The innovation is not technical but economic: it creates a new product (real-time pricing data) and a new business model (subscription service). The telegraph system becomes a data distribution network.

nodes.name: Stored program computer - code as data in memory
nodes.note: The conceptual breakthrough: a program is data. Instead of hand-rewiring circuits (ENIAC, 1945), the program sits in memory as numbers. The computer fetches each instruction, decodes it, and executes it. Changing the program is trivial (rewrite memory). This is Babbage's Analytical Engine concept finally realized in electronics. Every computer since has this architecture (von Neumann). This distinction (code vs. data, processor vs. memory) is fundamental. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Strowger automatic exchange - mechanical switching
nodes.note: A caller dials pulses on the handset (1=one pulse, 2=two pulses, etc). These pulses drive a stepper motor which rotates a wiper across a grid of contacts, selecting the called party's line. No human operator needed. The 1890 Strowger exchange was a mechanical marvel: 100 stepper units could handle 10,000 lines. Reliability was marginal (mechanical wear, misalignment), but no wage bill. Replaced manual exchanges over 30 years. The real innovation is replacing human labor with electromechanics. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: stepper motor and wiper-contact grid require precision mechanical steps]

nodes.name: Submarine telegraph cable
nodes.note: A copper core (signal), wrapped in gutta percha (insulator), wrapped in steel armour, laid on the ocean floor. PROBLEM: Gutta percha is unobtainable (tropical tree). SUBSTITUTE: Use rubber-impregnated cloth (expensive) or pitch-soaked jute, accepting higher leakage. The cable capacitance is enormous; signals attenuate and blur over 3000 km. Needs a relay every 500 km, but submersion makes access impossible. Solution: repeater amplifiers at each end only.

nodes.name: Superheterodyne receiver - fixed intermediate frequency design
nodes.note: Instead of amplifying the RF signal directly (hard at high frequencies), a mixer combines the received signal with a local oscillator, producing a difference frequency (intermediate frequency, typically 455 kHz or 10.7 MHz). Tuning changes only the local oscillator; the intermediate frequency is fixed and easy to amplify. This is the most important radio innovation after AM: it made high-gain, selective receivers practical. Nearly all radio since 1920 is superheterodyne.

nodes.name: Telegraph power supply - voltaic cells in series
nodes.note: Telegraph stations need reliable, large current (amps, not milliamps). A Daniell cell or Grove cell in series provides 1-2 volts. A telegraph key and relay need about 1 amp at 10-100 volts. The maintenance burden is high: cells need refilling, electrodes corrode, acid must be managed safely. This cost and complexity drives later adoption of central powerhouses.

nodes.name: Carbon microphone - pressure-to-resistance transducer
nodes.note: Sound waves move a diaphragm that presses down on loose carbon granules. Pressure changes resistance. A steady current through the carbon, modulated by this resistance change, creates a modulated signal that can be sent down a telegraph wire. The key: carbon is cheap, robust, and changes resistance reliably from 100 to 1000 ohms with pressure. Early telephone transmitters were simple and effective.

nodes.name: Diaphragm receiver - electromagnet hearing aid
nodes.note: A thin iron diaphragm is magnetized by an electromagnet. Modulated current in the coil varies the magnetic field, moving the diaphragm in and out, creating sound waves. No power source needed at the receiver (signal current from the microphone drives it). Early telephone receivers were just magnets and thin iron discs, very similar to telegraph sounders. The diaphragm must be flat enough and thin enough to vibrate freely at audio frequencies.

nodes.name: Manual switchboard exchange
nodes.note: A grid of copper jacks (one per subscriber line), with plug cords and a central battery supplying current to all lines. An operator plugs a caller's line into the called party's line, completing a circuit. The breakthrough: no longer does each person need a separate wire to every other person. A central office with 100 operator positions can switch 10,000 customers with 100 lines. Manual exchanges require hundreds of staff and are limited by operator speed (one plug per second).

nodes.name: Teleprinter - automated telegraph typing
nodes.note: Operator types on a keyboard (like a typewriter). Solenoids pull levers that position type wheels for each character, a hammer fires on command, the character prints on paper, and the whole sequence is transmitted as electrical pulses down the telegraph line. The receiving teleprinter receives the same pulses and reproduces each character. No skilled Morse operator needed; anyone who can type can use a teleprinter. Slower than Morse (40 words/minute vs. 100+), but usable by clerical staff. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: character wheel indexing mechanism needs mechanical precision]

nodes.name: Triode oscillator - audio and RF frequency synthesis
nodes.note: A triode with feedback can generate any frequency from audio (10 Hz) to microwave (1000 MHz), tuned by the LC circuit. The oscillation amplitude is limited by the triode's power supply and efficiency. Used in radio transmitters, local oscillators for superheterodyne receivers, and audio oscillators for music synthesis. The triode is THE electronic oscillator until solid-state transistors arrive. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: vacuum tube oscillator needs high vacuum for electron operation]

nodes.name: Trunk lines - long-distance telephone routes
nodes.note: Heavy-gauge copper wire strung on poles between cities, with loading coils every 2 km. A trunk line connects two exchanges, not individual subscribers. Calls are routed: local exchange A -> trunk to distant exchange B -> local delivery. The killer problem: telephone signals attenuate badly over distance. A 50 km trunk line needs repeater amplifiers every 15 km, which requires vacuum tubes (not available until 1915). Before that, trunk lines were limited to 50-100 km range. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Tuned LC circuit and resonance
nodes.note: An inductor (coil) and capacitor in series, tuned so that capacitive and inductive reactances cancel at a chosen frequency. At resonance, the impedance is minimum (current maximum), and the circuit selects only that frequency, rejecting others. This is THE solution to radio crowding: without tuning, all radio stations interfere. With tuning, each receiver selects one station and rejects the rest. Frequency = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). A variable capacitor lets listeners tune across the band.

nodes.name: Electronic camera tube (iconoscope) - real-time image capture
nodes.note: A vacuum tube where an electron beam scans a photosensitive mosaic (thousands of tiny silver-mica capacitors). Light on each capacitor charges it; the beam discharges each spot sequentially, producing a current proportional to light. This is a camera: it converts an optical image to an electrical signal suitable for transmission. The iconoscope was unreliable (mosaic damage, burn-in), but it launched electronic television and was the standard for decades. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e6 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: iconoscope tube requires very high vacuum to achieve usable photoemission]

nodes.name: Mechanical television scanning - early image transmission
nodes.note: A spinning disc with holes arranged in a spiral (Nipkow disc) scans an image line by line. Light from the scene passes through a hole onto a selenium photocell, which modulates current proportional to brightness. This signal is transmitted by radio; a receiver feeds it to a similar spinning disc, with light shining behind it, reconstructing the image on a screen. The whole system is mechanical, unreliable, and limited to about 30 lines of resolution. Electronic television replaced it by 1935. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: Nipkow disc hole pattern must be precise for image resolution]

nodes.name: Raster scan and synchronisation
nodes.note: The beam scans left-to-right (fast sweep), then retraces to the left (blanking), then drops one line down (slow sweep). It repeats 60 times per second (60 Hz frame rate), scanning 525 lines (NTSC) or 625 lines (PAL). At the receiver, an oscilloscope (CRT) must scan in exact synchronism. A sync pulse in the transmitted signal tells the receiver when each line begins and when each frame begins. Without tight synchronisation, the image tears and jitters. This is engineering at the microsecond level.

nodes.name: Vacuum tube computer - high-speed electronic switching
nodes.note: ENIAC (1945): 18,000 vacuum tubes, 150 kilowatts, does 5,000 additions per second (instead of 1 per second with relays). The tube acts as an electronic switch: no moving parts, microsecond speed. The killer limitation: reliability. Tubes fail constantly (one failure every 30 minutes). Maintenance requires replacing tubes and debugging. This drove the search for a smaller, more reliable switch: the transistor.

nodes.name: Pentode vacuum tube - suppressor grid output stage
nodes.note: A tetrode with a fifth electrode (suppressor grid, at cathode potential) that prevents secondary electrons from the anode reaching the screen. This was a problem in tetrodes (screen current wasted power). A pentode has higher efficiency and better linearity. It became the standard audio output tube and RF power tube from 1930 onward. Five or more grids became common in specialized tubes (hexode, heptode) for mixing and frequency conversion. nodes.name: Tetrode vacuum tube - screen grid amplifier
nodes.note: A triode with an added fourth electrode (screen grid), held at a positive but lower voltage than the anode. The screen shields the anode from the control grid, preventing feedback and allowing higher gain without oscillation. A tetrode is more stable and more powerful than a triode, better for RF amplifiers. The voltage between screen and cathode must be regulated, adding circuit complexity. By the 1930s, tetrodes replaced triodes in most high-power applications. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]
