nodes.name: Understanding and testing soil composition
nodes.note: Test soil pH, organic matter, and nutrient content via chemical analysis or simple tests. Informs liming, fertilizer, and crop choices. Precision farming based on data rather than guess.

nodes.name: Sourdough starter culture maintenance
nodes.note: Maintain a living culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in flour and water. Feed it regularly and use it to leaven bread. Improves flavor and digestibility compared to unleavened bread. Requires discipline but produces superior bread.

nodes.name: Sugar cane cultivation and juice extraction
nodes.note: Grow sugar cane in warm coastal regions, crush stalks with ox-powered mill to extract juice. Simmer juice to crystallize sugar. Imported from Mediterranean and later from tropical colonies. Labor-intensive but high value product.

nodes.name: Superphosphate from bones and sulfuric acid
nodes.note: React bone meal with sulfuric acid to convert insoluble phosphates into soluble form. More effective than guano but requires acid production and handling. Arrives in late agricultural revolution when industrialized.

nodes.name: Tea import and trade channels
nodes.note: Establish merchant contacts for tea via trade routes (by late Roman era via Parthia from China). Expensive, luxury item, consumed hot. Requires trade infrastructure and wealth. Demand creates mercantile networks.

nodes.name: Three-field crop rotation with fallowing
nodes.note: Grain, legume, fallow rotation sustains soil nitrogen and allows continuous cultivation on two-thirds of land; fallow fields provide grazing for animals, multiplying manure. Requires written record-keeping and community coordination.

nodes.name: Mechanical threshing machine
nodes.note: Flailed drum rotating against fixed comb beats grain from heads mechanically, replacing hand flailing. Powered by horses treading or pulled by oxen. Three to five fold increase in threshing speed. Multiplies bottleneck from threshing to grinding.

nodes.name: Tin plate cans for food preservation
nodes.note: Roll thin iron sheet and coat with tin to prevent rust and corrosion from acidic food. Seal with solder or lead. Can be sealed hot for sterilization without glass fragility. Requires rolling mill, tin coating process, and soldering skill. Cans are reusable if handled carefully.

nodes.name: Turnips as storable winter animal feed
nodes.note: High-yield root crop stores in cool cellars through winter, feeding oxen and sheep when pasture dies. Single biggest gain in animal husbandry: overwintered animals produce manure year-round and retain strength for spring ploughing and hauling. Revolutionary.

nodes.name: Oil extraction from seeds and olives
nodes.note: Press rapeseed, walnut, or sesame with mechanical screw press to extract oil for cooking and lamps. Olive oil already exists (tier 0). New seed crops provide additional supply. Oil keeps several months in sealed vessels.

nodes.name: Vinegar production via acetification
nodes.note: Pass fermented wine or weak ale through wood shavings and let acetic bacteria oxidize alcohol to acetic acid. Slower than heating but requires no energy. Preserves excess wine as vinegar for cooking and cleaning. Used medicinally as well.

nodes.name: Organized whaling industry for oil and meat
nodes.note: Organize fleets of whaleboats and processing ships to hunt large whales. Render whale blubber into oil for lamps (the best non-animal oil light). Whale meat is tough but provides protein. Dangerous work; whales fight back. Requires capital and international coordination. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Mechanical winnowing fan
nodes.note: Rotating fan or hand-cranked blower separates grain from chaff with controlled airstream. Manual winnowing baskets remain for small quantities, but the machine handles output from mechanical threshing. Driven by hand crank or powered by oxen.

nodes.name: Pure yeast culture isolation and maintenance
nodes.note: Isolate yeast strain from wild fermentation by serial dilution and propagation in sterile medium. Maintain culture in sealed glass vials. Enables reproducible beer and bread fermentation without wild cultures. Looks like alchemy; requires careful technique and documentation. nodes.note: Needs an oxy-hydrogen flame at roughly 1700-2000 C. nodes.name: Galena cat's whisker point-contact rectifier
nodes.note: A working semiconductor device in Rome, using mineral lead sulfide straight out of the mine and a springy wire. No purification, no doping, no vacuum, no theory. It is nearly free, it is a genuine rectifier, and it is the proof-of-concept that justifies a two-century programme to a sceptical patron. Build it the moment you have a cell and fine wire. It depends on the crude brine cell, not on the voltaic pile, which is what makes the year-three claim in 00_NONOBVIOUS_TRICKS actually true. nodes.name: Coordinate geometry and trigonometric tables
nodes.note: Hipparchus and Ptolemy already have chord tables, so this lands on prepared ground.

nodes.name: Germ theory of disease
nodes.note: The bead microscope makes this demonstrable rather than assertable, which is the whole difference. Galen's humoral theory is the obstacle and it is defended by the entire medical profession.

nodes.name: Germanium concentrate from flue dust and coal ash
nodes.note: Germanium is 1.6 ppm in the crust and essentially never occurs as its own workable ore in reach. Zinc flue dust and certain coal ashes are the realistic sources. The spectroscope is how you find it at all: without emission spectroscopy you would be searching blind for an element nobody has ever seen.

nodes.name: Single-bead microscope
nodes.note: Cost is trivial and the payoff is germ theory, cell biology and a demonstration nobody can dismiss. Build this in your first year. Van Leeuwenhoek out-resolved compound microscopes with it for fifty years.

nodes.name: Borosilicate glass
nodes.note: Needs boron. The Larderello fumaroles in Tuscany emit boric acid and are inside the Empire, which is a genuinely lucky break if it holds; verify on arrival before planning around it. Low thermal expansion is the difference between a laboratory and a pile of broken retorts. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Corned gunpowder
nodes.note: 75/15/10 by mass, and the ratio is worthless without corning: wet the mix, press the cake, break it into grains, sieve. OPTIONAL AND DANGEROUS. It buys imperial favour instantly and it makes every future usurper more dangerous, including during the Third Century Crisis when you most need the Empire to hold. Recommended: develop the chemistry, withhold the corning, and keep it as a survival card.

nodes.name: Regenerative and forced-draught furnaces to 1600 C+
nodes.note: Siemens regenerative preheat recycles flue heat into the incoming air and is the cheapest route past what charcoal and a bellows can do. Gate on fused quartz, on high-grade steel, and on most of Module 50. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. nodes.name: Attar of roses
nodes.note: Distilled rose oil (4 kg of petals for 1 g of oil). Extremely expensive and high-margin. Attar is one of the best early revenue products: small weight, non-perishable, high demand from the wealthy. Bulgarian and Persian atar dominate the market.

nodes.name: Bath with piped hot water
nodes.note: A boiler (steam-driven or later electric) supplies hot water on demand. Luxurious; middle-class homes gain hot water later than wealthy houses. Requires pressurised pipes and heating infrastructure. Modern thermostatic mixing valves prevent scalding.

nodes.name: Board games, dice games, and pieces
nodes.note: Latrunculi (small stones on a board), duodecim scripta (twelve marks, ancestor of backgammon), and knucklebones for gaming. Dice are carved bone or stone.

nodes.name: Button with eyelet
nodes.note: Buttons exist in Rome but are rare and made of stone or bone. The eyelet (sewn loop) adds cost. Horn buttons become viable later with better tools. Buttons displace expensive brooches, freeing wealth.

nodes.name: Beeswax candle
nodes.note: Expensive, clean-burning, fragrant. Beeswax is a byproduct of honey extraction and remains expensive through the early modern period.

nodes.name: Tallow candle
nodes.note: Cheap animal-fat candles; smoky and foul-smelling but accessible to the poor. Tallow is rendered from beef and mutton fat.

nodes.name: Carpet sweeper
nodes.note: Wheeled frame with rotating brush underneath. Push it across carpet to collect dust and lint. No electricity needed. Precedes vacuum cleaners; faster than hand-brushing. Carpet sweepers are labour-replacing and displace sweeping servants. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Cosmetics with safety warnings
nodes.note: Once germ theory and toxicology establish that white lead causes chronic poisoning, cosmetics reformulate. Lead face paint is phased out; zinc oxide and iron oxides replace it. Labels warn of hazards. Modern cosmetics prioritise safety and truthful marketing. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Roman cosmetics
nodes.note: Powders, kohl eyeliner, rouge, and white lead face paint (cerussa). The white lead is cosmetically effective but chronically poisoning users. No warning label exists.

nodes.name: Deodorant
nodes.note: Alum or zinc oxide in a fat or powder base. Alum acts as an astringent, reducing sweat and odour. Roman use of alum for textiles; applied to skin for personal use. Modern antiperspirants require aluminium chloride (20th century).

nodes.name: Dishwasher, mechanical and electric
nodes.note: Cochran's 1886 machine uses pressurised water spray, hot water, and soap. Requires a pressurised water supply (pump), a heat source (steam or electric), and a motor. Hot water and soap do most of the work; the machine's innovation is automation and pressure. Kitchen staff is displaced.

nodes.name: Fashion doll with clothing sets
nodes.note: Articulated wooden or bisque doll with interchangeable clothing. Allows girls to dress dolls in fashionable gowns. Drives textile consumption and toy industry growth. Later porcelain and plastic dolls command higher prices; bisque allows fine detail.

nodes.name: Double glazing (two panes)
nodes.note: Two panes of glass with an air gap reduces heat loss by half. Expensive to produce and install; assembly requires careful spacing and lead frame. Widespread only in the 18th-19th centuries as glass prices fall.

nodes.name: Electric fan for air circulation
nodes.note: Small electric motor drives a blade assembly. Expensive initially; prices fall with mass production. Rome would value this enormously in a Mediterranean summer; ceiling punkah fans pulled by servants are the low-tech precursor.

nodes.name: Electric lighting in home
nodes.note: Incandescent bulbs (Edison carbon, then tungsten filament) or arc lamps. Grid electricity required. Replaces gas lamps and kerosene. Cost per lumen falls; brightness increases. Urban electrification spreads from 1880s onward. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: incandescent filament requires vacuum to prevent oxidation]

nodes.name: Eraser, breadcrumb substitute
nodes.note: Breadcrumbs (white bread preferred) erase pencil marks by mechanical abrasion. Later rubber erasers require natural rubber, which is UNOBTAINABLE. Breadcrumb remains the substitute through the 19th century in resource-limited settings.

nodes.name: Fireplace and chimney
nodes.note: Rome never develops the chimney. The innovation is the flue and draft that draws smoke out of a room while allowing air intake from below. Transforms cold-weather living. Early chimneys are smoky and dangerous; the design improves over centuries.

nodes.name: Flush latrine with running water
nodes.note: Rome has flush latrines connected to running water and sewers, but lacks the water trap. Sewer gas backs up into the house at night when flow stops. This is the fatal gap.

nodes.name: Flush toilet with S-bend water trap
nodes.note: The water trap is the non-obvious critical innovation: standing water in an S-bend or U-bend below the bowl blocks sewer gas from backing into the house. Crapper patents an improved design in 1884. Modern plumbing code mandates traps.

nodes.name: Fountain pen
nodes.note: Ink reservoir under the nib, with capillary feed. Early designs leak; improved feeds (Waterman, Parker) in the 1880s fix this. Replaces dip pens and quills. Refillable or cartridge designs follow; mass production drives prices down.

nodes.name: Wooden furniture
nodes.note: Chairs, tables, beds, and chests. Quality varies from crude to fine (imported citrus wood). Beds are typically frames with rope supports, no springs.

nodes.name: Gas lamp and gasolier
nodes.note: Coal-gas (coke-oven gas) piped to rooms. Brighter than oil lamps but smoky and dangerous (carbon monoxide, explosions). Gas lighting spreads in cities; rural areas remain oil-lit for decades. Gasolier chandeliers replace candles in urban mansions.

nodes.name: Glass windows, wealthy houses
nodes.note: Rare and expensive. Glassblowing technology exists, but glass remains thick, poorly transparent, and valuable. Most windows are oil-paper or shutters.

nodes.name: Central heating by hot water radiator
nodes.note: Boiler in basement or furnace room heats water, which circulates through cast-iron radiators in all rooms. Replaces fireplaces and central stove heating. Enables uniform comfort; transforms house design. Requires piping, a circulating pump, and constant fuel supply.

nodes.name: Hypocaust underfloor heating
nodes.note: Hot air from a furnace flows through hollow spaces beneath the floor. Expensive; only wealthy houses and public baths use it. Rome never develops the chimney, so room heating otherwise requires a brazier and open flame. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Jigsaw puzzle
nodes.note: Hand-cut wooden jigsaw (using a saw, hence the name). Early puzzles are mounted hand-coloured prints glued to wood, then sawn into interlocking pieces. Expensive and educational for wealthy families.

nodes.name: Kitchen range (cast iron)
nodes.note: A fireplace-integrated cooking structure with a hot surface (cooking plate) and an oven. Cast iron conducts heat evenly. Requires blast furnace for casting; transforms cooking from dangling pots over flames. Labour-displacing for kitchen servants (negative gov).

nodes.name: Argand oil lamp
nodes.note: The flat circular wick and glass chimney allow air circulation from both sides of the flame, increasing brightness 3x over simple lamps. The chimney creates draft, keeping the flame in the hot zone. Oil consumption stays the same; light output soars.

nodes.name: Kerosene lamp
nodes.note: Kerosene (paraffin) burns hotter and cleaner than whale oil or plant oil. Brighter than Argand lamps with less smoke. Requires refined petroleum; supply depends on oil fields and distillation capacity.

nodes.name: Latrine water trap (S-bend)
nodes.note: The water trap is the critical innovation: standing water in an S-bend or U-bend below the toilet bowl blocks sewer gas from backing into the house. Non-obvious but essential for sanitary plumbing. Rome discovers this late or not at all in the West.

nodes.name: Lead and ceramic plumbing
nodes.note: Rome masters lead pipe-making and ceramic drainage. The lead slowly poisons users; Rome's elite show signs of lead poisoning but attribute it to other causes.

nodes.name: Locks and keys
nodes.note: Pin-tumbler locks exist in Egypt; Rome develops excellent examples in bronze and iron. Locks are expensive and a sign of wealth (or slavery).

nodes.name: Mangle and wringer
nodes.note: Paired hard rollers (wood or stone) squeeze water from cloth under pressure. Early mangling flattens linen; later wringer versions extract water faster. Eliminates the wringing-by-hand step; hand-wringer maids face unemployment.

nodes.name: Friction matches
nodes.note: White phosphorus matches ignite easily but cause phosphorus necrosis (rotting jawbone) in workers from chronic exposure. Safety matches use red phosphorus instead, less toxic. Early matches are dangerous to makers and users alike.

nodes.name: Mechanical clock for home
nodes.note: Escapement mechanism converts continuous power (falling weight or spring) into regulated ticks. Medieval clocks are weight-driven with iron verge escapement; later designs use springs. Accuracy improves from hours to minutes as escapements advance.

nodes.name: Metronome
nodes.note: Pendulum-driven clock ticking at adjustable rates for musical practice. Inverted design pivots the weight on a rod. Musicians find it essential; composers use metronome markings to standardise tempo. Early metronomes are wooden; later all-metal designs are more durable.

nodes.name: Mirror, polished bronze
nodes.note: Polished bronze reflects poorly (70-80% at best) and tarnishes. Small, expensive, and slowly replaced by silvered glass mirrors.

nodes.name: Mirror, silvered glass
nodes.note: Mercury and tin amalgam fused to glass back creates a reflective layer (90%+ vs 70% for bronze). Expensive and technically demanding; production moves to Venice in the 13th century. Frames are precious metal or fine wood.

nodes.name: Musical instruments
nodes.note: Lyres, kitharas, flutes, Pan pipes, and percussion. All handmade; quality varies by maker. String instruments require catgut or sinew from animals.

nodes.name: Oil lamp, simple
nodes.note: Rome has simple clay and bronze oil lamps, burning olive oil or animal fat. The innovation ahead is the flat wick and glass chimney, which doubles brightness.

nodes.name: Pencil, graphite in wood
nodes.note: Graphite pencils arrive in the 16th century after graphite discovery in Cumberland. Early designs slot graphite into wood holders; later hexagonal wood casing is carved around it. Graphite is cheap once located; supply is the constraint.

nodes.name: Perfume, distilled alcohol base
nodes.note: Alcohol dissolves and carries fragrance far better than fat alone. Volatile alcohols evaporate, leaving scent on skin and clothes. Concentrated distilled perfumes (attar) command high prices and excellent margins. The innovation is distillation, not enfleurage.

nodes.name: Perfume by enfleurage
nodes.note: Flower petals are laid on cold fat, which absorbs fragrance. Repeated; expensive and used by the wealthy. Yields poor revenue; the innovation is distillation for concentrates.

nodes.name: Piano with hammer action
nodes.note: Struck strings with escapement mechanism allowing rapid re-strike. Cristofori invents the hammer action around 1700, replacing plucked harpsichords. Touche and dynamic range enable entirely new music. Expensive; requires years of training to play well.

nodes.name: Playing cards, printed
nodes.note: Woodcut or engraved cards printed in volume. Early printed decks (15th century) are hand-coloured. Standardised designs (Italian, Spanish, French suits) emerge later. Cards were originally hand-painted and very expensive.

nodes.name: Pocket watch
nodes.note: Miniaturized spring-driven mechanism with balance wheel (spiral spring regulating oscillation). Requires high precision machining and jeweled pivots to reduce friction. Early watches lose 5-10 minutes per day; later escapements improve accuracy.

nodes.name: Pressure cooker (Papin's digester)
nodes.note: A sealed vessel where steam pressure raises water boiling point, accelerating cooking 3x. Papin invents the digester in 1679 to demonstrate steam power; it becomes both a cooking device AND the conceptual ancestor of the steam engine. Requires safety valve.

nodes.name: Printed books for home
nodes.note: Printed volumes replace hand-copied manuscripts. Early books are expensive; gradually price falls as standardisation and competition reduce costs. Literacy spreads; libraries become personal, not institutional.

nodes.name: Public bath (thermae)
nodes.note: The thermae are social centers with heated water pools, caldarium and frigidarium. Rome's public hygiene infrastructure is remarkable for its era; yet most private homes lack hot water.

nodes.name: Ceiling punkah, servant-pulled
nodes.note: A large cloth fan suspended from the ceiling, pulled by a cord to and fro by a servant. Provides air circulation and cooling in hot climates. Entirely mechanical and labour-intensive; electric fans are the obvious 19th-century replacement.

nodes.name: Refrigeration, mechanical ice machine
nodes.note: Ammonia or ether evaporation in a compressor cools an ice chamber. Requires a steam engine to drive the compressor. Early mechanical ice-makers (Carve, 1850s) free wealthy households from dependence on natural ice harvesting and storage.

nodes.name: Home refrigerator, electric
nodes.note: Domestic refrigerator with electric compressor. Freon (CFC) replaces ammonia for safety (1930s). Standard feature in wealthy homes by 1950s; middle-class penetration spreads with electrification and price falls. Transforms food preservation and cooking.

nodes.name: Safety pin
nodes.note: Bent iron wire with a catch. Simpler than brooches and more secure for fastening cloth or diapers. Mass production requires drawn wire and stamping, both later innovations.

nodes.name: Safety razor
nodes.note: Replaceable blade held at a fixed angle in a handle guard, preventing deep cuts. Earlier straight razors require stropping and honing; safety razors are simpler for users. Gillette disposable blades (early 1900s) create a consumable product with huge margins.

nodes.name: Sewer separated from stormwater drain
nodes.note: Sewage and rain runoff follow separate pipes to prevent sewage backup during storms. Public health innovation; requires city-scale investment. Many 19th-century cities combine sewers (causing problems); separation is a later upgrade. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Sewing machine, hand-crank
nodes.note: Reciprocating needle driven by crank mechanism. Howe and Singer commercialize sewing machines in the 1850s; hand-crank models precede treadle and electric drives. Stitches much faster than hand-sewing; domestic servants' value plummets.

nodes.name: Shampoo, soap-based
nodes.note: Soap solution with perfume. Romans wash hair with lye (harsh) or oil. Soap-based shampoo is gentle and effective. Liquid and powdered forms compete; bars arrive later. Fragrance matters for premium products.

nodes.name: Hard soap, sapo
nodes.note: Hot saponification of animal fat and plant oil with caustic lye, producing hard soap. Rome lacks this; soap is invented in the Eastern Mediterranean around 6th century. Labour-intensive but small-scale.

nodes.name: Spectacles, corrective lenses
nodes.note: Convex lenses for presbyopia (age-related farsightedness) arrive around 1300. Concave lenses for myopia come later. The hinge and bridge are crafted from brass. Spectacles are luxury goods until mass production.

nodes.name: Sprung mattress
nodes.note: Coiled iron springs in a wood frame topped with ticking and stuffing (wool, horsehair, or coconut fiber). Dramatically more comfortable than rope-frame beds. Requires drawn wire and coil-forming tools. Mass production follows industrial tooling.

nodes.name: Enclosed stove
nodes.note: A metal or ceramic box with fire inside, heating room air by radiation and conduction. More efficient than open fireplace because less heat escapes up the chimney. Requires cast iron or tile manufacture. [FIXED after independent audit: it consumed 40 kg of cast iron at tier 1. There is no cast iron in the Roman West; it needs the blast furnace and cannot be a cheap early win.]

nodes.name: Toothbrush
nodes.note: Bone or wood handle with bristles of horsehair or bamboo fiber. Romans use twigs and charcoal powder for dental cleaning. The toothbrush format is luxury; mass adoption requires cheap bristles and handles.

nodes.name: Toothpaste, commercial formulation
nodes.note: Soap base with abrasive chalk or pumice powder, flavoured. Early toothpastes are gritty; fluoride is added in the 1950s. Toothbrushes + paste replace charcoal and salt rubbing. Marketing drives adoption; modern formulations include whiteners and stain removers.

nodes.name: Toys and dolls
nodes.note: Carved wooden dolls with jointed limbs or cloth bodies. Lead and tin soldiers for boys; fashion dolls for girls. Decoration and articulation increase cost. Toys become a significant retail category in the 18th and 19th centuries.

nodes.name: Umbrella
nodes.note: Wood frame with linen canopy. Rome and later cultures have parasols (sun protection); rain umbrellas arrive in northern Europe around 1500s. Widespread adoption requires industrial metal frames and waterproof cotton textiles.

nodes.name: Vacuum cleaner
nodes.note: Electric motor drives a suction fan that pulls dirt through a cloth bag filter. Replaces carpet sweepers and hand-brushing entirely. Servants become redundant. Cord length and motor noise are early limitations; wireless and quiet models come later. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Vacuum flask, thermos
nodes.note: Double-walled glass with vacuum between walls and silvered inner surface. Dewar invents it in 1892 for laboratory use; commercial thermos bottles follow. Keeps hot drinks hot for hours; cold drinks cold. Expensive; mass production eventually lowers cost.

nodes.name: Washing machine, electric-powered
nodes.note: Motor-driven drum or agitator. No cranking required. Faster cycles, cooler operation, less wear on fabric. Laundry becomes a household task rather than a full-time servant job. Early motors are noisy and prone to breakage; reliability improves.

nodes.name: Washing machine, hand-powered
nodes.note: A wooden or metal tub with paddles or rollers rotated by crank. Hot soapy water and mechanical action replace hours of hand-scrubbing. Laundry maids become surplus; wealthy households buy machines rather than slaves.

nodes.name: Zip fastener
nodes.note: Interlocking teeth or loops fastened by sliding slider. Whitcomb L. Judson invents the 'clasp locker' in 1891; Gideon Sundback perfects the modern zip in 1913. Requires precision stamping and assembly. Replaces buttons for boots and jackets.

nodes.name: Rigid padded horse collar, whippletree, nailed horseshoe
nodes.note: Roman throat-and-girth harness chokes a horse under heavy draught. The size of the improvement is disputed in modern scholarship, so claim a real but modest gain, not the old textbook figure of four times. Politically the safest technology in this document: it feeds people and moves army supplies and threatens nobody.

nodes.name: Hot air balloon for observation
nodes.note: Low technology, moderate cost, high spectacle, and the State wants it for siege observation and signalling. Also one of the fastest ways to be accused of sorcery, so fly it first for the army with the governor watching, never privately at night. Linen sized with oil is the envelope; Rome has excellent sailcloth. [FIXED after independent audit: paper and distilled spirits were listed and neither is load-bearing. An oiled linen envelope over a wood fire needs Roman sailcloth and oil, both tier 0.]

nodes.name: Hydrochloric acid and aqua regia
nodes.note: Salt plus oil of vitriol. The salt-cake residue is the feedstock for the Leblanc soda process, so nothing is wasted. Aqua regia dissolves gold, which is a demonstration that will terrify the mint and delight your patron; use it carefully.

nodes.name: Hydrofluoric acid
nodes.note: Lead or wax vessels only; it eats glass, which is also what makes it useful. Extreme and insidious toxicity: it penetrates skin painlessly, seeks calcium in bone, and kills hours later. You have no calcium gluconate. Treat it as the most dangerous substance in your laboratory.

nodes.name: Establish the Alexandrian physician-philosopher persona
nodes.note: Buy books, a house, clothes, a Greek freedman secretary, and a reputation for piety. Reduces all future suspicion.

nodes.name: Adiabatic demagnetization apparatus
nodes.note: Cooling power limited by entropy of spin system; achieves 0.01 K from starting 1 K. Requires precision heat switches and careful thermometry.

nodes.name: Aerial camera: gyro-stabilized mount
nodes.note: Focal length and shutter speed set by altitude and aircraft speed; sidelap and endlap of frames ensures stereoscopic overlap.

nodes.name: Alidade: sight ruler for plane table
nodes.note: Telescope provides magnification and collimation; eyepiece must be designed to give clear view of distant point while keeping edge of ruler in sight.

nodes.name: Analytical balance: equal arm
nodes.note: Sensitivity depends on balance arm length and pivot sharpness. Rider on beam allows fractional weights.

nodes.name: Aneroid pressure gauge: evacuated bellows
nodes.note: No liquid; portable and rugged. Accuracy 2-3 percent typical for barometers. Frequency response for recording dynamic pressure is much better than mercury column.

nodes.name: Antireflection coating single wavelength
nodes.note: A single quarter-wave layer of the right index nearly halves losses at design wavelength; this doubled the effective aperture of telescopes and microscopes. Multicoatings extend bandwidth. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Artificial horizon: bubble level
nodes.note: Bubble much more visible than faint horizon at twilight; altitude star not twice-the-bubble correction because half the motion needed.

nodes.name: Balance spring: spiral hairspring
nodes.note: Isochronism (period independent of amplitude) requires specific curve shape. Compensation for thermal expansion uses bimetallic rim. Precision chronometer rates to seconds per week.

nodes.name: Baseline measurement: apparatus and calibration
nodes.note: Baseline length accuracy sets precision of entire survey; errors in baseline are magnified by triangulation. Careful temperature and tension control during measurement.

nodes.name: Beam splitter dichroic mirror
nodes.note: Evaporated metal films or dielectric coatings create partial reflectors. Dichroic effect (color-dependent reflection) requires interference; multilayer coatings achieve sharp wavelength separation. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Bolometer: blackened platinum resistance
nodes.note: Time constant must be < 0.1 second to follow modulated light; thermal mass vs sensitivity tradeoff.

nodes.name: Bourdon tube pressure gauge
nodes.note: Works up to 1000 bar with steel tubes. Nonlinearity and hysteresis are issues; C-tube, spiral, and helical forms trade span for linearity.

nodes.name: Cassegrain reflector telescope
nodes.note: Effective focal length can be very large; physical tube is short and stiff. Secondary blockage costs light; useful for high magnification and spectroscopy. Cassegrain and Gregorian differ in secondary curvature (convex vs concave). [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Measuring chain: steel links
nodes.note: Standardization of link length was critical; earlier chains varied between regions. Stretch under tension; calibration against standard required.

nodes.name: Chronometer rate observation
nodes.note: Greenwich time determined independently; comparison over several days averages out daily variations.

nodes.name: Claude cycle: air liquefaction with work extraction
nodes.note: Expander is efficiency gain: gas does external work while cooling. Allows higher input temperature before liquefaction. Industrial version dominates after 1920.

nodes.name: Cloud chamber: Wilson expansion chamber
nodes.note: The kernel: ions seed condensation; alcohol vapor becomes cloud along particle tracks. Photographs record tracks: alpha particles thick and straight, beta particles thin and curved, gamma rays occasional electron recoils.

nodes.name: Condenser: sub-stage aperture control
nodes.note: Iris diaphragm controls numerical aperture of illumination; matching it to objective NA maximizes contrast and depth of field. Substage height adjustment focuses the light.

nodes.name: Cooke triplet photographic lens
nodes.note: Symmetry means left and right aberrations cancel; the central meniscus acts as field flattener. Astigmatism and coma are small across a wide field. This design persisted unchanged into the 1970s. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Creep furnace: constant load at high temperature
nodes.note: Creep rate accelerates with time; elongation logarithmic or power-law in time. Material structure changes under stress; microstructure analysis explains rate.

nodes.name: Cryostat: dewar flask double-walled
nodes.note: Vacuum insulation much better than solid foam (which didn't exist); radiation baffle reduces heat transfer. Silver coating reflects infrared.

nodes.name: Cyclotron accelerator: magnet and RF coil
nodes.note: Synchronism between particle orbit period and RF frequency is automatic; frequency stays constant as particle spirals outward and gains energy. Enables 10-20 MeV beam, impossible with accelerators.

nodes.name: Dark field condenser: oblique illumination
nodes.note: Unstained samples are nearly invisible in brightfield because they scatter little and absorb little. Dark field cuts direct light; scattered light from particles appears bright on black background. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Diffraction grating: ruled reflective
nodes.note: The kernel: fine pitch (20,000-50,000 lines/inch) requires a master screw with error < 0.1 micron over its full length. Groove uniformity is critical; defects scatter light.

nodes.name: Doublet achromatic lens
nodes.note: Red and blue light have different refractive indices; flint glass bends them oppositely. A concave flint inside a convex crown cancels the dispersion while keeping convergence. Cemented joint must be optically contacted. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Echo sounder: acoustic depth finder
nodes.note: Sound speed in water 1500 m/s; modern instruments use frequency sweep. Early spark sounders were intermittent; later continuous recordings possible.

nodes.name: Electron diffraction camera: LEED
nodes.note: Electron wavelength < 1 Angstrom; very small diffraction angles. Phosphor screen detects diffraction pattern. Low-energy electrons (50-500 eV) scatter strongly from top layers. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Electron microscope: column and lens assembly
nodes.note: Electrons have wavelength 1000x smaller than visible light; 2000x higher resolution. Requires high vacuum, high voltage (50-100 kV), and magnetic lenses. Sample preparation and observation technique are complex. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Electron source: heated cathode
nodes.note: Filament life determined by evaporation rate; higher temperature gives more current but shorter life. Wehnelt cap focuses emission. Tungsten chosen for high melting point and low evaporation. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Electroscope: gold leaf detector
nodes.note: Leaf must be thin and light; damped oscillation with critical damping optimal. Used to detect radioactivity by ionisation of air.

nodes.name: Eyepiece: Erfle wide field
nodes.note: The kernel: five elements can be tuned to flatten field and correct all aberrations across a wide angle. Previous 3-4 element designs limited to 50 degrees. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Eyepiece: Huygens
nodes.note: Lens separation equals the sum of focal lengths; real image forms between elements. Long eye relief and wide field for low powers; chromatic aberration high.

nodes.name: Eyepiece: Kellner
nodes.note: Achromatic eyelens corrects the Huygens problem; large field of view; good eye relief. Became standard for 19th-century microscopes.

nodes.name: Eyepiece: Orthoscopic
nodes.note: All aberrations well corrected; distortion nearly absent. Best planetary observation eyepiece until the Erfle; good for telescopes of any focal ratio. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Eyepiece: Ramsden
nodes.note: Real image forms between lenses; reticle can be placed there. Simpler than Kellner and Huygens. Used for surveying instruments where a graticule is essential.

nodes.name: Fatigue test machine: rotating bending
nodes.note: Specimen rotates through constant bending moment; every point sees same stress cycle. Failure always begins at stress concentration; S-N curve (stress vs cycle count) defines fatigue limit.

nodes.name: Gas thermometry: absolute temperature scale
nodes.note: Kernel is that gas pressure or volume change is linear with absolute temperature. Primary standard used to calibrate mercury and resistance thermometers. Requires careful control of gas amount.

nodes.name: Geiger-Müller counter: proportional region
nodes.note: Pulse output independent of input energy (above threshold); excellent counting efficiency. Dead time 100-300 microseconds limits count rate.

nodes.name: Geodetic survey apparatus complete
nodes.note: National survey requires coordination of many teams over years. Control points must be stable; pillar stability checked periodically.

nodes.name: Gravimeter: spring balance portable
nodes.note: Gravity variation 0.3 percent across Earth; instrument detects 0.01 percent. Thermal compensation by bimetallic strips essential.

nodes.name: Gyro horizon: attitude indicator
nodes.note: Gyroscopic inertia holds attitude; erection mechanism cancels slow drift. Precession rate ~ mass imbalance * gravity.

nodes.name: Gyrocompass: spinning rotor
nodes.note: North-seeking property is automatic once spinning; no magnetic compass needed. Gyroscopic inertia suppresses ship's motion effects.

nodes.name: High pressure cell: diamond anvil or autoclave
nodes.note: Diamond anvil for optics; hardened steel for liquids. Seal design and pressure measurement calibration are critical.

nodes.name: Immersion objective: oil lens
nodes.note: Oil (n=1.52) matches glass closely; light bent less at air-glass interface, allowing higher NA. Allows numerical apertures above 1.0, finer resolution. Standard for 1000x magnification. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Interference filter coated
nodes.note: Alternating high and low index layers create destructive interference outside the pass band. Extremely narrow passbands possible; sharp edges. Requires vacuum evaporation and strict thickness control. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Interferometer: Fabry-Pérot etalon
nodes.note: Multiple reflections enhance sharpness; useful for spectral lines separated by nanometers. Parallelism and surface flatness required to better than 0.1 wavelength.

nodes.name: Interferometer: Michelson
nodes.note: Adjustment is finicky; mirror angle must be within microradians. Fringe visibility depends on path difference being small. Used to measure length by counting fringes as mirror moves.

nodes.name: Ionisation chamber: gas filled detector
nodes.note: Signal proportional to energy; used to measure radiation intensity. Electrode spacing and voltage fixed; gas filling critical.

nodes.name: Joule-Thomson expansion valve
nodes.note: Cooling power depends on entering pressure and temperature; for most gases, Joule-Thomson coefficient is positive (cooling). Throttle design (capillary or sintered restriction) controls expansion.

nodes.name: Linde cycle: expansion engine and recuperator
nodes.note: Each stage drops temperature; tail gas cools incoming gas. Requires pure, dry air (CO2 and water freeze out). Liquefaction rate 1-10 liters/hour.

nodes.name: Magnetometer: sensitive compass
nodes.note: Temperature and vibration affect needle; declination charts required for navigation. Magnetic latitude determines angle of dip.

nodes.name: Marine chronometer: spring balance compensation
nodes.note: Chronometer rate (gain/loss per day) must be < 1 second; observed rate used to correct while at sea. Ship's motion and temperature gradients are constant challenges.

nodes.name: Mass spectrograph: deflection
nodes.note: Radius of curvature proportional to mass; spot positions give isotope masses and abundances. Requires high vacuum, stable voltage, and precise ion source.

nodes.name: McLeod gauge: compression manometer
nodes.note: Measures 1 to 1e-4 torr. Requires careful construction and leveling. Provides absolute calibration for other gauges.

nodes.name: Mercury barometer: column height
nodes.note: Standard atmosphere = 760 mm Hg at 0 C and 45 degrees latitude. Correction for latitude, temperature, and mercury density variation required for precision.

nodes.name: Microbalance: quartz oscillator frequency shift
nodes.note: Sensitivity nanogram range; frequency stable to 0.01 Hz. Used for film thickness measurement and chemical detection.

nodes.name: Microtome: rotary feed
nodes.note: Screw advance per rotation is fixed and precise; blade remains stationary; hundreds of consecutive micron-thick sections from one specimen. Required for neuroanatomy. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Microtome: sliding blade
nodes.note: Tissue freezes on stage; blade slides at angle; spring deflection determines slice thickness. 50-200 micron sections for hand microscopy.

nodes.name: Newtonian reflector telescope
nodes.note: Simple and cheap; no secondary mirror obstruction. Off-axis aberrations manageable up to f/4. The flat (Newtonian diagonal) must be very small (5-15% blockage) and precisely angled. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Optical comparator: magnified shadow projection
nodes.note: Magnification 10x-100x; edge sharpness depends on light source coherence. Faster than microscope for many parts; no contact with surface.

nodes.name: Orifice plate: differential pressure flow measurement
nodes.note: Cheap and simple; but discharge coefficient depends on Reynolds number and geometry. Pressure recovery poor.

nodes.name: Oscilloscope: cathode ray tube display
nodes.note: Deflection sensitivity and time-base linearity are critical. Phosphor persistence determines trace brightness and flicker. High voltage supply must be stable.

nodes.name: Petzval portrait lens
nodes.note: The kernel is that a convergent group behind the aperture stop naturally focuses field curvature to a curved surface, which is acceptable for portrait work where central sharpness matters. f/3.5 was revolutionary for 1840s photography. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: pH meter: glass electrode potentiometer
nodes.note: Glass electrode potential is logarithmic in [H+]; high impedance requires vacuum tube amplifier. Slope and zero-point calibration against known buffers essential.

nodes.name: Phase contrast objective and annuli
nodes.note: Transparent samples have tiny amplitude differences that the eye cannot detect; phase differences are huge but invisible. Phase plate retards diffracted light; interference makes phases visible. Revolutionary for biology. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Photocell: vacuum photoelectric
nodes.note: Quantum efficiency 5-10 percent; spectral response depends on cathode material. Cathode sensitivity to residual gas vapor is problem. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Photogrammetry: stereoscope and comparator
nodes.note: Optical axis separation and focal length known from calibration; parallax difference = height difference. Systematic errors from camera tilt must be corrected.

nodes.name: Photographic emulsion detector
nodes.note: Emulsion provides permanent record and extreme position resolution (< 1 micron). Quantitative analysis requires careful grain counting and calibration against known energies.

nodes.name: Photometer: visual brightness comparison
nodes.note: Standard candle defined (1 candela); distance squared from unknown source matched to known distance from standard.

nodes.name: Photomultiplier: secondary emission cascade
nodes.note: Gain 10^6 typical; enables detection of single photons. Dark current (thermioni emission) limits low-light sensitivity; cooling essential.

nodes.name: Pitot tube: total and static pressure difference
nodes.note: Yields velocity directly from pressure difference. Sensitive to flow angularity; probe design critical for accuracy in turbulent flow.

nodes.name: Plane table: graphical surveying
nodes.note: Immediate feedback on map; errors caught in field. Slope corrections and magnetic declination must be handled separately. Useful for small-area mapping.

nodes.name: Polariser: Nicol prism calcite
nodes.note: Natural birefringence of calcite; extraordinary ray and ordinary ray have different refractive indices. Carving and cementing a prism at the Brewster angle transmits one, reflects the other internally. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Precise levelling: rod and staff
nodes.note: Backsight and foresight must balance to third decimal place; systematic errors (refraction, curvature) cancel only if distances equal. Levelling bench marks established every km.

nodes.name: Telescope primary mirror parabolic
nodes.note: The parabola corrects spherical aberration; a sphere would have offaxis focus. Speculums corrode; silvered glass requires maintenance every few years. Precision to 0.1 wavelength required for good focus. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Prism: Amici roof prism
nodes.note: The roof angle must be precisely 90 degrees; any error causes the two roof faces to produce a split image. Coating the roof faces was later improvement. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Prism: Porro prism binocular
nodes.note: Porro gives longer eyepiece separation than roof; better for binoculars where one prism arm doubles as the barrel. Internal reflections must not degrade contrast. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Quartz resonator: piezoelectric oscillator
nodes.note: Frequency stability better than 1 part per million per year. Replaced tuning forks for precise timekeeping. Frequency depends on crystal cut and temperature.

nodes.name: Radio direction finder: loop antenna
nodes.note: Dipole pattern of loop gives sharp null; bearing is direction of null. 180-degree ambiguity resolved by sense antenna or manual observation.

nodes.name: Resistance thermometer: platinum RTD
nodes.note: Accuracy better than thermocouple; slow response. Industrial platinum RTDs have 0.1 C accuracy. Insulation resistance can limit precision.

nodes.name: Reticle: crosshair or graticule
nodes.note: Etching with diamond point or photographic reduction defines the graticule. Registration of crosshairs to optical axis is the precision step.

nodes.name: Ruling engine: precision screw diamond
nodes.note: The most demanding instrument before 1950. Screw must advance uniformly against spring loading; spindle runout < 0.5 micron over 200 mm stroke. Most sophisticated mechanical device of its era.

nodes.name: Schmidt corrector plate
nodes.note: A spherical mirror has severe offaxis aberrations. A thin aspheric plate near the center of curvature corrects all of them. Requires precision figuring to waves; small deviations ruin image. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Scintillation detector: crystal and photomultiplier
nodes.note: Energy resolution better than Geiger counter; pulse height gives particle energy. Decay time of scintillation limits count rate (1000 cps typical).

nodes.name: Sextant: arc and optical system
nodes.note: Optical path via fixed and moving mirrors allows 60 degree field in 120 degree arc. Reading to 0.1 arcminute requires careful eyepiece and vernier.

nodes.name: Shock tube: driven and dump sections
nodes.note: Temperature behind shock is predictable from gas properties and compression ratio; brief duration allows measurement at extreme conditions. Diaphragm timing is precise.

nodes.name: Simple plano-convex lens
nodes.note: The kernel is that a single spherical surface converges parallel light to a point. Aberrations are severe; useful only for low magnification. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Sounding machine: lead line and marks
nodes.note: Sample of bottom (sand, mud, shells) helps identify location when fog prevents sight navigation. Deep sea (> 300 fathoms) requires stronger line.

nodes.name: Spectral radiometer: grating and photocells
nodes.note: Array of detectors measures entire spectrum; much faster than scanning monochromator. Calibration against blackbody standard essential.

nodes.name: Spectrograph: grating camera
nodes.note: Grating gives linear wavelength scale and multiple orders; more light concentrated. Requires grating of very high quality; defects are invisible to eye but ruin spectrum.

nodes.name: Spectrograph: prism camera
nodes.note: Photography captures the spectrum without eye; much fainter lines visible. Comparison spectra on same plate enable precise wavelength measurement.

nodes.name: Spirit level: bubble in tube
nodes.note: Curvature of tube determines sensitivity; tighter curve = smaller bubble movement for given tilt. Sensitivity 1 minute of arc typical.

nodes.name: Strain gauge bridge amplifier
nodes.note: Bridge balance point shifts with strain; amplified output is linear over useful range. Temperature drift in gauges and electronics is a constant problem.

nodes.name: Strain gauge: bonded resistance wire
nodes.note: Temperature compensation via dummy gauge. Bridge circuit nulls initial resistance; strain produces bridge imbalance. Gauge factor (delta-R/R per unit strain) is material-dependent and reproducible. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tacheometer: distance and elevation measurement
nodes.note: Stadia interval subtends known angle; staff distance = staff reading / tangent of angle. Avoids chain for rough work; less accurate but much faster.

nodes.name: Steel measuring tape: wound on reel
nodes.note: Tape sags under its own weight; standard tension (100 lbs) specified in manuals. Thermal expansion significant for steel; correction tables provided.

nodes.name: Telephoto lens principle
nodes.note: The interval between front and rear elements is shorter than focal length; magnification and physical compactness are the point. Rear element separation tunes back working distance. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tessar compound photographic lens
nodes.note: The rear doublet is cemented; front elements air-spaced. Tessar corrects all primary aberrations (spherical, coma, astigmatism, field curvature) and controls distortion. f/4.5 was standard for hand cameras 1902-1950. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Theodolite: angle measurement
nodes.note: Circles divided 360 degrees with minute precision; verniers read to 10 seconds. Optics give magnification; telescope focuses on distant point.

nodes.name: Thermocouple: junction EMF measurement
nodes.note: Seebeck coefficient and reference junction temperature define sensitivity. High-temperature range extends to 1600 C with platinum-platinum/rhodium.

nodes.name: Torsion balance: vertical fiber suspension
nodes.note: No knife edge; fiber can twist billions of times. Used to measure gravitational constant and test inverseness of gravitational law.

nodes.name: Towing tank: model boat resistance measurement
nodes.note: Model-to-full-scale scaling requires Reynolds number matching; separate friction and pressure drag requires careful measurement of local pressure.

nodes.name: Travelling microscope for length measurement
nodes.note: Magnification gives visual precision on micrometer screw. Kernel is matching optical resolution to mechanical precision of the screw.

nodes.name: Triangulation: station marker
nodes.note: Centering error contributes to position error; forced centering (rotating theodolite over fixed point) necessary for high precision.

nodes.name: Triplet apochromatic lens
nodes.note: Flint-crown-flint sandwich with carefully chosen thicknesses eliminates both primary and secondary chromatic aberration. Air gaps between elements are essential; spacing is critical. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tuning fork: acoustic resonator
nodes.note: Frequency stable to 0.1 percent; frequencies 100 Hz to 1000 Hz common. Used as timekeeping standard before quartz.

nodes.name: Ultracentrifuge: high-speed rotor
nodes.note: Rotor imbalance is catastrophic; dynamic balancing to < 1 gram-cm required. Vacuum jacket reduces drag and heating.

nodes.name: Ultramicroscope: dark field with slit lamp
nodes.note: Colloid particles smaller than visible wavelength scatter light; ultramicroscope can detect particles 10-100 nm, below direct visibility limit. Used to verify kinetic theory of matter. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Van de Graaff static generator
nodes.note: Belt isolation makes voltage independent of corona losses; millions of volts achievable. Originally thought impractical; elegant principle that charges accumulate without external energy beyond motor to drive belt.

nodes.name: Venturi tube: smooth convergent-divergent flow
nodes.note: Better pressure recovery than orifice; more stable discharge coefficient. Smooth internal surface essential for accuracy.

nodes.name: Vibration table: shaker with electromagnet
nodes.note: Mechanical resonances of specimen must be understood; forced excitation can produce nonlinear effects. Force and displacement must both be measured.

nodes.name: Wave plate phase retarder
nodes.note: Quarter wave plate shifts phase by 90 degrees; half wave by 180. Thickness controls retardation. Mica easily cleaves to controlled thickness; later crystals like quartz are more stable. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Wide angle photographic lens
nodes.note: Large field angle means massive distortion if not corrected. Symmetrical designs minimize distortion at the cost of vignetting. Focal length/image diagonal ratio defines angle of view. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Wind tunnel: subsonic test section
nodes.note: Boundary layer thickness and pressure gradient are critical to realistic results. Model blockage ratio must be < 5 percent. Inlet contraction and honeycomb reduce turbulence.

nodes.name: X-ray diffraction camera: Bragg geometry
nodes.note: Bragg angle = arcsin(wavelength / 2d); both angle and intensity must be measured. Requires collimated X-rays and precision rotation stage.

nodes.name: Oxygen and hydrogen in quantity
nodes.note: Zinc or iron with acid gives hydrogen; heating manganese dioxide or a chlorate gives oxygen. Needed for the oxy-hydrogen torch, for fused quartz, for balloons, and later for reducing germanium oxide to metal. Hydrogen and air is an explosive mixture over a very wide range; be disciplined.

nodes.name: Tolerances, jigs, fixtures and interchangeable manufacture
nodes.note: A management and measurement innovation more than a mechanical one, and it is what turns a workshop into an industry. The army will want it for weapons before anyone else does, which is your funding argument. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. THE STATE WILL RESIST THIS. Interchangeable manufacture visibly replaces free urban artisans with unskilled hands and gauges. Suetonius, Vespasian 18: an engineer offers a cheap machine for hauling columns to the Capitol, and Vespasian rewards him but declines to use it, saying he must be allowed to feed his poor commons. Site it in the provinces, staff it conspicuously with freedmen, and frame it as arming the legions rather than as saving wages. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: manufacturing tolerance standard based on 0.1mm precision]

nodes.name: Grown and alloy junction transistors
nodes.note: The point-contact device is a laboratory curiosity. The junction transistor is manufacturable, rugged and reproducible, and it is what actually replaces the vacuum tube. If you only get one generation past the goal, get this one. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_10um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: emitter and collector regions require 10-50 micrometer manufacturing precision]

nodes.name: A working laboratory: retorts, baths, lutes, crucibles, fume management
nodes.note: Alexandrian alchemy already looks like this, so it is culturally normal, which is your cover. Fume management is not optional; the classic way a bootstrapper dies is chlorine or nitrogen dioxide in a closed room.

nodes.name: Lead chamber sulfuric acid at industrial scale
nodes.note: Burn sulfur with saltpetre in a lead-lined chamber; the nitrogen oxides shuttle oxygen catalytically. Lead is the only Roman-available material that survives the conditions, and Rome has a great deal of cheap lead. This is the node that turns chemistry from a laboratory curiosity into an industry. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Lead sheet, pipe, litharge and cupellation control
nodes.note: Rome does this already and does it well. You need lead in bulk for the lead chamber process, for cable sheathing, for accumulators, and for acid plumbing. Also secures your galena supply for the crystal detector. [SCALED: this is an INDUSTRY, not a demonstration. At 200 tonnes of product a year it consumes about 300 tonnes of charcoal annually, derived from the physical ratio in data/world/resources.json rather than guessed. At 0.75 tonnes of charcoal per hectare of coppice per year that is roughly 400 hectares of forest under permanent management, which you must own before you light it.]

nodes.name: Ground and polished spherical lenses
nodes.note: Reading spectacles for a literate elite that goes presbyopic at forty and has no remedy. Enormous margin, obvious utility, zero threat. This is your best year-one revenue product and it also buys you your first patron.

nodes.name: Air brake (locomotive and train)
nodes.note: Compressed air from the engine applies brake pressure to all wheels simultaneously through pipes. Without it, trains over ten cars cannot stop reliably. This is the prerequisite for modern freight.

nodes.name: Assembly line and mass production
nodes.note: Workers do one task repeatedly as car moves on conveyor. Each worker becomes highly skilled at one assembly step. Huge overhead but makes cars affordable for ordinary people.

nodes.name: Automobile (self-propelled carriage)
nodes.note: Engine drives wheels through gearbox. Steering wheel controls front wheels. Four-wheel suspension. Replaces horse-drawn carriages. Major social disruption from independence and speed.

nodes.name: Pivoting front axle
nodes.note: ROME POSSIBLY HAS THIS but is disputed. Turning is impossible without it; evidence in Roman relief carvings is ambiguous. Assume present but mark confidence low.

nodes.name: Ball bearing
nodes.note: Steel balls in a cage roll between races. Reduces friction in wheel hubs and pedal cranks by 90 percent. Makes the bicycle practical and comfortable for long rides. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Block system (railway safety)
nodes.note: Divide the line into blocks with signals; only one train per block. This is not a mechanical invention; it is an information system. Railway safety is fundamentally a communication problem.

nodes.name: Boneshaker (pedal bicycle)
nodes.note: Pedals drive the front wheel directly via crank. Frame and wheels are wood and cast iron, hence the name. Rider feels every rock; suspension comes later. Speed gain over walking is 2x. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Bridge
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Stone arch bridges, magnificent examples, part of road network. This is why Roman roads are faster than mountain paths.

nodes.name: Carburettor
nodes.note: Fuel nozzle sprays petrol into an air stream at variable rates. Mixture must be tuned to engine speed. Precise ratio is critical; too rich or too lean and the engine stalls. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Caterpillar track (crawler)
nodes.note: Steel shoes on chains loop around drive sprockets. Distributes weight over ground to reduce sinking in mud. Allows cross-country movement on otherwise impassable terrain.

nodes.name: Chain drive (for bicycle)
nodes.note: Roller chain connecting pedal sprocket to rear wheel. Allows gearing: the rear wheel turns multiple times per pedal stroke. Reduces effort and enables comfortable cruising speed. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Coach
nodes.note: Enclosed four-wheel carriage with seating inside, drawn by horses. No suspension yet, so routes must be smooth roads. This is personal transport for the wealthy.

nodes.name: Coal tar gas (coal gas)
nodes.note: Coke and steam passed through hot coal produces combustible gas. Used for lighting and early engines. Supply is local and pipeline-dependent; replaced by petrol in vehicles. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: steam-coke reaction at 900-1000C for coal gas production]

nodes.name: Cursus publicus courier service
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Imperial dispatch relay using stations and fresh horses. Shows that Rome recognizes speed of information matters; this logic applies to freight.

nodes.name: Diesel cycle (compression ignition)
nodes.note: Compress air to 500 psi, inject fuel which ignites by heat alone. No spark plugs needed. More efficient than Otto cycle but requires massive precision in boring. Heavier and more expensive.

nodes.name: Diesel supply chain
nodes.note: Heavy-oil fraction from crude, more energy-dense than petrol, flows at cold temperatures. Essential for trucks and industry. Distribution network similar to petrol but slightly different specifications.

nodes.name: Differential (rear axle)
nodes.note: Bevel gear system that allows both rear wheels to turn at different speeds during cornering. Without it, inside wheel scrapes and car is hard to steer. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Fishplate rail jointer
nodes.note: Iron plates bolted across a rail joint prevent gaps and shearing. Eliminates the bump and clatter of wheels crossing joints. Maintenance of alignment becomes predictable. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Flanged wheel
nodes.note: The flange is on the WHEEL, not the rail. Inward-facing rim keeps the wheel on track. This is the counterintuitive choice that makes all railway systems work. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Four-wheeled cart
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Four-wheel design allows steering the front axle independently, a fundamental shift from two-wheel carts. Capacity and maneuverability.

nodes.name: Atmospheric gas engine (Lenoir)
nodes.note: Mix illuminating gas with air, ignite, expansion drives piston, atmospheric pressure returns it. Inefficient but quieter than steam. Industrial benchmark before petrol engines.

nodes.name: Gearbox and clutch
nodes.note: Friction clutch allows engine to spin freely when disengaged. Gear trains multiply torque at low speed and allow high speed at high RPM. Without gearing, a small engine cannot move a heavy car. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Harness of throat and girth type
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Rope and leather harness distributes pull across the shoulders and chest. Impedes breathing but enables pulling; the rigid collar is later and better.

nodes.name: Hobby horse (pedal-less bicycle)
nodes.note: Rider straddles a frame with two wheels and propels by pushing feet on the ground. Faster than walking, no pedals. Proof of concept for the bicycle, then abandoned as impractical.

nodes.name: Horse saddle (basic)
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Basic saddle with cloth and leather distributes rider weight. Allows long-distance mounted travel. Stirrups come later.

nodes.name: Nailed horseshoe
nodes.note: Iron shoes nailed to hoof allow horses to work on stone roads for weeks without going lame. This is not efficiency; this is making the horse usable on paved ground instead of destroying it.

nodes.name: Iron edge rail
nodes.note: Cast iron rails with one edge raised to guide flanged wheels. First used in mines. The innovation is the raised edge, not the metal; it prevents derailment and reduces friction.

nodes.name: Litter
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Pole-carried passenger carriage used by the wealthy. Humans as motive power but avoids the discomfort of horseback for dignitaries.

nodes.name: Macadam road surface
nodes.note: Broken stone, graded by size, compacted without binding agent. Much cheaper to build and maintain than Roman dressed-stone roads but degrades faster in wet. An economic trade-off, not an improvement.

nodes.name: Magneto (ignition system)
nodes.note: Rotating magnet in coil generates high-voltage spark without needing a battery. Works on any engine speed. This simple approach powered all early cars. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Milestone
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Stone pillars marking distance along roads. Enables speed prediction, time scheduling, loss prediction. Information infrastructure.

nodes.name: Road network for motor vehicles
nodes.note: Smooth, level roads with safety markings, regular maintenance, and drainage. Cars need better surface than macadam; tarmac wears out faster under car weight but is faster to repair.

nodes.name: Mule transport
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Mules are preferred for mountain work because they are surefooted and eat less than horses. The pack mule is the backbone of supply in rough terrain.

nodes.name: Omnibus (motor bus)
nodes.note: Large motor carriage for 20-50 passengers. Replaces horse-drawn omnibus. Speed, capacity, and lack of animal waste transform urban public transport.

nodes.name: Otto cycle four-stroke engine
nodes.note: Intake, compression, power, exhaust in four strokes per cycle. More efficient than atmospheric engines. Forms the foundation of all automotive engines.

nodes.name: Ox transport
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Oxen pull heavier loads than horses at slower speed and cost less to feed. Used for slow supply and field work; horses for speed.

nodes.name: Paved trunk road network
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. The via system of stone-laid trunk roads is the network substrate for everything below. Permits high-speed carriage travel and reliable supply movement.

nodes.name: Penny farthing (high-wheel bicycle)
nodes.note: Huge front wheel, tiny back wheel. Higher wheel passes obstacles; one turn of the crank moves you further. Unstable and dangerous but fast. Rider height makes it impractical for most. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Pneumatic tyre (rubber tyre)
nodes.note: REQUIRES NATURAL RUBBER (tier 9 unobtainable in Rome). Air-filled tube and tyre absorb shocks perfectly. Solid rubber or leather tyre is a poor substitute: rides are harsh and efficiency is lost. This is an honest limitation. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Point and switch
nodes.note: Movable rails allow a train to switch between two tracks. The mechanism must be sturdy enough to guide a moving train cleanly. Enables sidings and branch lines.

nodes.name: Safety bicycle (chain drive)
nodes.note: Equal-size wheels with chain drive; seat low and central. The chain and the differential-free rear drive are the inventions. Safe, stable, and fast. Modern bicycle geometry. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Railway signal
nodes.note: Semaphore arms and flag signals allow operators to communicate over distance. Necessary before trains run on tight schedules; without them, collisions are inevitable.

nodes.name: Spark plug (spark ignition)
nodes.note: Electric spark across a gap ignites fuel mix at the exact moment of compression. Timing is everything; even small errors cause misfires and loss of power. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Leaf spring
nodes.note: Flexing steel leaf under a carriage absorbs shocks and bumps. This single innovation makes long-distance travel on rough roads bearable. Suspension is what makes the journey tolerable, not the speed.

nodes.name: Stagecoach
nodes.note: Coach with leaf-spring suspension and scheduled stops; a business model for passenger transport. The springs change everything: bumpy roads become tolerable for long hours.

nodes.name: Standard gauge (railway)
nodes.note: All railways must use the same track spacing for freight transfer between lines. Without standardisation, each line is an island. The cost of standardisation is high; the cost of not doing so is higher.

nodes.name: Steam locomotive
nodes.note: Steam engine mounted on rails propels itself and train. Requires constant water and fuel stops. The locomotive does not pull faster than horses until distances exceed 30 miles; then volume and fuel logistics matter.

nodes.name: Steering geometry (Ackermann)
nodes.note: Front wheels must turn at different angles during a turn so both follow the same curved path. This geometry is counterintuitive but essential for stable handling. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Stirrup
nodes.note: Metal foot-loops hanging from saddle revolutionise horseback riding. Rider can brace legs, rise from seat, and deliver force in combat or work. This is as much a military technology as a transport one. [FIXED after independent audit: the horse collar is draught harness and has nothing to do with a mounted rider's balance. The real missing input is a framed saddle.]

nodes.name: Superheater (steam locomotive)
nodes.note: Heat the steam further after leaving the boiler to expand it more in the cylinder, improving efficiency 20 percent. Complexity and maintenance cost are high; only justified on long-distance engines. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tarmacadam road surface
nodes.note: Macadam with tar binding is cheaper to build than Roman stone but still degrades. The advantage is speed of repair, not quality. Honest assessment: it is an economic choice for volume, not engineering superiority.

nodes.name: Tender (coal and water car)
nodes.note: Water and coal are consumed continuously; a dedicated car attached to the engine carries supplies. Without the tender, the engine range is measured in tens of miles. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tractor (motor field vehicle)
nodes.note: Powerful engine mounted on crawler tracks for traction in mud. Can pull multiple ploughs or work in woods. Changes farmwork from oxen to machines; entire labour class displaced.

nodes.name: Truck (motor freight vehicle)
nodes.note: Heavy-duty chassis with open cargo bed. Diesel engine for economy and torque. Replaces the mule and the railway for regional freight. Speed and flexibility change logistics entirely.

nodes.name: Turnpike
nodes.note: Private or chartered toll road maintained by toll gate revenue. Creates incentive to maintain roads better than government roads. Improves speed and reliability. Some hostility from smugglers and bandits.

nodes.name: Two-wheeled cart
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Simple two-point suspension, lighter than four-wheel for local work, used everywhere by farmers and traders.

nodes.name: Iron tyre (tire)
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Iron band shrunk hot onto the rim protects the wooden wheel and spreads road impact. Vastly extends wheel life over bare wood.

nodes.name: Spoked wheel
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Radial spokes in tension carry load far better than solid wood. This invention alone made fast carriages possible.

nodes.name: Wheelbarrow
nodes.note: One-wheel handcart, invented in China, allows manual labour to move bulk goods. Rome does not have this; it is surprisingly absent. An enormous productivity gain once adopted.

nodes.name: Whippletree
nodes.note: The whippletree, or evener, is a pivoting bar that distributes pull evenly between two horses, preventing one from shirking. Without it, tandem teams do not work.

nodes.name: Logarithms and computed tables
nodes.note: The 40,000 scribe-hours are real: Napier spent 20 years and Briggs employed computers. This is a pure money-for-time trade and it is worth it, because every engineer and astronomer after you saves a factor of ten on arithmetic.

nodes.name: The first accurate screw, and thread standards
nodes.note: The bootstrap problem: to cut an accurate screw you need an accurate screw. Escape it by wrapping a strip round a cylinder to generate a first rough helix, then correcting a master by lapping with a long nut, which averages out the errors. Slow, fiddly, and it is the gate on all measurement. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: lapping master screw with a long nut requires file and gauge precision to average errors]

nodes.name: Alum
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Melos. Mordant, styptic, sizing.

nodes.name: Aluminium
nodes.note: Hall-Heroult in a molten fluoride bath. Cryolite is Greenlandic and unobtainable, so you must synthesise the bath from your own hydrofluoric acid. Before electricity aluminium is a precious metal; after it, it is roofing. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: Hall-Heroult bath must be maintained at 950-1000 C]

nodes.name: Ammonia
nodes.note: Ammonia liquor is a by-product of coking coal, so it is nearly free once you coke. Fertiliser, refrigeration, nitric acid via Ostwald oxidation.

nodes.name: Asbestos
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Cyprus. Pliny describes it. Useful, and it will kill your workers slowly.

nodes.name: Bakelite (phenol formaldehyde)
nodes.note: The first fully synthetic plastic, from coal tar phenol. Electrical insulation, housings, and the thing that makes mass-produced electrical goods possible.

nodes.name: Beeswax
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Lost wax casting, luting, acid-proof coating.

nodes.name: Bitumen and naphtha seeps
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea. Cable insulation, waterproofing, and the seed of petroleum chemistry.

nodes.name: Blister steel
nodes.note: Bar iron packed in charcoal at about 1000 C for days. Carbon penetrates on the order of a millimetre a day, so use thin bars.

nodes.name: Brass (by cementation)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS, made by heating copper with calamine and charcoal WITHOUT ever seeing zinc metal. See mat_zinc for why.

nodes.name: Bronze
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Casting, bearings, statuary, instruments.

nodes.name: Bulk steel (converter and open hearth)
nodes.note: Thousands of tonnes instead of kilogrammes. NOTE THE PHOSPHORUS PROBLEM: an acid lining cannot remove it and most European ores carry it, so you need a basic dolomite lining (Thomas and Gilchrist). Knowing this in advance saves you the years it cost Bessemer.

nodes.name: Calamine (zinc carbonate/silicate ore)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS and already smelts it into brass. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Camphor (traded)
nodes.note: Reachable via the Indian Ocean and Chinese trade, expensive. Needed for celluloid and for smokeless powder.

nodes.name: Carbon black and lampblack
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Ink pigment, and much later the reinforcing filler that makes rubber into tyres.

nodes.name: Cast iron
nodes.note: Brittle, cheap, castable, 3-4% carbon. Rome has none in the West; Han China has had it for 500 years. Pipes, pots, cannon, machine frames, stoves.

nodes.name: Celluloid (nitrocellulose plastic)
