nodes.name: Fuel oil (heavy fraction)
nodes.note: Heavy oil from the still bottom: too thick to burn in lamps, but a boiler fuel for ships and stationary engines. Higher energy density than coal by weight; viscous, needing heating to flow and atomization to burn. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Gas engine and internal combustion
nodes.note: Coal gas is sucked in, mixed with air, sparked, and exploded. Much lighter and simpler than a steam engine. No boiler, no furnace, no engineer. Otto and Diesel engines follow. Early models are unreliable; ignition is the problem. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Gas main and gas network
nodes.note: Seamless iron pipe laid underground, distribution on a town or city scale. Requires precision joints, testing for leaks, and reliable supply. Gas is lighter than air: pipes must slope and have drains for condensed tar.

nodes.name: Gas meter
nodes.note: A wet meter with pistons in a sealed chamber, gas pushing them round, a dial recording revolutions. Charges customers fairly and identifies leaks. Requires careful assembly and sealed joints.

nodes.name: High voltage transmission
nodes.note: Power loss in a wire is proportional to I squared; raising voltage and lowering current for the same power reduces losses dramatically. Remote hydro becomes economic only with high voltage. Requires transformers, insulators, and careful design.

nodes.name: Hydroelectric power station
nodes.note: A dam, penstock, turbine, and dynamo coupled: water flow becomes rotary motion becomes electrical current. The scale is decided by head and flow. Long-distance transmission at high voltage makes remote hydro economical.

nodes.name: Indicator diagram (Watt's instrument)
nodes.note: A small pump coupled to the engine cylinder; a pencil draws a closed curve on a moving drum of paper. The area inside is work; the height is pressure. This turns thermodynamics from guessing into measurement: you can see what the engine actually does.

nodes.name: Kerosene (paraffin) lamps
nodes.note: Kerosene is a clear liquid fraction with a clean flame, brighter than candles or whale oil. Cheaper to refine than to ship coal. Lamps are simple: wick, chimney, brass fitting. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Lead-acid storage battery
nodes.note: Lead oxide and lead plates in sulfuric acid: charge with DC, discharge to get power. Rechargeable, robust, stores significant energy. The acid eats organic matter and corrodes copper; wood cases and lead terminals are necessary. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Leat and weir
nodes.note: The leat is a conduit bringing water from higher up the valley, often in an aqueduct on stonework or timber. The weir diverts water from the river. Together they concentrate flow and head at the mill site.

nodes.name: Load factor and grid economics
nodes.note: Load factor is average demand over peak demand. A grid with high load factor is economical: fixed costs (wires, transformers) are spread over more revenue. Time-of-use tariffs and reservoir storage improve load factor.

nodes.name: Millpond and storage
nodes.note: A dam and reservoir upstream of the mill, holding water during low flow, releasing it when needed. This gives you power when the stream does not: seasonal agriculture, milling, mining.

nodes.name: Nickel-iron battery
nodes.note: Nickel oxide and iron electrodes in caustic soda solution. Tougher than lead-acid, tolerates abuse and overcharge, but lower voltage and self-discharge. Edson and Tesla championed it; it is still used in harsh environments. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Horizontal waterwheel (Norse)
nodes.note: The rotor spins on a vertical axis, driven by a direct vertical jet. No complex gearing needed, no right-angle transmission. Rugged, efficient for small streams with drop.

nodes.name: Nuclear fission and power
nodes.note: Honest assessment: nuclear power requires uranium enrichment to weapons-grade purity (99.9999+%), neutron physics at a level unknown to Rome, materials research for radiation damage, and a national security programme. The reactor is the easy part. Start this only if you have a state programme with decades and billions to spare.

nodes.name: Oil refinery and distillation
nodes.note: Crude oil boils at different temperatures; fractional distillation separates light fractions (petrol, kerosene) from heavy (fuel oil, tar). Requires large copper stills, careful heating control, and condensers. The fractions are products, not wastes.

nodes.name: Oil shale and bitumen deposits
nodes.note: Oil shale and bitumen seeps exist; heating shale gives a bituminous liquid. The yield is poor and transport is heavy, but it is available without drilling if you find the deposits.

nodes.name: Overshot waterwheel
nodes.note: Rome has this too, notably the 16-wheel Barbegal complex. Weight of the water does the work; it needs a significant drop but delivers more power per wheel.

nodes.name: Peat extraction and burning
nodes.note: Bog digging gives you fuel where forest is scarce. Peat burns slower and wetter than wood but is abundant in northern Europe. Not Rome's world yet, but available in the North.

nodes.name: Pelton wheel
nodes.note: A jet of water hits a double-cup bucket at high speed, splitting the jet tangentially to the wheel. Ideal for very high heads with low flow. The bucket profile is critical; casting is easier than machining but requires controlled cooling to avoid cracks.

nodes.name: Petroleum seeps and collection
nodes.note: Oil seeps from rock faces and pools in low ground. Early collection by bucket and pit. No pressure, no depth, just ambient flow. Pitch, naphtha, light oil; use depends on locality. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Oil pipeline
nodes.note: Welded steel pipe from well to refinery, hundreds of km. Oil is thick; transport by pipeline is cheaper than rail or ship. Requires high pressure seamless pipe, welding skill, and multiple pump stations.

nodes.name: Post mill
nodes.note: The entire mill building pivots on a post to face the wind. It is portable, fits anywhere, and gives you wind power without a tall fixed tower. The miller rotates it by hand or rope from a tail pole. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Pumped storage hydroelectric
nodes.note: Two reservoirs at different elevations: pump water up when power is cheap, run it down to generate when demand is high. Stores energy as gravitational potential; no battery needed. Requires two dams and good geology.

nodes.name: Rotary drilling
nodes.note: A spinning drill bit on a hollow rotating rod; drilling mud circulates down the pipe, cooling and carrying cuttings up. Faster, deeper, better for hard rock. Needs precise engineering and circulation pumps. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Safety valve and pressure gauge
nodes.note: A weighted spring-loaded valve that lifts at a set pressure, and a Bourdon or liquid gauge to read it. Early boiler explosions killed many; this is the honest lesson that machines need observation and limits. Requires calibration and maintenance. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Screw press
nodes.note: The screw and nut multiply force: oil, wine, coins. Rome has perfect screw threads; this is a force multiplier, not power generation.

nodes.name: Selenium photovoltaic cell
nodes.note: A sealed cell with selenium on iron or copper, a back contact and a semi-transparent front. Too fragile and slow for power; used in light meters, exposure control, light-activated switches. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Selenium metal extraction
nodes.note: Selenium is a trace element in copper ores. Roasting and selective reduction yields grey metallic selenium. The metal is brittle and toxic; handling requires care. Essential for photovoltaic effects. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Selenium photovoltaic effect
nodes.note: Selenium exposed to light generates a voltage. The effect is real but tiny; a palm-sized cell produces microamps. Photo-electric light meters were the first practical use. The efficiency is under 1 percent. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Sails on ships
nodes.note: Rome uses wind to move ships. This is free power once mastered; the wind will not supply electricity or mechanical work directly ashore without new capture technology.

nodes.name: Efficiency measurement of waterwheels
nodes.note: Smeaton built test wheels and measured their output vs input with weights and pulleys, not guessing. This is the birth of hydraulic engineering as a science: quantitative, reproducible, publishable.

nodes.name: Steam turbine (Parsons)
nodes.note: Stages of rotor and stator blades; steam expands through each stage, doing work and accelerating. Above a few hundred kW, this beats reciprocating engines: no reciprocating masses, no vibration, compact, efficient. Blade tolerances and metallurgy are severe.

nodes.name: Stirling engine
nodes.note: Two cylinders with a hot end and cold end, connected via a regenerator. Displacement and timing are offset so heat is recycled. External combustion, any fuel, but complex mechanics and modest power. Useful for stationary engines where simplicity matters. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Substation and distribution
nodes.note: Receives high-voltage transmission lines, steps them down via transformers to local distribution voltage, distributes to neighborhoods and industries. A hub between generation and use; switching and protection equipment required.

nodes.name: Superheating and steam drying
nodes.note: Heating saturated steam above boiling point increases its energy density. Dry steam does not corrode pipes and valve seats; water droplets do. Superheaters are pipe coils in the hottest part of the furnace. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Thermoelectric couple (Seebeck effect)
nodes.note: Two different metals joined, one end hot and one cold: a voltage appears. Seebeck discovered this by heating copper-bismuth junctions. Current is tiny but direct: a thermopile of 50 couples can ring a bell. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Thermopile as a current source
nodes.note: A stack of thermoelectric couples, all hot ends at a furnace, all cold ends at water, producing a steady voltage without zinc consumption. Early telegraph relays and electroplating work used thermopiles before batteries became cheap. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Three-phase AC and polyphase
nodes.note: Three AC waves 120 degrees apart, on three wires. Power delivery is constant instead of pulsing; motors start without a starter and run balanced. Tesla's innovation; it enabled power distribution at scale.

nodes.name: Tide mill
nodes.note: A mill at the estuary with gates that open on incoming tide, close on outgoing, releasing a head of water. Twice per 24 hours, not continuous, but free and predictable. Requires careful site and sluice design.

nodes.name: Tower mill
nodes.note: A fixed tapered brick or stone tower with a rotating cap. Taller and heavier than a post mill, it catches stronger winds and is more stable. The rotary bearing is now high stress, needing good metalwork. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Transformer (step-up/step-down)
nodes.note: Two coils on an iron core; AC in one induces AC in the other at a different voltage. No moving parts, highly efficient. Allows voltage conversion without rotating machinery, the key to AC distribution.

nodes.name: Treadwheel crane
nodes.note: Roman construction cranes driven by human walk inside the wheel. The mechanical advantage is immediate and the load is obvious to the worker.

nodes.name: Trompe (water-driven air blast)
nodes.note: Falling water entrains air in a angled tube, compressing it as the water drops. The compressed air separates from the water at the bottom, no valves, no moving parts. Ingenious; useful for furnace blast in a mine or forge where you cannot afford bellows labour. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Undershot waterwheel
nodes.note: Rome already operates these at scale. The water pushes on the bucket; it is simple, portable, and tolerates muddy water and sand.

nodes.name: Water turbine (Fourneyron)
nodes.note: The turbine runner spins fast, with fixed guide vanes and moving buckets, using the entire head at any flow. This beats a wheel because it accelerates the water to high speed and extracts the momentum, not just the weight. The penalty: it needs better tolerances and materials.

nodes.name: Windmill fantail and automatic furling
nodes.note: A small perpendicular fan on the tail of the cap automatically rotates the mill to face the wind. If the wind is too strong, the fan spins faster, which tilts a striker linkage that furls the sail. No miller attendance needed at night. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Band theory, doping, carriers, the p-n junction
nodes.note: The single largest time saving in the programme. Historically this took from 1900 to 1947 and several Nobel prizes. You carry the conclusions. Write them down in your first decade, in plain quantitative language, in many copies, because you will not live to see them tested.

nodes.name: Radio: spark, crystal set, then valve transmitters
nodes.note: Wireless communication over the whole Mediterranean, including to ships, which no empire has ever had. Strategically this is worth more than the electric telegraph and it is the second great gift to the State. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Rag paper from linen
nodes.note: Cai Lun's paper is 105 AD in China and will not reach the Mediterranean for centuries. Ret and lime the rags, beat them to pulp with a water-driven stamper, lift on a wire mould, press and size. Cheaper than papyrus, far cheaper than parchment, and it is the substrate of everything in Module 80.

nodes.name: Iron rail, locomotive and permanent way
nodes.note: Rome's road network is already excellent, so the marginal gain is smaller than it was in Britain, but bulk freight overland at a fortieth of the cost changes what can be built inland. Politically superb: it is unambiguously an imperial instrument. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. The 400 tonnes of rail steel is a demonstration line of roughly 4 km at about 100 kg per metre of track, not a network. A network is a further order of magnitude and is why the calendar floor here is a generation.

nodes.name: Fireclay, grog and silica refractories
nodes.note: Nothing hot happens without a vessel that survives it. Rome has excellent ceramics but no systematic refractory grading. Test candidate clays by firing to failure and record the results; this is your first real experimental programme.

nodes.name: Boiled water, handwashing, wound irrigation, quarantine
nodes.note: Costs an argument, not a denarius. Saves more Roman lives than every machine in this document combined. Sell it to the legions first: the army already has valetudinaria and an officer class that measures results.

nodes.name: Binomial theorem and binomial expansion
nodes.note: Newton discovered this; Pascal's triangle gives coefficients. Teaching: why does (x+y)² = x² + 2xy + y²? Draw a square divided into four. Why does (x+y)³ work the same way? Induction proof follows. Adoption: fast, because it saves multiplication.

nodes.name: Complex numbers: a + bi where i² = -1
nodes.note: Cardano's cubic formula forced complex intermediate steps. Teaching: geometry (rotation and scaling in the plane) makes it tangible. Adoption: fast in AC electricity and physics.

nodes.name: Determinants and matrix inversion
nodes.note: Ancient roots in solving simultaneous equations. Teaching: area and volume interpretation. Adoption by applied mathematicians first.

nodes.name: Infinite series and convergence
nodes.note: Zeno's paradox and medieval scholars debated infinities. Newton and Leibniz used series for trig and exp. Teaching requires the limit concept first. Convergence tests (ratio, integral, comparison) come later.

nodes.name: Polynomial interpolation and finite differences
nodes.note: Computing machines depend on difference tables. Teaching: Lagrange vs. Newton forms. Adoption: essential for any function tabulation.

nodes.name: Least squares method and curve fitting
nodes.note: Gauss and Legendre derived independently (1805-1812). Teaching: why squares? They weight large errors heavily and math is neat. Adoption: fast in geodesy and later in all experimental science.

nodes.name: Logarithm as inverse exponent: log₁₀(1000) = 3
nodes.note: Napier invented this to replace multiplication with addition: multiply by looking up logs, adding, looking up antilog. Teaching: understand exponent rules first. Then log is just naming the exponent. The product rule is obvious once you see it.

nodes.name: Matrices and matrix multiplication
nodes.note: Cayley formalized (1858). Teaching: transforms (rotation, scaling); systems of equations as Ax = b. Adoption: slow until computers make it practical.

nodes.name: Numerical methods: Newton-Raphson, bisection, iteration
nodes.note: Requires testing convergence by hand before computers. Teaching: graph on paper, subdivide, iterate. Adoption: essential for any real design calculation.

nodes.name: Polynomial equations and factoring
nodes.note: Cubics and quartics have closed formulas (Cardano, Ferrari), but they are ugly. Quintics do not have formulas (Galois, Abel). Teaching: show a cubic solved by substitution and depression. Adoption: essential for engineering, slow elsewhere.

nodes.name: The quadratic equation and solution formula
nodes.note: Babylonians completed the square geometrically. Al-Khwarizmi had the method. Descartes proved it algebraically. Teaching: deriving the formula from completing the square takes an hour and feels like discovery. The ± notation is key.

nodes.name: Symbolic algebra and letter variables
nodes.note: Al-Khwarizmi and medieval scholars used words; Vieta brought letters. Teaching replaces arithmetic drill with symbolic manipulation: instead of 'find the number such that when you add 5 and triple it you get 24,' write 3x + 5 = 24 and show x = 19/3. Adoption fast in universities, slow elsewhere.

nodes.name: Tensors and tensor notation
nodes.note: Einstein summation convention hides indices. Teaching requires patience. Adoption: essential for solid mechanics and general relativity.

nodes.name: Vectors and vector algebra
nodes.note: Gibbs and Heaviside developed notation independently in the 1880s. Teaching: forces, velocities, displacements. Adoption: essential for 3D mechanics.

nodes.name: The derivative as instantaneous rate of change
nodes.note: Newton's fluxions, Leibniz's differential notation (df/dx) is cleaner. Teaching: slope of a curve at a point, velocity as change of position, acceleration as change of velocity. First application to physics and engineering. Adoption: essential for all quantitative science.

nodes.name: Fourier series: decomposing periodic functions
nodes.note: Fourier solved heat equation using this. Teaching: mechanical analogy using tuning forks and resonance. Adoption: electrical engineering relies on it for AC power.

nodes.name: Fourier transform and continuous frequency spectrum
nodes.note: Integral form goes to infinity. Teaching requires confidence with Fourier series first. Adoption is late 20th century for digital signal processing.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem: differentiation and integration are inverses
nodes.note: Proven by Newton and Leibniz independently. Teaching is the eureka moment: derivative and integral undo each other. Adoption is fast because it makes calculations feasible.

nodes.name: The integral as area under a curve
nodes.note: Riemann formalized it; Lebesgue generalized later. Teaching: Archimedes estimated area with inscribed and circumscribed rectangles. Calculus makes it algebraic. Adoption: once differentiation exists, integrals follow for work, volume, mass.

nodes.name: The limit and convergence to a value
nodes.note: The foundation of modern calculus, formalized by Cauchy and Weierstrass. Medieval debates about infinitesimals; Newton and Leibniz avoided the rigour. Teaching: intuitive first ('get as close as you want'), then epsilon-delta proof for one simple case. Adoption is graduate-level.

nodes.name: Ordinary differential equations and solution methods
nodes.note: Newton's laws are ODEs. Teaching: simple cases first (y' = 2y has solution e^(2x)). Adoption: essential for physics and engineering.

nodes.name: Partial differential equations
nodes.note: d²u/dt² = c² d²u/dx² (wave equation); solutions require boundary conditions. Teaching is hard; Fourier series helps. Adoption is by mathematical physicists first.

nodes.name: Conic sections: circles, ellipses, parabolas, hyperbolas
nodes.note: Apollonius knew them geometrically. Descartes wrote them algebraically. Teaching: derive from plane cutting a cone, or as locus of points. Adoption: essential for understanding planetary orbits.

nodes.name: Coordinate geometry and the Cartesian plane
nodes.note: Descartes and Fermat, early 1600s. Teaching: each point is a pair (x,y); equations become curves. Adoption: fast in university, slow in practical surveying.

nodes.name: Descriptive geometry and engineering drawing
nodes.note: Monge formalized it for military engineering (1780s). Teaching: start with wooden blocks, draw them, build from the drawing. Adoption: universal by 1850 in all engineering.

nodes.name: Differential geometry: curves and surfaces
nodes.note: Gauss and Riemann. Teaching requires calculus and linear algebra. Adoption by theoretical physics and later differential geometry becomes essential.

nodes.name: Non-Euclidean geometry: hyperbolic and elliptic
nodes.note: Shocking because Euclidean seemed necessary. Teaching requires intrinsic vs. extrinsic curvature. Adoption: slow until Einstein (1915) makes gravity a curved spacetime.

nodes.name: Spherical trigonometry and navigation formulas
nodes.note: Essential for celestial navigation and map-making. Teaching requires globe and accurate diagrams. Adoption: fast among navigators and cartographers.

nodes.name: Trigonometric functions and tables
nodes.note: Hipparchus computed chord tables; Indians used sines. Modern tables (7-decimal, 15-decimal) require thousands of hours to compute and check. Manufacturing tables is expensive; printing enables adoption.

nodes.name: Citation and bibliographic reference
nodes.note: Standard notation evolved over centuries (now many styles). Teaching: plagiarism vs. citation. Adoption: fast once journals exist.

nodes.name: Curriculum and course sequence
nodes.note: Universities formalized in medieval period. Teaching: what order? Arithmetic before algebra, geometry before calculus. Adoption: slow because schools resist change.

nodes.name: Doctorate and research degree
nodes.note: German universities formalised (1800s). Teaching: what counts as original? How evaluate quality? Adoption: now universal marker of research qualification.

nodes.name: Examination and credentialing
nodes.note: Universities began written exams in 19th century. Teaching: standardises quality. Adoption: slow because it threatens existing credentials.

nodes.name: Funded research programme
nodes.note: NIH, NSF, DFIR modern examples. Teaching: how write proposal. Adoption: became essential by 1950s as research became expensive.

nodes.name: Scientific journal and periodical
nodes.note: Philosophical Transactions (1665) first. Teaching: establishes priority and enables distant researchers. Adoption: fast once printing enables it.

nodes.name: Learned society and academy
nodes.note: Royal Society (1660), Academie des Sciences (1666). Teaching: creates community and authority. Adoption: fast among elite, slow elsewhere.

nodes.name: Patent as disclosure and property right
nodes.note: English statute 1624. Teaching: why disclose? Fear of copying drives secrecy. Patent law forces choice: publish or abandon claim. Adoption is slow and contested.

nodes.name: Referee and peer review
nodes.note: Formalised in 20th century (Nature and Science). Teaching: why anonymous matters (prevents conflicts). Adoption: slow because refereeing is unpaid.

nodes.name: Research group and principal investigator
nodes.note: Liebig's group (1830s) was model. Teaching: how supervise and credit work. Adoption: fast in universities, slow in industry.

nodes.name: Textbook and codified knowledge
nodes.note: Euclid's Elements (300 BC) set standard. Teaching: distill knowledge into digestible form. Adoption: slow because good textbooks take years to write and refine.

nodes.name: Controlled experiment and causality
nodes.note: Foundation of empirical science. Teaching: why matters (isolates cause from correlation). Adoption is slow because it requires surrendering real-world complexity.

nodes.name: Hypothesis and prediction
nodes.note: Explicit prediction, not 'let's see what happens.' Teaching: why falsifiable matters. Adoption: becomes standard in quantitative science.

nodes.name: Laboratory notebook and data recording
nodes.note: Legal requirement for patent disputes. Teaching: why matters (reproducibility, chain of custody). Adoption: fast in experimental labs.

nodes.name: Negative result and null finding
nodes.note: Publication bias: journals reject negatives. Teaching: why matters (saves others' time). Adoption: slow because negatives disappoint.

nodes.name: Peer criticism and expert review
nodes.note: Royal Society tradition. Teaching: why defensiveness fails. Adoption: fast in university but slow in industry and government.

nodes.name: Replication and repeatability
nodes.note: Validates findings and catches fraud. Teaching: why peer skepticism matters. Adoption: slow because replication is unglamorous and often unrewarding.

nodes.name: Decimal fractions
nodes.note: Al-Kashi described this in the 15th century; Simon Stevin formalized it. The point or comma is merely convention. Teaching: counting by tens extends below unity. Adoption slow because it competes with fractions.

nodes.name: The decimal point convention
nodes.note: Napier used a period; Stevin used a circle. The point won. Adoption is fast once stakes are printing. Different countries use comma still.

nodes.name: Dimensional analysis and unit checking
nodes.note: Fourier first formalized this. Benefits: catch algebra errors (multiplying meters and kilograms is wrong), derive relationships from dimensional guess. Teaching requires algebra first.

nodes.name: The equals sign
nodes.note: Recorde introduced = around 1557; it replaced 'is equal to'. Before this, sentences: 'x plus 5 is the same as 12.' Afterward: x + 5 = 12. This tiny change enables algebra as a visual system.

nodes.name: Error propagation and uncertainty arithmetic
nodes.note: Requires calculus and statistics both. Teaching is graduate-level. Adoption is by research groups first, later by engineering. Key insight: combine uncertainties as root-sum-square when independent, linearly when correlated.

nodes.name: Exponent notation
nodes.note: Vieta used q for quadratum (square), c for cubus. Descartes switched to superscripts. Typesetting superscripts is hard; printing adoption is slow.

nodes.name: Metric system: standard meters, kilograms, seconds
nodes.note: French Revolution, 1790s. Requires redefining all trade measures simultaneously; no gradual adoption. Professions that stake identity on old systems resist hardest: British inch, American pound. Teaching: why base 10? Because fingers. Adoption: must be enforced by law and remaking every measuring tool.

nodes.name: Negative numbers
nodes.note: Chinese and Hindu texts have them. Europe resists: 'I cannot have negative sheep.' Teaching requires understanding debt as negative property, temperature below a reference point, or mathematical convenience. Adoption requires replacing intuition with rule-following.

nodes.name: Operator symbols: +, -, *, /
nodes.note: Germany adopted + and - in 15th c. for accounting. Multiplication: earlier × (Oughtred) and · (Leibniz) both persist. Division: ÷ (Obelus) is late 17th c. Adoption is printing-driven.

nodes.name: Positional notation and place value
nodes.note: Babylonians and Indians used this. Rome has it for decimals and whole numbers already. Not universal yet in all trades.

nodes.name: Root symbols and radical notation
nodes.note: Medieval √ is a stylized r for radix. Alternative: fractional exponents (1/2 power). Teaching competing notations until one wins printing.

nodes.name: Scientific notation and powers of ten
nodes.note: Saves writing and makes comparison of magnitudes visual. Adoption requires slides rules and tables to persist; hand calculators will make it standard.

nodes.name: Significant figures and precision rules
nodes.note: Requires actually knowing your apparatus uncertainty first. Teaching: students must measure things badly and see the rule explain results. Adoption in labs is slow because it exposes poor work.

nodes.name: Zero as a number
nodes.note: The Hindus and Arabs have this. Europe thinks zero is dangerous or meaningless. Teaching means replacing 'no tens' with 'zero tens': algebra becomes possible. Adoption slow because it threatens calculators' livelihoods.

nodes.name: Acoustics and sound propagation
nodes.note: Newton and Laplace debated whether sound is isothermal or adiabatic. Teaching: waves, not particles. Adoption: slow until mechanical reproduction creates demand.

nodes.name: Aerodynamic lift and wing design
nodes.note: Kutta-Joukowski theorem (1902-1906). Teaching requires wind tunnel or theoretical derivation. Adoption: transforms aviation from dream to engineering.

nodes.name: Blackbody radiation and Planck's law
nodes.note: Ultraviolet catastrophe and Planck's quantum fix (1900). Teaching: experiment shows curve; classical theory predicts infinite intensity at high frequency. Teaching point: sometimes you must invent new physics.

nodes.name: Boltzmann distribution and thermal equilibrium
nodes.note: Everything is exponential: molecular speeds, electron energy levels, reaction rates. Teaching: why ln(k) vs 1/T is linear (Arrhenius equation). Adoption: universal in chemistry and physics.

nodes.name: Diffraction and Fraunhofer patterns
nodes.note: Fraunhofer (1819-1823). Teaching: how gratings work (parallel slits). Adoption: transforms spectroscopy.

nodes.name: Elasticity and Hooke's law
nodes.note: Hooke (1678) discovered spring law; generalized to materials by Thomas Young (1807). Teaching: why materials behave differently. Adoption: foundation for structural engineering.

nodes.name: Electrostatics and Coulomb's law
nodes.note: Coulomb (1785). Teaching: electric field is the concept; force follows. Adoption: foundation for all electric phenomena.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic wave and radiation
nodes.note: Light IS an electromagnetic wave. Teaching: Hertz demonstrated (1887-1888). Adoption: transforms radio and later all wireless communication.

nodes.name: Kinetic energy and potential energy
nodes.note: Leibniz introduced vis viva (living force). Teaching: energy is useful even when forces are complex. Adoption: fast in engineering.

nodes.name: Fluid statics and buoyancy
nodes.note: Archimedes and Hero knew it. Teaching: submerged objects. Adoption: immediate in navigation and dam engineering.

nodes.name: Geometric optics and ray tracing
nodes.note: Fermat's principle (light takes fastest path) explains both laws. Teaching: mirrors and lenses. Adoption: immediate in designing instruments.

nodes.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
nodes.note: Explains Kepler's laws. Teaching: derives planetary orbits. Adoption: transforms astronomy and physics into unified science.

nodes.name: Hydrodynamics and Bernoulli's equation
nodes.note: Bernoulli (1738). Teaching: high velocity means low pressure (why wind lifts roofs). Adoption: essential for pumps, pipes, and aerodynamics.

nodes.name: Kinematics: position, velocity, acceleration
nodes.note: Ancient scholars attempted this without calculus. Teaching is trivial after derivatives exist. Adoption: immediate in physics and engineering.

nodes.name: Kinetic theory of gases
nodes.note: Clausius, Maxwell, Boltzmann (1860s-1870s). Teaching: one molecule has no pressure; billions do. Adoption: transforms thermodynamics from empirical to theoretical.

nodes.name: Magnetostatics and magnetic field
nodes.note: Ampere and Gauss. Teaching: bar magnet, compass, current loop. Adoption: immediate in motors and generators.

nodes.name: Maxwell's equations and electromagnetic theory
nodes.note: Maxwell (1861-1862). Teaching: each equation is comprehensible; together they are profound. Adoption is slow because it requires accepting light is electromagnetic.

nodes.name: Momentum and impulse
nodes.note: Descartes understood conservation; Newton formalized. Teaching: collisions and explosions. Adoption: immediate.

nodes.name: The neutron
nodes.note: Completes the picture: nucleus is protons and neutrons. Teaching: beta decay produces electron and antineutrino (not just released from nucleus). Adoption: opens path to fission.

nodes.name: Newton's three laws of motion
nodes.note: Principia (1687). Teaching: Galileo and Descartes prepared the ground. Adoption: transforms all engineering from qualitative to quantitative.

nodes.name: Nuclear fission and chain reaction
nodes.note: Meitner and Frisch (1938-1939); Manhattan Project (1942-1945). Teaching: Einstein's E = mc², mass defect, reaction rates. Adoption: immediate military application (bomb and reactor).

nodes.name: The nucleus and radioactivity
nodes.note: Rutherford (1911); radioactivity discovered by Becquerel, explained by Rutherford and Soddy. Teaching: gold foil experiment shows nuclear structure. Adoption: opens nuclear physics.

nodes.name: Photoelectric effect and stopping potential
nodes.note: Millikan measured stopping potential (1916). Teaching: light intensity does not matter, only frequency. This seemed absurd to everyone. Adoption took Einstein's Nobel Prize (1921) as proof.

nodes.name: The quantum and photon concept
nodes.note: Planck (1900) solved blackbody; Einstein (1905) applied to photoelectric effect. Teaching: why is h so small? Why can't we see energy packets in everyday light (because intensity is huge). Adoption: slow, even Einstein was reluctant.

nodes.name: Reynolds number and flow regime
nodes.note: Reynolds (1883). Teaching: same flow pattern works at all scales if Re is same. Adoption: essential for aerodynamics and pipeline design.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic spectrum
nodes.note: Visible is tiny fraction (400-700 nm). Teaching: infrared feels like heat, UV causes sunburn, X-rays penetrate flesh. Adoption: telescopes and later radio.

nodes.name: Speed of light as fundamental constant
nodes.note: Galileo, Roemer, Foucault, Bradley all attempted measurement. Teaching: why is it special? Adoption: slow until Einstein.

nodes.name: Statics and forces in equilibrium
nodes.note: Archimedes knew this. Rome has it thoroughly. Teaching is engineering curriculum baseline.

nodes.name: Statistical mechanics and ensemble theory
nodes.note: Boltzmann, Gibbs (1870s-1890s). Teaching requires probability and quantum mechanics for full understanding. Adoption by theoretical physicists first.

nodes.name: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
nodes.note: Heisenberg (1927). Teaching: not instrument limitation, but fundamental. Adoption: slow because it contradicts intuition.

nodes.name: Viscosity and Newton's law of friction
nodes.note: Newton described it qualitatively; Stokes derived drag force on spheres (1851). Teaching: oiliness is measurable. Adoption: essential for lubrication and later fluid mechanics.

nodes.name: Wave mechanics and Schrödinger equation
nodes.note: Schrödinger (1926). Teaching is technically hard and philosophically confusing (wave vs particle). Adoption: slow but now universal in quantum chemistry.

nodes.name: Wave motion and the wave equation
nodes.note: d'Alembert (1746). Teaching: mechanical analogy (vibrating string) then abstract. Adoption: essential for understanding vibration, sound, and later light and matter waves.

nodes.name: Work, power, and efficiency
nodes.note: Defining work and power makes engine efficiency measurable. Teaching: mechanical advantage vs. power (pulleys help force, not power). Adoption: immediate and universal.

nodes.name: Probability axioms and conditional probability
nodes.note: Formalized by Kolmogorov (1933). Teaching starts with dice and urn problems. Adoption: essential for statistics once this century opens.

nodes.name: Central limit theorem
nodes.note: Explains why normal distribution is universal. Teaching requires multiple simulations to convince. Adoption: theoretical foundation for all inferential statistics.

nodes.name: Permutations and combinations
nodes.note: Ancient roots; Pascal systematized. Teaching: counting in two ways (order matters or not). Adoption: fast in gambling and later in all statistics.

nodes.name: Normal (Gaussian) distribution and the bell curve
nodes.note: Gauss, Laplace, de Moivre. Teaching: derive from sums of dice or measurements. Adoption: universal in any quantitative field.

nodes.name: Analysis of variance (ANOVA)
nodes.note: Fisher (1920s). Teaching: one-way then multi-way. Adoption by agricultural and later all experimental science.

nodes.name: Blinding and double-blind experiments
nodes.note: Placebo effect is real and unconscious bias is universal. Teaching: show a color-changing experiment (nothing actually changed) then 'explain' it to subjects, whose reports change. Adoption is slow because it requires admitting fallibility.

nodes.name: Blocking and stratification in experiments
nodes.note: Fisher (1925). Teaching: you know some subjects are different (male/female, old/young); use this. Adoption: standard in agricultural and medical experiments.

nodes.name: Confidence interval and margin of error
nodes.note: Common misunderstanding: the interval is random, not the parameter. Teaching requires clarification. Adoption: standard in polls and clinical trials.

nodes.name: Control chart and statistical process control
nodes.note: Shewhart (1920s) at Western Electric. Teaching: time series is as important as variation. Adoption: transforms quality control from inspection to prediction.

nodes.name: Control group and negative control
nodes.note: Medical tradition going back centuries (though not formalized). Teaching: without it, cannot distinguish treatment from natural history. Adoption is slow in medicine because 'denying' treatment feels unethical.

nodes.name: Correlation and covariance
nodes.note: Galton and Pearson (1880s). Teaching: scatter plot with best-fit line. Adoption: essential for social science and medicine.

nodes.name: Mean, variance, and standard deviation
nodes.note: Quetelet popularized mean and variance (1830s). Teaching: compute by hand for small datasets. Adoption: fast in any measurement discipline.

nodes.name: Mortality table and actuarial science
nodes.note: Graunt (1662) from London bills of mortality. Teaching: data is public; computation is rote. Adoption: fast in insurance once mathematics spreads.

nodes.name: Randomisation and random assignment
nodes.note: Fisher advocated it for agricultural trials. Teaching: why matters (controls bias), how to do it (draw lots, random number table). Adoption is slow because it requires surrendering control.

nodes.name: Linear regression and the line of best fit
nodes.note: Legendre and Gauss (1805-1812); refined by Pearson. Teaching: fit to data, predict new y from new x. Adoption: universal in experiments.

nodes.name: Sampling theory and the standard error
nodes.note: Practical foundation for all surveys. Teaching: simulate draws from a population. Adoption: fast in quality control.

nodes.name: Significance test and p-value
nodes.note: Fisher popularized p-value; Neyman-Pearson developed hypothesis testing framework. Teaching: both ideas matter but are often confused. Adoption: dominant but controversial by end of 20th century.

nodes.name: Student's t-test for mean differences
nodes.note: Gosset (pseudonym 'Student', 1908) working in brewing. Teaching requires Student's t distribution tables. Adoption: universal in comparing experiments.

nodes.name: Found the school (the Museum)
nodes.note: The pivot of the entire game. Converts your hours into other people's hours permanently. Every year of delay here costs more than any single technology. Grants +4 scholars and +2 scholars/yr thereafter. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. OPTIONAL. Nothing in the technical tree requires it. It is simply the highest-leverage thing you can spend money on, because it converts your hours into other people's hours permanently. You may decline to found it and hire craftsmen forever instead; the simulator will let you, and will show you the cost.

nodes.name: Controlled experiment, hypothesis, replication, publication
nodes.note: The hard part is not stating it, it is displacing Aristotelian authority. Risk is high because the failure mode is cultural, not technical. Multiplier on every research node thereafter. Contradicting Aristotle and Galen in public is a social act before it is an intellectual one, and their defenders hold the chairs, the patronage and the medical guild. Expect organised opposition, not curiosity.

nodes.name: Screw-cutting lathe with lead screw and slide rest
nodes.note: The machine that makes machines. Everything after this gets easier, and each generation of lathe builds a better one. Maudslay's insight is the slide rest: take the tool out of the operator's hand and the accuracy stops depending on his wrist.

nodes.name: Anchor
nodes.note: Heavy iron-shank anchor with wooden flukes; holds a ship in sand or mud; chains and cable are rope, which cost money to replace.

nodes.name: Astronomical tables
nodes.note: Pre-compute the position of the sun, moon, and stars for centuries ahead; used for latitude, longitude by lunar distances, and checking accuracy; the Nautical Almanac. nodes.name: Backstaff for latitude
nodes.note: Observe the sun's shadow rather than looking at it; more accurate than the cross-staff; still limited by eye and wind movement; typically accurate to 0.3 degrees.

nodes.name: Water-tube boiler
nodes.note: Tubes carry hot combustion gases; water flows in separate tubes; higher heat transfer and safety; pressures to 300 psi and higher; faster steam production than fire-tube boilers.

nodes.name: Bowsprit
nodes.note: A spar extending forward from the bow to which jibs are attached; spreads the sail plan and improves balance; very exposed to breaking in heavy seas.

nodes.name: Buoy
nodes.note: A floating marker anchored to a rock or sandbar; guides ships around hazards; a coded system of colors and shapes lets pilots recognize them at distance. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. nodes.name: Canal lock
nodes.note: An enclosed chamber with gates; fill to float a boat up, drain to lower it down; allows ships to traverse rivers with different water levels and connects seas at different heights.

nodes.name: Carvel planking
nodes.note: Planks laid edge-to-edge and edge-fitted flush; smoother and stronger than clinker, allows larger ships; requires excellent carpentry and precise tools.

nodes.name: Navigation charts
nodes.note: Systematically plot known coastlines, harbours, and hazards; use magnetic compass rose; accumulate centuries of observation; early charts are crude but better than guesswork. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Clinker planking
nodes.note: Planks overlap like roof shingles and are rivetted at the overlap; easier to build than carvel, lighter, more flexible; popular in northern Europe.

nodes.name: Coastal pilotage
nodes.note: Experienced pilots guide ships via visual landmarks, tides, and memory; safe within sight of land; at sea they are lost.

nodes.name: Compartmented hull
nodes.note: Watertight bulkheads divide the hull into sections; if one section is breached, it floods but does not sink the ship; saves more lives than lifeboats.

nodes.name: Compound and triple expansion engine
nodes.note: Multiple cylinders at different pressures; steam expands through each in turn; triples fuel efficiency compared to a simple engine; coal consumption becomes the limiting factor.

nodes.name: Copper-sheathed hull
nodes.note: Thin copper sheet nailed over the hull below the waterline; resists shipworm better than lead and does not pit; very expensive but saves years of ship life. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. nodes.name: Cross-staff for latitude
nodes.note: Hold a calibrated wooden cross at arm's length; move the cross-bar until it aligns the sun with the horizon; read the angle; gives latitude to within a degree or so.

nodes.name: Diesel engine ship
nodes.note: Internal combustion engine burning fuel oil; more efficient than steam turbines and no need to carry water or boilers; standard in merchant ships by 1920.

nodes.name: Diving bell
nodes.note: An air-filled bell lowered to the seafloor on a rope; a diver climbs in, breathes the air, works for a few minutes, then is pulled up; depth limited to 40 feet and time to 15 minutes. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Diving suit and air pump
nodes.note: Waterproof suit with helmet, fed air by hose from a steam-driven pump on the surface; allows work at 200 feet for an hour; nitrogen narcosis and decompression sickness are poorly understood.

nodes.name: Dredging
nodes.note: Mechanically scoop mud and sediment from a harbour or river bottom; deepens channels and prevents silting; essential for maintaining harbours over decades.

nodes.name: Dry compass card
nodes.note: A card with 32 points marked, pivoted on a needle magnetized by rubbing with lodestone, enclosed in a box; far more stable than a wet compass floating in oil.

nodes.name: Drydock
nodes.note: An enclosed basin with gates; flood to float the ship in, then pump or drain to expose the hull for repairs and careening; very expensive, worth it only for major harbours.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic wave theory
nodes.note: Maxwell showed that light is an electromagnetic wave; this understanding underpins sonar, radar, and radio; converts acoustic and optical problems into a unified framework. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Fore-and-aft rig
nodes.note: Sails set along the length of the mast rather than across it; requires stronger masts and better carpentry; allows true beating to windward with multiple tacks.

nodes.name: Lighthouse with Fresnel lens
nodes.note: A stepped glass lens focuses light from a lantern into a parallel beam visible for 20 miles; vastly brighter than a simple lens; standard by 1850.

nodes.name: Fuel oil burner
nodes.note: Atomize fuel oil and spray it into a furnace; burns cleaner and hotter than coal; enables diesel engines and high-pressure steam boilers; requires fuel oil supply infrastructure. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Artificial harbours in hydraulic concrete
nodes.note: Rome builds harbours at Portus and Caesarea using pozzolanic concrete that sets underwater; breakwaters and jetties protect anchorages.

nodes.name: Iron hull
nodes.note: A ship built entirely of iron plates riveted together; floats because the average density is low (air inside); immune to shipworm and rot; three times the tonnage of wood for the same structural weight.

nodes.name: Jib sail
nodes.note: Triangular sail forward of the mast; helps turn the ship and improves windward work; adds to total canvas with minimal weight.

nodes.name: Lateen sail
nodes.note: A triangular sail rigged along the mast at an angle, known in the Mediterranean; can sail 6 to 8 points from the wind, not 11-12 like modern fore-and-aft, but a real improvement over square.

nodes.name: Lead-line and hydrographic survey
nodes.note: Systematically map harbour depths and holding ground; use a marked line with lead weight and hollow underside (carries samples of sand, shells, mud); plot on charts.

nodes.name: Lead sheathing against shipworm
nodes.note: Lead sheet nailed over the underwater hull prevents shipworm (Teredo) boring into timber; Rome has done this for decades; it is perishable and must be renewed regularly.

nodes.name: Lifeboat
nodes.note: A strong open boat carried on davits (cranes); can be launched quickly; holds a fraction of the crew; crew discipline and adequate numbers matter far more than equipment.

nodes.name: Lodestone knowledge
nodes.note: Rome knows that lodestones attract iron; the knowledge that this is true even when spinning, and points north, is not yet recorded in the literature.

nodes.name: Log line for speed
nodes.note: A light wooden board (the log) on a long knotted line; thrown overboard, it stays in place while the ship moves; count the knots paid out in a sand-glass interval to find speed.

nodes.name: Lunar distance method for longitude
nodes.note: Measure the angle between the moon and a known star; look up the time of that angle in pre-computed tables; convert time to longitude; works without a chronometer but requires superlative tables and a calm hand.

nodes.name: Magnetic compass
nodes.note: A pivoted compass card with a magnetized needle shows north in any weather, by day or night, independent of landmarks; one of the pivotal inventions for open-sea navigation. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.]

nodes.name: Marine chronometer
nodes.note: A clock that keeps time to better than 1 second per day at sea despite temperature swings and ship motion; solved by Harrison via bimetallic compensation and friction balance; the breakthrough for longitude.

nodes.name: Mercator projection
nodes.note: Project the globe onto a cylinder; latitude and longitude become straight lines; a rhumb line (constant compass heading) becomes straight; game-changing for charts.

nodes.name: Large merchant sailing ships
nodes.note: Rome already operates grain ships of 350 tonnes or more to Alexandria; the Fayum papyri and wrecks confirm sophisticated hull design and large crews.

nodes.name: Monsoon route to India
nodes.note: The Red Sea and Indian Ocean route is now known to sail southwest with summer monsoon to India, return northeast with winter monsoon; still hazardous and slow.

nodes.name: Mortise-and-tenon hull construction
nodes.note: Rome's Mediterranean shipwrights already lock planks edge-to-edge with interlocking joints; this is shell-first construction, building the hull shell before framing.

nodes.name: Multiple masts
nodes.note: Ships with two or three masts can carry more sail, balance trim better, and sacrifice fewer sails if one mast is damaged; requires significantly stronger hulls.

nodes.name: Paddle wheel
nodes.note: Large wheels with flat paddles on each side, driven by a steam engine; inherently inefficient (submerges too much water near the surface) and loses power in a heavy sea.

nodes.name: Pharos lighthouse
nodes.note: The great tower at Alexandria with fire beacon at night; one of Rome's most famous navigational aids; visible for miles at sea.

nodes.name: Screw propeller
nodes.note: A helical blade (like an Archimedean screw) beneath the stern, spinning at high speed; far more efficient than a paddle wheel, especially in heavy seas and at full speed.

nodes.name: Sextant for latitude and more
nodes.note: Uses mirrors and a vernier scale; measure angles up to 120 degrees; accurate to 0.1 degree; also measures stellar altitudes for latitude at night; the standard instrument for three centuries.

nodes.name: Skeleton-first hull construction
nodes.note: Build the frame (ribs) first, then plank over it, not vice versa; cheaper and faster, scales to much larger ships, and uses timber more efficiently; requires a fundamental rethinking of carpentry.

nodes.name: Sonar and echo sounding
nodes.note: Transmit an acoustic pulse into water, listen for the echo; measures depth and detects underwater objects; replaces the lead-line and adds a new dimension to navigation. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_measure_time_ms added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: echo sounding requires millisecond timing for distance measurement]

nodes.name: Sounding lines
nodes.note: A knotted rope with a lead weight; tossed overboard to measure water depth and bottom type; pilots memorize landmarks and feel the bottom.

nodes.name: Spritsail
nodes.note: A sail rigged diagonally across the mast with a spar (the sprit); gives some directional control compared to pure square rig.

nodes.name: Square sail with brails
nodes.note: The square sail hangs from a yard; brails (lines running to the yard) gather it up when not needed; it cannot work to windward.

nodes.name: Steam turbine at sea
nodes.note: Steam jets hit curved blades on a fast-spinning rotor; much smaller, lighter, and cheaper than reciprocating engines for the same power; direct drive to a propeller.

nodes.name: Steel hull
nodes.note: Steel is stronger and tougher than iron; allows thinner, lighter hulls for the same strength; standard by 1890; vastly better fatigue resistance than iron.

nodes.name: Steering oars
nodes.note: Large oars mounted on each quarter (side) of the stern, worked by pilots; slow and inefficient on large hulls with a following sea.

nodes.name: Sternpost rudder
nodes.note: A single flat board hung vertically at the stern from iron pintles, turned by a tiller; much more responsive than steering oars on large hulls, especially in following seas.

nodes.name: Submarine
nodes.note: A small strong hull that submerges; propelled by electric motors on batteries or a diesel on the surface; requires precise depth control, air supply, and crew training; first military use in WWI. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_10um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: pressure hull requires slide rest and micrometer precision for structural integrity at depth]

nodes.name: Submarine telegraph cable
nodes.note: Copper conductor insulated with gutta percha (unobtainable), wrapped in iron armor; gutta percha fails, so use bitumen and later synthetic rubber instead, accepting higher loss. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: insulation uniformity critical for underwater telegraph signal quality]

nodes.name: Torpedo
nodes.note: A self-propelled warhead driven by a small steam engine or compressed air, launched from a tube; detonates on contact or by timed fuse; extends the range of naval combat beyond line of sight.

nodes.name: Traverse board
nodes.note: A board with holes and a peg; log the ship's course and speed every hour; sum them at the end of the watch to estimate position; crude but systematic.

nodes.name: Optical semaphore chain
nodes.note: Chappe's chain did Paris to Lille, 230 km, in minutes. Rome to the Rhine in a day instead of a month is worth more to an emperor than any weapon. THIS is the demonstration that buys imperial patronage. Requires the telescope to read the arms at distance.

nodes.name: Four-point probe, Hall effect, carrier measurement
nodes.note: You cannot purify what you cannot measure. Resistivity to four significant figures and a Hall measurement for carrier type and density are the feedback loop that makes the entire purification programme convergent instead of blind. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_measure_elec added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: four-point probe and Hall effect require electrical measurement]

nodes.name: Silicon: trichlorosilane purification and high-temperature crystal growth
nodes.note: Silicon is everywhere, which is why it wins in the end, and it melts at 1414 C against germanium's 938 C, needs far better crucible chemistry, and its purification runs through trichlorosilane. Germanium first is the right bootstrap order and history agrees for exactly these reasons. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_measure_temp_hi added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: 1414 C crystal growth requires high-temperature pyrometry]

nodes.name: Czochralski single crystal growth and controlled doping
nodes.note: Dip a seed into the melt and pull slowly while rotating. Grain boundaries destroy carrier lifetime, so polycrystalline germanium will never make a working transistor no matter how pure it is. Add the dopant to the melt in weighed traces; this is where the analytical balance earns its keep two centuries later. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_measure_temp_hi, cap_tol_10um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: Czochralski pulling requires high-temperature pyrometry at melting point and slide rest precision for seed control]

nodes.name: Hard soap from oil and causticised lye
nodes.note: Rome has sapo only as a Gallic hair pomade (Pliny NH 28.191). Causticise wood-ash lye with slaked lime and boil with olive oil to a hard bar. Sells to baths and fullers. Early cash, teaches your staff basic process control, and it is completely unthreatening.

nodes.name: Leblanc and later Solvay soda
nodes.note: Frees you from the Egyptian natron supply and gives alkali in industrial quantity for glass, soap, paper and textiles. Leblanc is filthy: the hydrogen chloride and sulfide waste caused genuine environmental disasters in Britain. Condense the acid gas from the start; you will want the hydrochloric acid anyway. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Prism and grating spectroscope
nodes.note: Highest information yield per denarius of any instrument you can build. Emission lines identify elements you have no other way to detect, and much later it is how you verify that your germanium is actually germanium. [FIXED after independent audit: a ruled grating needs the finest screw you own; the node declared no tolerance rung.]

nodes.name: Averages, error, sampling, controlled comparison
nodes.note: Enables the medical trials that make germ theory persuasive rather than merely correct, and enables census and annona work that buys imperial favour.

nodes.name: Newcomen atmospheric engine
nodes.note: Appallingly inefficient, around 0.5 to 1 percent, but it does not care: its job is pumping water out of coal and metal mines, where the fuel is free at the pithead. Do not attempt this before water power is exhausted; Italy and Gaul have rivers. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: High pressure steam and adequate boilers
nodes.note: Power density enough for locomotives and ships. Be honest with your students about how many people early boilers killed, and build a hydraulic test and a relief valve into the very first one. A boiler explosion in Rome will be read as divine judgment on the whole programme. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Separate condenser and rotative engines
nodes.note: Roughly a fourfold fuel saving, plus rotative motion via the sun and planet gear, which puts an engine anywhere rather than only at a pithead. This is the node that lets industry leave the riverbank. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: piston-cylinder precision for efficient sealing and smooth operation]

nodes.name: Oil of vitriol by dry distillation of green vitriol
nodes.note: The master key to all chemistry. Green vitriol lies in heaps at every pyrite mine as a weathering product and Rome has no idea what it is for. High risk because the retorts fail constantly at the temperature required. Small scale, expensive acid, but it bootstraps the chamber process. [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_heat_0700 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: green vitriol dehydration at approximately 480 C requires pottery kiln scale heat]

nodes.name: Electric telegraph
nodes.note: The killer application for an empire and the thing that makes your programme permanently indispensable to the State. Glass or ceramic insulators on poles, relays every few tens of kilometres, Daniell cells at each station. Once the Rhine frontier can answer Rome in an hour, no emperor will ever let your institute be closed. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Refracting telescope
nodes.note: Military and naval value is immediate and obvious, which makes it one of the safest impressive things you can make. Chromatic aberration forces long tubes until you have flint glass for achromats.

nodes.name: Buttons and buttonholes
nodes.note: Buttonholes cut and sewn by hand initially, later machine-cut. Buttons turned from bone, wood, or cast metals. Enables fitted garments that open and close easily, replacing laces and ties. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Calico printing with blocks
nodes.note: Hand-carved wooden blocks print colors onto cloth by pressing into dye paste then cloth. Each color requires separate block and pass. Produces decorative cotton fabrics. Hand skill and artistic eye essential. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Canvas cloth
nodes.note: Heavy, tightly-woven linen cloth for sails, tents, and durable goods. Weave density and thread weight matter more than fiber fineness.

nodes.name: Carding fibers
nodes.note: Wooden carding combs with wire teeth card wool into parallel fibers ready for spinning. Increases fineness of yarn but slower than combing.

nodes.name: Chlorine bleaching of cloth
nodes.note: Cl2 gas or hypochlorite solution bleaches cloth in hours instead of weeks. 100x speedup ends field bleaching bottleneck. Risks fabric damage if concentration not controlled. Requires chlorine production (electrolytic or chemical) from heavy industry. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Chrome tanning of leather
nodes.note: Chromium salts cross-link collagen in hides in days instead of weeks (vegetable tanning). Produces soft, supple leather resistant to heat. Requires chromium compound production and process control. Overtakes vegetable tanning by early 1900s. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Combing fibers
nodes.note: Iron-toothed combs arrange long fibers in parallel. Faster and cleaner output than carding, produces stronger yarn. Older technique than carding.

nodes.name: Cotton gin with saw
nodes.note: Rotating saw cylinder draws lint through spacing slots while stationary brush removes lint. Whitney saw gin (1793) produces 50 lbs/day vs 1 lb/day by hand. Game-changing for cotton profitability, tragically driving slavery expansion.

nodes.name: Cotton by trade
nodes.note: Cotton imported from India and traded in Roman markets. Small quantities, expensive.

nodes.name: Drop spindle
nodes.note: Simple weighted spindle suspended by thread. Skill-dependent, slow. Standard Roman spinning method.

nodes.name: Dyeing with madder root
nodes.note: Madder root (Rubia tinctorum) produces reds and oranges. Requires mordanting to set dye. Standard Roman dye.

nodes.name: Murex purple dyeing
nodes.note: Purple dye from murex snail gland secretion. Tyrian purple, supremely expensive, only for imperial and elite garments.

nodes.name: Dyeing with woad
nodes.note: Woad (Isatis tinctoria) produces blues. Leaves fermented then oxidized. Common and relatively cheap blue dye.

nodes.name: Felting
nodes.note: Matting wool fibers with moisture and heat to create felt. Ancient technique for hats, cloaks, armor padding.

nodes.name: Field bleaching with sun
nodes.note: Spreading wet cloth on grass, rewetting daily, exposed to sunlight for weeks. Oxidizes and bleaches fibers white. Bottleneck of textile production: chlorine bleaching is 100x faster. Weather dependent. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Fitted garment tailoring
nodes.note: Cutting and sewing cloth to body shape instead of wrapping rectangles. Requires pattern pieces scaled to measurements. Enables close-fitting tunics and garments.

nodes.name: Flying shuttle
nodes.note: Mechanical shuttle box throws shuttle left-right via spring or lever, eliminating need to reach across loom. One weaver now handles wide looms. Kay 1733. Triples weaving speed. Labor displacement sparks Luddite unrest.

nodes.name: Fulling cloth
nodes.note: Hand fulling: beating woven cloth in lye-filled tub to felt and shrink fibers. Labor-intensive, done by fullers.

nodes.name: Water-powered fulling mill
nodes.note: Water-driven heavy mallets or rollers beat cloth in lye to felt and shrink. Replaces hand fullers working for hours in tubs. Enables fuller scale production. Requires water power site and capital infrastructure.

nodes.name: Hand ginning cotton
nodes.note: Removing seeds from cotton by hand using a stick or roller. Slow: produces about 1 lb clean cotton per day. Mechanical ginning is revolutionary leap.

nodes.name: Horizontal loom
nodes.note: Refined horizontal loom with better shaft control and cloth beam tension. Slightly faster than two-beam. Intermediate step toward mechanized looms.

nodes.name: Hosiery production
nodes.note: Production of stockings and socks via knitting frame. Enables mass market for close-fitting legwear. Comfort and fit improve dramatically over hand-knit. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Indigo dyeing
nodes.note: Indigo vat requires reduction (removal of oxygen) with lime and charcoal. Color sets by oxidation in air after dipping. Produces brilliant fast blue superior to woad. Imported indigo becomes available medieval period onward.

nodes.name: Jacquard loom with punched cards
nodes.note: Punched cards control which warp threads rise per pick. Each card has holes engaging or disengaging hooks. Complex patterns woven without hand shaft control. Cards must be hand-prepared; later inspires computer punch-card era. Transforms pattern-weaving from artisanal to systematic. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Knitting frame
nodes.note: Stocking frame (William Lee, 1589). Reciprocating needles with closing latches, hand or foot powered. Produces stockings mechanically. Displaces hand knitters, enables mass hosiery. Complex precision mechanism.

nodes.name: Linen fiber from flax
nodes.note: Linen from flax after retting and breaking. Rome produces linen cloth routinely.

nodes.name: Mercerisation of cotton
nodes.note: Treating cotton yarn or cloth with sodium hydroxide under tension causes fibers to swell and straighten, increasing luster and dye uptake. Mercerized cotton resembles silk. Requires caustic soda production and careful process control. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Mordanting dyes with alum
nodes.note: Alum mordant fixes dyes to fiber. Cloth treated with alum before dyeing absorbs color much more effectively and resists fading. Standard practice for madder and other dyes.

nodes.name: Nylon fiber
nodes.note: Polyamide fiber synthesized from coal tar via complex organic chemistry (Carothers, 1935). Requires high-temperature reactors, vacuum conditions, precise monomer synthesis, and polymerization control. Strongest fiber yet, endless customization. Fully replaces some natural uses. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: polyamide polymerization requires rough vacuum to remove water and ammonia byproducts]

nodes.name: Standard pattern cutting and sizing
nodes.note: Standardized paper patterns for garment pieces scaled to common sizes (small/medium/large). Enables fast cutting and consistent fit without measuring individuals. Speeds production and reduces skilled labor in cutting. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Power loom
nodes.note: Water-driven loom with automatic shuttle throw and shaft control via cams. Weaving speed increases 4-5x. Cloth quality variable until tension control perfected. Enormous labor displacement.

nodes.name: Rayon from nitrocellulose
nodes.note: Dissolving nitrocellulose in ether-alcohol, forcing through spinnerets into acid coagulant, regenerating cellulose. First synthetic fiber, 1889 (Chardonnet). Requires precise chemistry, temperature, and concentration control. Somewhat fragile in wet state.

nodes.name: Rayon from viscose
nodes.note: Dissolving wood pulp in alkaline sulfide creating viscose paste, aging, forcing through spinnerets into acid bath regenerating cellulose fiber. By 1900 displaces much nitrocellulose. More robust than nitro-rayon. Requires wood pulp supply and chemical process control.

nodes.name: Roller printing of cloth
nodes.note: Engraved copper or steel rollers rotate through dye paste then press pattern onto cloth continuously. Replaces block printing entirely: 100x faster, consistent patterns, multiple colors per pass via multiple rollers. Requires precision engraving and gear coordination.

nodes.name: Rope walk and cordage
nodes.note: Long building (300-400 ft) where fiber strands are twisted together while walking backward. Produces rope and cordage at scale. Standard for ship rigging and maritime use.

nodes.name: Sailcloth
nodes.note: Heavy linen or hemp cloth used for sails. Rome produces for naval fleet. Requires tight weave and strong yarn.

nodes.name: Sewing machine with lockstitch
nodes.note: Two non-obvious inventions: lockstitch (needle passes through cloth-held loop made by shuttle beneath, creating loop for next pass) and eye-pointed needle (eye at tip, not butt). Hand or treadle powered. Serrated presser foot holds fabric. Replaces hand sewers, mostly women.

nodes.name: Shoddy and recycled wool
nodes.note: Shredding old wool cloth into fibers, then re-carding and re-spinning into new yarn. Produces weaker yarn but enables reuse of scrap wool for cheaper cloth.

nodes.name: Silk by trade
nodes.note: Silk traded via Silk Road, closely guarded by Persia. Rare, luxury good.

nodes.name: Spinning jenny
nodes.note: Hand-cranked machine with 8-16 spindles on one rail, all driven by single crank. One operator spins multiple threads simultaneously. Hargreaves 1764. Enables 8-16x labor displacement. Massive unemployment among spinners.

nodes.name: Spinning mule (jenny plus frame)
nodes.note: Hand-cranked carriage on rails moves in-out while spindles rotate. Moving carriage stretches roving as spindles twist, producing finer, stronger thread than jenny or frame alone. Can produce very fine yarn. Later steam-powered. Skilled operation essential.

nodes.name: Spinning wheel with flyer
nodes.note: The flyer is the invention, not the wheel. The flyer twists and winds yarn simultaneously rather than alternately, roughly tripling output per spinner. Hand or foot powered. Displaces many spinners.

nodes.name: Synthetic aniline dyes
nodes.note: Aniline dyes (Mauveine and successors) from coal tar offer brilliant colors, lower cost, and consistency vs natural dyes. No mordanting required for most. Destroys market for madder, indigo, cochineal. By-product of coal industry. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tape measure standardization
nodes.note: Flexible calibrated tape in inches or centimeters with brass end caps. Enables rapid precise body measurements for fitting. Standardization of units also enables pattern size labeling. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Textile mill and factory system
nodes.note: Multi-story water-powered mill integrating spinning, weaving, finishing under one roof. Centralized production, child and female labor prevalent. Requires water power, capital, organization, and transportation. Birth of industrial production system.

nodes.name: Treadle loom
nodes.note: Foot pedals control loom shafts via connecting rods and cams, freeing hands to throw shuttle. Speeds weaving noticeably. Weaver must still operate shuttle by hand.

nodes.name: Two-beam loom
nodes.note: Horizontal loom with warp tensioned between two beams. Faster than warp-weighted, standard for linen and wool in Roman period.

nodes.name: Vegetable tanning of leather
nodes.note: Tanning hides with oak or chestnut bark tannins in vats over weeks. Produces flexible, durable leather resistant to rot. Process is standardized by medieval period but knowledge of bark selection and timing matters. [AUDIT: this node does not declare the capability rung it needs. An automated pass once inferred one, and an independent review found that EVERY inferred rung it sampled was wrong, so all of them were reverted. The gap is left visible on purpose: a missing prerequisite you can see beats a wrong one you cannot.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Warp-weighted loom
nodes.note: Vertical loom with weights hanging on warp threads. Slow but reliable for narrow textiles and tapestries.

nodes.name: Water frame spinner
nodes.note: Water-powered spinning: spindle shaft driven continuously by water wheel via gearing. Produces tightly twisted warp yarn suitable for looms. Arkwright 1769. Requires factory-scale capital. Transforms spinning from cottage to factory.

nodes.name: Wool fiber
nodes.note: Wool fiber from sheep, available in Roman households. No processing required beyond shearing and basic cleaning.

nodes.name: Wool combing machinery
nodes.note: Water-powered rollers with metal pins comb wool fibers to parallelism. Produces cleaner, stronger yarn than hand combing. One machine replaces many combers. Requires substantial capital and water power.

nodes.name: Heat, energy, entropy, the gas laws
