nodes.note: Requires the thermometer to be more than words. Without it you cannot design an efficient engine or a controlled furnace.

nodes.name: Sealed liquid-in-glass thermometer with fixed points
nodes.note: Melting ice and boiling water as fixed points. Without a repeatable temperature scale not one recipe in this guide can be transmitted to anyone who is not standing beside you. Prerequisite for thermodynamics being real rather than rhetorical.

nodes.name: Ackermann steering geometry
nodes.kb: Front wheels steered so inner wheel turns more than outer
nodes.note: Inner wheel scrubs less at full lock; eliminates tire wear in corners and improves cornering stability. All modern steering uses this.

nodes.name: Air filter: intake cleaning
nodes.kb: Cloth or paper element traps dust from intake air
nodes.note: Prevents sand and dirt from scoring cylinders; must be cleaned frequently. Clogged filter reduces power.

nodes.name: Anti-siphon valve in fuel line
nodes.kb: One-way valve prevents fuel from siphoning back to tank
nodes.note: Prevents carburettor flooding when pump is idle; ball check or spring-loaded disc. Simple and reliable.

nodes.name: Articulated trailer: semi-trailer
nodes.kb: Unpowered trailer coupled with fifth wheel to powered tractor
nodes.note: Trailer carries 10 to 20 tonnes; fifth wheel distribution allows tractor to navigate tight corners. Payload efficiency gains 50 percent.

nodes.name: Automatic transmission: hydraulic
nodes.kb: Hydraulic torque converter shifts gears automatically
nodes.note: Torque converter uses hydraulic fluid as transmission medium; pressure regulator shifts gears by engaging clutch packs. Complex and smooth.

nodes.name: Ball bearing: spherical
nodes.kb: Hardened steel balls in cage on hardened grooved races
nodes.note: Spheres conform to race geometry; friction is 1/100th of plain bearing. Requires tolerance and hardness. Standard in bicycles and motors.

nodes.name: Brake shoe: curved pad
nodes.kb: Curved cast iron pad presses on wheel rim or drum by lever
nodes.note: Curved form conforms to wheel; friction coefficient is 0.3 to 0.4. Wears smooth; brake fade if overheated. Standard on carts and coaches.

nodes.name: Caliper brake: side-pull
nodes.kb: Twin arms pivot at pivot bolt; pads squeeze rim from sides
nodes.note: Cable-actuated lever pulls arm; return spring releases. Friction pads require constant replacement. No brake fade on light speeds.

nodes.name: Cam follower and tappet
nodes.kb: Hardened follower rides on camshaft lobe and operates valve
nodes.note: Roller followers reduce friction compared to flat or spherical; hardness prevents wear under high Hertzian stress.

nodes.name: Cambered road and drainage
nodes.kb: Road surface slopes from centre to edges; ditches along sides
nodes.note: Water runs off to sides instead of pooling; eliminates mud pits and wheel ruts. Simple geometry; the slope is a few per cent.

nodes.name: Carbide headlamp
nodes.kb: Acetylene gas from carbide and water burns with bright flame
nodes.note: Calcium carbide reacts with water to produce acetylene; bright white flame. Generates heat inside lamp; safety valve required.

nodes.name: Carburettor: fuel atomiser
nodes.kb: Moving air through venturi creates vacuum to atomise fuel
nodes.note: Bernoulli effect pulls fuel into airstream; float chamber maintains level. Throttle valve controls air flow and mixture ratio.

nodes.name: Caterpillar track: endless belt
nodes.kb: Linked steel shoes on driving sprockets distribute load over wide area
nodes.note: Tracks climb steep slopes and cross soft ground; mud does not cling to shoes. Higher traction than wheels. Used on tanks and heavy dozers.

nodes.name: Chain drive: roller chain
nodes.kb: Rollers on links mesh with sprockets to transmit power
nodes.note: Decouples crank size from wheel size; enables small wheel with high speed. Rollers reduce wear on sprockets; chain stretches with use.

nodes.name: Coil ignition: battery and breaker
nodes.kb: Battery powers coil; breaker points open to induce spark at plug
nodes.note: Breaker points are mechanical; timing is set by cam lobe. Requires battery maintenance. More reliable than magneto at high speeds.

nodes.name: Coil spring: helical wire
nodes.kb: Wire or steel rod wound in helix; compresses under load
nodes.note: Uniform spring rate over travel; no friction loss like leaf springs. Compact; fits inside axle tubes. Oscillates without damping.

nodes.name: Reinforced concrete road
nodes.kb: Steel-reinforced Portland cement slab laid on prepared base
nodes.note: Monolithic slab eliminates rutting and stone rattle; steel prevents cracking under load. Lasts 40 years. Expensive but fast traffic.

nodes.name: Cone clutch: friction surface
nodes.kb: Male and female cones interlock; axial force engages drive
nodes.note: Conical geometry increases normal force and torque capacity at shallow angles. Slipping heats both surfaces; requires cooling time.

nodes.name: Connecting rod: piston link
nodes.kb: Steel link connects piston to crankshaft; transfers reciprocal motion to rotary
nodes.note: I-beam section resists bending; pin holes at each end. Mass must be balanced for high-speed rotation or vibration is severe.

nodes.name: Cooling fan: mechanical drive
nodes.kb: Spinning blades pull air through radiator fins
nodes.note: Fan speed follows engine speed via belt; high-speed spinning creates significant parasitic drag. Viscous fan clutch reduces load at idle.

nodes.name: Dead axle: non-driven
nodes.kb: Axle does not rotate; wheels spin freely on bearings
nodes.note: Used for steering and rear trailer axles; no power transmission. Simpler than live axle.

nodes.name: Derailleur: chain shifter
nodes.kb: Pivot arm shifts chain between sprockets; cable controlled
nodes.note: Lever or cable shifts chain sideways onto cogs; tension arm maintains chain slack. Requires precise cable routing and spring tuning.

nodes.name: Differential: bevel gears
nodes.kb: Four-gear spider lets driven wheels turn at different speeds in corners
nodes.note: Without this the inside wheel scrubs 15 percent and the axle twists; with it, smooth cornering. Essential for motor vehicles and powered carts.

nodes.name: Disc brake: pad on disk
nodes.kb: Brake pads squeeze rotating disk; high friction, excellent cooling
nodes.note: Disk cools by convection; no fade even in continuous braking. Linear force; no self-energizing issues. Modern standard.

nodes.name: Distributor: switching contacts
nodes.kb: Rotating contact arm sends voltage to each spark plug in sequence
nodes.note: Synchronous with engine rotation; rotor opens and closes circuits. Must handle thousands of switching cycles per minute.

nodes.name: Drum brake: shoes in cylinder
nodes.kb: Two shoes inside rotating drum; hydraulic or cable pulls them out
nodes.note: Enclosed brakes protect from water and mud; self-energizing if shoes are wedged into drum. Fade if overheated; requires cooling time.

nodes.name: Dynamo: rotary power generator
nodes.kb: Spinning armature in magnetic field generates voltage to charge battery
nodes.note: Engine drives dynamo via belt; output voltage must exceed battery voltage for charging. Regulator disconnects if voltage is too high.

nodes.name: Electric starter motor
nodes.kb: Battery-powered motor with pinion gear engages flywheel
nodes.note: Eliminates hand-crank; starter disengages when engine fires. Bendix drive uses overrunning clutch for safety.

nodes.name: Tram: electric powered
nodes.kb: Electric motor powered from overhead wires via trolley pole
nodes.note: DC motor efficiency and smooth control are superior to steam. Trolley pole reaches overhead conductor; braking recovers energy.

nodes.name: Elliptic spring: single curved
nodes.kb: Single curved plate hung from axle; smooth compliance
nodes.note: Smoothly distributes bump energy; eliminates stacking friction loss. Used front and rear; lighter and quieter than leaf springs.

nodes.name: Engine block: cast cylinder
nodes.kb: Cast iron monolithic block holds cylinders and bearing supports
nodes.note: Single casting eliminates many seams; cooling jackets are sand-cored. Boring and honing cylinders to tolerance requires careful tool control.

nodes.name: Epicyclic gearbox: planetary
nodes.kb: Small gears orbit around central sun gear; multiple ratios by holding components
nodes.note: Very compact; ratios determined by which element is held fixed. Used in early automatic transmissions and in-wheel motors.

nodes.name: Exhaust valve with spring
nodes.kb: Heat-resistant valve opens and closes exhaust port
nodes.note: Exhaust valve sees combustion temperature; must withstand thermal cycling. Nickel and chromium alloying required. Valve seating is critical.

nodes.name: Fan belt and pulley drive
nodes.kb: V-belt wrapped around pulleys drives cooling fan
nodes.note: Belt must be tensioned correctly; slipping causes loss, breakage causes overheating. Replaceable; tension checked periodically.

nodes.name: Fifth wheel coupling
nodes.kb: Articulated hitch between tractor and trailer via rotating disk
nodes.note: Low-friction pivot lets trailer turn independently; no stress on kingpin. Enables articulated rigs and half-tracks.

nodes.name: Freewheel: ratchet hub
nodes.kb: Hub spins freely when pedals stop; mechanical ratchet
nodes.note: Pawl and ratchet; wheel keeps spinning downhill without pedaling. Eliminates pedal speed constraint; coasting is essential.

nodes.name: Friction damper: sliding block
nodes.kb: Spring-loaded block dragged by spring motion; dissipates energy
nodes.note: Slides against fixed surface; friction converts oscillation to heat. Simple and robust; damping is velocity-independent.

nodes.name: Fuel pump: mechanical
nodes.kb: Cam-operated diaphragm pump lifts fuel from tank to carburettor
nodes.note: Diaphragm flexes in and out; check valves direct flow. Operates at engine speed; pressure regulator diverts excess back to tank.

nodes.name: Grease cup with screw plunger
nodes.kb: Cup on bearing with spring plunger; screw forces grease down shaft
nodes.note: Periodic manual screw-turn adds grease; spring pressure keeps old grease out. Prevents bearing starvation and water ingress on wagon axles.

nodes.name: Half-track vehicle
nodes.kb: Tracks at rear, steered wheels at front
nodes.note: Front wheels steer; tracks handle traction. Lower cost than full track; faster on roads. Used in WW2 for soft-ground transport.

nodes.name: Handbrake: lever and cable
nodes.kb: Operator lever pulls cable to engage brake; ratchet holds locked
nodes.note: Ratchet lets driver hold vehicle on slope; release is manual. Simple and reliable. Works at parking.

nodes.name: Headlamp: electric light
nodes.kb: Parabolic reflector and incandescent or arc lamp for road lighting
nodes.note: Dip and main beam control low and high intensity. Reflector focus determines beam pattern. Carbide lamps use chemical reaction; electric is cleaner.

nodes.name: Rigid padded horse collar
nodes.kb: Padded frame that lets horse pull from shoulders not neck
nodes.note: Pressure on chest, not neck blood vessels; a horse can then pull 5 times its own weight. The yoke was strangulation efficiency.

nodes.name: Tram: horse-drawn
nodes.kb: Carriage running on rails pulled by horses
nodes.note: Rails reduce rolling resistance and allow heavier load than roads. Wheels flange the rail; tracks are laid in city streets and paved.

nodes.name: Nailed horseshoe
nodes.kb: Iron U-shaped shoe nailed to hoof perimeter
nodes.note: Nails grip hoof wall without driving into sensitive tissue; the curve distributes load. Works where ground is wet or rocky. Unshod horses slip.

nodes.name: Hub gear: internal speeds
nodes.kb: Planetary gears inside hub allow multiple speed ratios
nodes.note: No derailleur; gears inside sealed hub. Shift under load; no chain slip. More complex than derailleur; self-repairs are difficult.

nodes.name: Hydraulic brake line and cylinder
nodes.kb: Fluid pressure in hose transmits braking force to four wheels equally
nodes.note: Eliminates cable routing and friction; equal pressure on all wheels prevents skew and locks. Requires bleed valves to remove air bubbles.

nodes.name: Hydraulic shock absorber
nodes.kb: Piston in oil cylinder; orifice restricts flow and damps motion
nodes.note: Oil viscosity and orifice size control damping rate; velocity-dependent. Smooth ride; eliminates spring bounce; separate piston rod for return.

nodes.name: Ignition timing advance mechanism
nodes.kb: Mechanical advance shifts spark timing with engine rpm
nodes.note: Weights or springs move contact breaker forward as rpm rises; spark must advance for combustion to complete before piston rises. Late spark kills power.

nodes.name: Indicator light: direction signal
nodes.kb: Flashing light or arm signals intent to turn
nodes.note: Flashing relay opens and closes circuit; amber lens is standard. Arm-based indicators fold down when turn is complete.

nodes.name: Inner tube: rubber bladder
nodes.kb: Separate air-holding tube inside tyre; prevents pinch-flats
nodes.note: Valve stem allows inflation and deflation; seals against tyre bead. Pinch-flats occur when rim hits bump with low pressure.

nodes.name: Intake valve with cam
nodes.kb: Conical valve opens and closes intake port via camshaft lobe
nodes.note: Cam lobe pushes tappet and rod; valve lifts against spring. Timing is fixed by cam profile; wrong timing kills efficiency.

nodes.name: Iron tyre band
nodes.kb: Forged iron band shrunk onto wooden wheel rim
nodes.note: Iron hardness resists ground wear and stone damage; shrink-fit creates friction grip. Wheel lasts 10 times longer than bare wood on stone.

nodes.name: Kerb and gutter edge
nodes.kb: Stone edge strip separates carriageway from sidewalk
nodes.note: Defines edge; prevents water and debris escaping onto pavements. Protects pedestrians and controls vehicle paths.

nodes.name: Kingpin and steering arm
nodes.kb: Vertical pivot pin through steering knuckle with ball bearing
nodes.note: Ball bearing lets front wheel turn freely; kingpin takes axial thrust. Caster angle puts turning axis ahead of contact patch for stability.

nodes.name: Leaf spring: stacked flat
nodes.kb: Curved flat steel leaves stacked and clamped at ends
nodes.note: Flat geometry is easy to forge; stacked layers share load and provide damping. Leaf separation under impact; requires periodic re-tensioning.

nodes.name: Level crossing: road and rail
nodes.kb: Road surface raised or lowered to meet rail level at grade
nodes.note: Eliminates grade separation cost; risk is collision. Signals, gates and lookouts required. Works only for light traffic or short crossings.

nodes.name: Live axle: powered driving
nodes.kb: Axle rotates with wheels; power delivered through shaft inside
nodes.note: Propshaft spins inside the axle tube; differential is built into axle casing. Standard on motor vehicles from 1900.

nodes.name: Macadam road surface
nodes.kb: Layers of small stones compacted into solid binding mass
nodes.note: Each stone layer is smaller; compaction by weight and traffic creates shear-lock. Natural road binding without tar; lasts 20 years.

nodes.name: Magneto ignition: coil armature
nodes.kb: Rotating magnet induces high-voltage pulse in coil at each cylinder
nodes.note: Magneto generates its own power from engine rotation; no battery. Timing must advance with rpm for full power.

nodes.name: DC electric motor
nodes.kb: Rotating coil in permanent magnet field powered by DC current
nodes.note: Commutator and brushes switch current direction as coil rotates; torque is continuous. Brushes require maintenance; arcing causes wear.

nodes.name: Motor lorry: gasoline truck
nodes.note: Cab over engine or conventional layout; payload 2 to 5 tonnes. Four-speed gearbox and live axle. Air brake lines for trailer.

nodes.name: Motorcycle: two-wheeled motor
nodes.kb: Single-cylinder engine in bicycle frame with motorcycle tyres
nodes.note: Three to 8 horsepower typical; motorcycle tyres must have grip. Lightweight and manoeuvrable; no weather protection. Sidecar extends payload.

nodes.name: Muffler: silencer pipe
nodes.kb: Chamber with baffles absorbs exhaust noise
nodes.note: Expansion and baffle design attenuate pulsations; silencing is incomplete. Backpressure aids low-end torque.

nodes.name: Oil bath: submerged bearing
nodes.kb: Bearing runs submerged in oil; oil clings to parts by capillary action
nodes.note: No manual lubrication; oil circulates by splashing. Water and dirt sink to the bottom. Standard on high-speed bicycle hubs and motor bearings.

nodes.name: Oil pump: pressure lubrication
nodes.kb: Geared pump pressurises oil to lubricate engine bearings
nodes.note: Pump creates 20 to 60 psi; feeds main gallery and branch lines. Pressure relief valve prevents overpressure. Low pressure warning by float valve.

nodes.name: Omnibus: passenger coach
nodes.kb: Large open or enclosed carriage seating 10 to 30 passengers
nodes.note: Spring suspension carries multiple passengers smoothly; seats are arranged lengthwise or in rows. Public transport standard from 1820.

nodes.name: Penny-farthing: large wheel
nodes.kb: Huge front wheel with pedal cranks, tiny rear wheel
nodes.note: Wheel diameter reaches 60 inches; one pedal turn covers 15 feet. Speed is possible; instability and rider height are hazards.

nodes.name: Piston with rings
nodes.kb: Cast iron cup with sealing rings slides in cylinder bore
nodes.note: Compression ring seals gases; oil ring wipes cylinder wall. Rings must slide freely or friction is excessive and compression leaks past.

nodes.name: Plain journal bearing
nodes.kb: Soft metal sleeve around rotating shaft; oil film reduces friction
nodes.note: Bronze wears instead of the shaft; replaceable. Oil film is hydrodynamic; bearing runs hot if oil starves. Standard in wooden carts.

nodes.name: Plate clutch: disk friction
nodes.kb: Spring-loaded disk with friction material squeezes between plates
nodes.note: Friction material burns if slipped excessively; wear changes pedal feel. Diaphragm spring reduces effort; self-adjusting for wear.

nodes.name: Pneumatic tyre: air-filled
nodes.kb: Rubber envelope filled with air; sidewalls flex to absorb bumps
nodes.note: Air spring is light and effective; pinch-flats require inner tube. Rotation must be balanced or vibration results. Puncture repair by patching.

nodes.name: Pressure relief valve: oil system
nodes.kb: Spring-loaded valve diverts oil back to sump if pressure exceeds limit
nodes.note: Spring preload determines cracking pressure; higher pressure means more oil flow. Chattering if spring is weak; no flow if stuck closed.

nodes.name: Propshaft: transmission shaft
nodes.kb: Long shaft with universal joints connects gearbox to differential
nodes.note: Must be balanced to avoid vibration; spins 1000 to 6000 rpm. Tube and solid shaft designs; solid is simpler but heavier.

nodes.name: Radiator: water cooler
nodes.kb: Thin brass tubes and fins cool hot water by exposure to air
nodes.note: Fins increase surface area; water flows in at base and out at top by thermosiphon circulation. Cooling must match engine heat output.

nodes.name: Steam road roller
nodes.kb: Heavy steam-powered cylinder compacts stone and asphalt
nodes.note: Steam piston drives the roller by crank; compaction force is thousands of tonnes. Human-powered rollers took teams of 20 men all day.

nodes.name: Roller bearing: cylindrical
nodes.kb: Hardened steel cylinders in cage rolling on hardened races
nodes.note: Rolling contact reduces friction to 1/10th of sliding; spin is almost frictionless. Cage holds cylinders in place and spacing.

nodes.name: Safety bicycle: chain-driven
nodes.kb: Equal-sized wheels with chain drive to rear wheel
nodes.note: Low seat position is stable; handlebar steering is direct. Chain and sprockets allow gear ratios; pedal force is efficient.

nodes.name: Shrink-fit tyre assembly
nodes.kb: Heat iron tyre to expand, slide onto rim, cool to grip
nodes.note: Radial pressure from cooling iron clamping the rim; the tyre cannot slip or loosen. Critical process failure if temperature is wrong.

nodes.name: Sliding gearbox: mesh shift
nodes.kb: Gears slide on shafts to engage different ratios
nodes.note: Gears crash if shifted under load; must rev-match or double-clutch. Four to six speeds typical. Crude compared to synchromesh.

nodes.name: Snow plough: powered blade
nodes.kb: V-shaped blade mounted on truck clears snow from road surface
nodes.note: Hydraulic lift raises or lowers blade; angling lifts pushes snow to side. Rock and gravel damage blades; steel edge replaceable.

nodes.name: Solid rubber tyre
nodes.kb: Thick rubber wheel without air; hard and durable
nodes.note: Does not puncture; very heavy and hard. Poor ride quality; vibration is severe. Bounce is minimal. Used on trolleys and industrial wheels.

nodes.name: Spark plug: electrode gap
nodes.kb: Insulated electrode with air gap in combustion chamber
nodes.note: Ceramic insulator withstands 1000 C and high pressure; central electrode is nickel-alloy. Gap requires precise machining and adjustment.

nodes.name: Improved spoked wheel
nodes.kb: Radial spokes under tension with metal rim band
nodes.note: Tensioned spokes are lighter and stronger than solid wood; the metal rim distributes braking and impact loads. Wheels survive rutted roads.

nodes.name: Tram: steam-powered
nodes.kb: Small steam engine on platform drives tram on rails
nodes.note: Small steam engine is compact; boiler must be insulated. Track fouling by coal dust is a nuisance. Electric power displaced steam in cities by 1910.

nodes.name: Stirrup with foot loop
nodes.kb: Metal loop hung from saddle to support rider foot
nodes.note: Allows rider to stand in saddle and apply weight and force; enables mounted combat and faster gaits. Foot placement adds stability.

nodes.name: Lead-acid storage battery
nodes.kb: Lead plates in sulfuric acid store electrical energy
nodes.note: Charging creates lead dioxide on positive plate; discharge converts it back. Sulfate buildup shortens battery life. Maintenance requires regular watering.

nodes.name: Synchromesh: synchronizer ring
nodes.kb: Friction cone syncs gear speeds before meshing; smooths shift
nodes.note: Friction ring accelerates or decelerates gear to match shaft speed; then dog clutch engages. Eliminates grinding and allows fast shifts.

nodes.name: Tandem harness for shafts
nodes.kb: Two horses in line sharing draft load via shaft trace system
nodes.note: Horses positioned one behind the other; the lead horse sets direction, rear horse pushes. Standard for coaches and heavy wagons.

nodes.name: Taper roller bearing
nodes.kb: Conical rollers in cage on matching conical races
nodes.note: Tapers allow combined radial and thrust loading; spreads force over long contact line. Wheel hub and differential support bearings.

nodes.name: Tarmacadam: tar-bound stone
nodes.kb: Macadam base with hot coal tar binder and top dressing
nodes.note: Tar fills voids and binds; prevents water penetration and dust. Lasts 30 years on trunk roads. Less noise and dust than macadam.

nodes.name: Thermostat: temperature valve
nodes.kb: Wax pellet expands with heat; valve restricts bypass to radiator
nodes.note: Wax expands at setpoint (around 82 C); opens gradually. Prevents engine overcooling at startup and overheating at full load.

nodes.name: Throttle valve: fuel control
nodes.kb: Butterfly valve controls fuel and air intake to engine
nodes.note: Cable or linkage to accelerator pedal; spring returns to idle. Mixture enrichment for cold start.

nodes.name: Tractor: agricultural motorvehicle
nodes.kb: Low-speed high-torque motor with power takeoff for implements
nodes.note: Three-point hitch connects implements; PTO shaft drives threshers, pumps, balers. Wide tyres and low centre-of-gravity for soft ground.

nodes.name: Transmission oil sump and drain
nodes.kb: Gear box filled with oil that bathes and cools gears
nodes.note: Oil viscosity must be chosen for ambient temperature; splash lubrication relies on gear teeth churning oil. Regular changes remove metal particles.

nodes.name: Trolleybus: electric bus
nodes.kb: Bus-sized vehicle with electric motor powered from overhead wires
nodes.note: No rails required; road steering allows flexible routing. Two trolley poles provide redundancy and steady power. Silent and clean.

nodes.name: Tyre bead: rim seat
nodes.kb: Reinforced edge of tyre seats onto wheel rim
nodes.note: Wire or cord-reinforced ring prevents tyre slipping on rim under load. Bead tension must match rim diameter for safe seating.

nodes.name: Tyre tread pattern
nodes.kb: Grooves carved into tyre surface channel water away from contact patch
nodes.note: Grooves remove water from contact patch and improve grip; sipes add biting edges at low temperatures. Tread wear is main tyre life limit.

nodes.name: Universal joint: Cardan shaft
nodes.kb: Double-jointed shaft transmits rotation at angles up to 30 degrees
nodes.note: Cruciform spider with needle bearings allows shaft to bend; speed is uniform if using double joints. Essential for connecting engine to axle.

nodes.name: Velocipede: pedal-driven wheel
nodes.kb: Cranks attached to hub of large wheel; pedals drive directly
nodes.note: Direct crank drive means pedal force is proportional to wheel size; large wheel needed for speed. Poor leverage and high pedal rate.

nodes.name: Vulcanized rubber
nodes.kb: Sulfur compound heated with rubber to cure and harden it
nodes.note: Sulfur cross-links rubber chains; hot vulcanization hardness is precise. Without vulcanization rubber is sticky and brittle in cold. Essential for tyres.

nodes.name: Water pump: centrifugal
nodes.kb: Spinning impeller pushes water through cooling circuit
nodes.note: Impeller blades fling water outward; centrifugal force creates pressure head. Thermostat bypass allows fast warm-up.

nodes.name: Whippletree and swingletree
nodes.kb: Hinged bar that pivots to equalize load across multiple animals
nodes.note: Each horse pulls equally even if they are different strengths; load distributes by a free pivot. Critical for heavy loads and team hauling.

nodes.name: Windscreen wiper: mechanical
nodes.kb: Camshaft-driven arm swings wiper blade across glass
nodes.note: Vacuum-operated versions use engine intake; direct cam drive is mechanically reliable. Blade must be soft rubber to avoid scratching glass.

nodes.name: Wire rope brake cable
nodes.kb: Steel wire rope transmits brake force from lever to shoe
nodes.note: Stranded rope accepts bending around pulleys; weaker than solid cable but easier to route around wheels and frame. Stretches and requires adjustment.

nodes.name: Wire spoke wheel
nodes.kb: Steel wire spokes replace wooden or iron spokes; lighter and stronger
nodes.note: Wire spokes under tension resist compression and bending; they are much lighter. Requires jigs for spoke tensioning and lacing. Standard on bicycles.

nodes.name: Articulated locomotive
nodes.kb: Two or more sets of driving wheels with separate boilers or joined at the boiler
nodes.note: Articulated locomotives have a pivot at the center, allowing the rear unit to rotate for curves. Two sets of cylinders pulling one boiler. The kernel is the pivot and steam pipes: the feedpipes to rear cylinders must flex or the pivot motion will rupture them. Modern articulated designs use flexible pipes and careful geometry to manage stress.

nodes.name: Automatic train stop
nodes.kb: Automatic alarm or brake activation if signal is passed at danger
nodes.note: A ramp or arm on the track activates a release or brake if the locomotive passes a stop signal. Driver hears a loud alarm and can take over. If the alarm is ignored, the brake applies automatically. The kernel is that this is the only purely automatic safety: all other safeguards require human adherence. Some systems use electromagnets; others use mechanical trip arms.

nodes.name: Axle bearing journal box
nodes.kb: Cast iron housing containing brass or bronze bushing
nodes.note: Bearing box contains the bushing that carries the axle. Must have drain hole for oil leakage; a clogged box overheats. The kernel is that hot boxes derail trains; inspection and re-oiling on schedule is essential maintenance.

nodes.name: Ballast tank system
nodes.kb: Sea water ballast tanks controlling ship trim and stability
nodes.note: Ballast tanks allow a ship to adjust its weight distribution without cargo. Ballast is seawater pumped in or out through gates. The kernel is that ballast must be carefully distributed; uneven ballast causes the ship to heel dangerously. Ballast tanks also allow ships to carry cargo efficiently despite variable load.

nodes.name: Bilge pump
nodes.kb: Hand-operated pump removing water from the hold
nodes.note: Bilge pump is a simple piston pump with flapper valves. Two sailors working alternately can keep a large ship dry. The kernel is that a ship always leaks; a crew must pump continuously during a long voyage. Without pumping, a wooden ship sinks in weeks.

nodes.name: Blastpipe for draught
nodes.kb: Exhaust steam nozzle in chimney creating suction on the firebox
nodes.note: Blastpipe is a small nozzle of steam in the chimney. Exhaust steam velocity creates low pressure, pulling hot gases through the firebox and tubes. Without it, a locomotive boiler makes barely enough steam to move itself. The kernel is this simple: a jet of steam pulls the fire. Diameter and shape matter; too tight and back-pressure rises, too loose and draught fails.

nodes.name: Block signalling system
nodes.kb: Dividing track into blocks, only one train per block
nodes.note: Track is divided into blocks; a signal at the entrance shows whether the block is occupied. Signalmen receive messages from block to block. The kernel is that this prevents rear-end collisions automatically: if a train fails to stop at a signal, it has already entered the block, so the signal behind is set to stop. The system requires discipline and communication between all signal boxes.

nodes.name: Block and tackle pulley
nodes.kb: Pulley blocks in series multiplying rope mechanical advantage
nodes.note: Multiple pulleys in wooden blocks distribute rope friction. A six-part tackle gives a six-fold mechanical advantage. The kernel is that each pulley adds weight and friction, so very large tackles lose efficiency; four to six parts is typical.

nodes.name: Bogie truck with leading wheels
nodes.kb: Four-wheel swiveling truck supporting front or rear of locomotive
nodes.note: Bogie is a small truck with four wheels; swivels on a central pin. Distributes weight over many wheels, reducing rail stress. The kernel is the pivot: it must allow the bogie to rotate for curves but cannot have play or the wheels will hunt side-to-side and derail. Friction damping is essential.

nodes.name: Bowsprit extension spar
nodes.kb: Spar extending forward from bow supporting jibs
nodes.note: Bowsprit is a large spar lashed to the bow, extending 10-40 feet. Jibs hang from it. The kernel is that the bowsprit is in compression from the jib load and tension from lashing; if the lashing fails, the bowsprit falls and often takes the foremast with it.

nodes.name: Brake shoe on wheels
nodes.kb: Cast iron shoe pressed against wheel rim by brake lever
nodes.note: Early brakes used wooden shoes; cast iron shoes are more durable. The kernel is that shoe friction converts kinetic energy to heat; excessive braking overheats shoes and reduces friction.

nodes.name: Bullhead rail
nodes.kb: T-shaped rail with bulbous head resisting vertical wear
nodes.note: Bulbous head can be turned over once worn on one side; reversible rail doubles its service life. Requires close-tolerance rolling and special chairs to clamp the head.

nodes.name: Canal lift water elevator
nodes.kb: Large tank lift carrying boats vertically up or down
nodes.note: Canal lift replaces a series of locks with a single vertical motion. Large tank holds the boat; steam engine or counterweight lifts it. The kernel is that this is mechanically complex and rarely used; locks are simpler and more reliable. Only justified where height difference is extreme.

nodes.name: Canal lock for water level control
nodes.kb: Pair of gates with pump or natural flow controlling water level
nodes.note: Locks allow boats to navigate waterfalls or height differences. Gates must seal perfectly; any leak drains the lock. The kernel is that operating a lock requires skill: chambers must be filled and drained at the right rate, and gates must close in sequence or water escapes.

nodes.name: Capstan for hauling
nodes.kb: Vertical rotating post with rope wrapped around hauling cargo
nodes.note: Capstan has a vertical axle on a sturdy base; rope is wrapped and sailors push bars to rotate it. Mechanical advantage is excellent: one turn around the capstan multiplies force. The kernel is that rope can slip if tension is uneven; capstan bars must be moved by sailors in synchronized rhythm, or the rope loosens.

nodes.name: Carvel planking hull construction
nodes.kb: Edge-to-edge hull planks fastened to internal frames
nodes.note: Planks meet edge to edge on the outside; frames inside hold the shape. Smoother hull than clinker, better for large vessels. The kernel is that seams must be perfectly caulked or the ship leaks. The planks are attached to frames with treenails (wooden pegs) or iron bolts; treenails are preferred because iron rusts and weakens the hull.

nodes.name: Overhead catenary for power
nodes.kb: Suspended cable overhead for pantograph to contact
nodes.note: Catenary wire sags naturally; a support cable above compensates for sag. Pantograph wheel rolls on the contact wire. The kernel is maintaining contact at speed: if the wire is too high the pantograph lifts off, if too low it sags into obstacles. Tension is maintained by weights on the suspension ends. Modern catenary uses elaborate linkages to keep tension constant as the wire stretches and temperature changes.

nodes.name: Caulking with oakum
nodes.kb: Loose fiber rope driven into seams and sealed with pitch
nodes.note: Oakum is unraveled rope fiber. Sailors drive it into seams with mallets and chisels, then seal over with tar. Leaks can be caulked at sea. The kernel is that the seam must be sealed from both sides, or water seeps past the caulking; hulls have internal seams that must also be caulked after the hull is built.

nodes.name: Chain cable
nodes.kb: Wrought iron chain for anchor cable replacing hemp rope
nodes.note: Chain cable is much stronger than rope, does not rot, and does not chafe. Requires chain windlass or capstan to handle weight. The kernel is that chain links must be perfectly closed or they open under cyclic load; link welding must be perfect or the chain fails suddenly.

nodes.name: Chair and key for bullhead rail
nodes.kb: Cast iron saddle clamping bullhead rail to sleeper with removable wedge
nodes.note: Chair sits on sleeper, the bulbous head of the rail slides into the chair, a wooden wedge or key is driven in to lock it. The kernel is that cast iron chairs can be removed and reused; cheaper than welding and allows track realignment. Keys must be replaced when they loosen.

nodes.name: Clinker planking hull construction
nodes.kb: Overlapping hull planks fastened edge to edge
nodes.note: Each plank overlaps the one below; fastened with iron rivets or treenails. Flexes with the hull movement. The kernel is that overlap provides some hydrodynamic benefit at speed, and the joint overlaps create a labyrinth that slows leaking. Clinker hulls are lighter and more flexible than carvel.

nodes.name: Compound expansion engine
nodes.kb: Two cylinders: high pressure first, then low pressure from exhaust
nodes.note: High-pressure steam in small cylinders expands, then exhausts into larger low-pressure cylinders. Receiver cooling improves efficiency.

nodes.name: Copper sheathing for wooden hulls
nodes.kb: Thin copper sheet covering hull below waterline
nodes.note: Copper is expensive but prevents marine growth (barnacles, weed) that increases drag. Needs copper nails for fastening; iron nails corrode and weaken the sheathing. The kernel is that copper is sacrificial: it oxidizes and protects the wood. Replacement is expensive but hull speed is preserved.

nodes.name: Diesel electric transmission
nodes.kb: Diesel engine driving an electrical generator, motor drives wheels
nodes.note: Diesel engine inefficient at low speed; generator produces electrical power, electric motor drives wheels. Electric transmission allows smooth power delivery.

nodes.name: Double bottom hull structure
nodes.kb: Inner hull separated from outer hull by empty space
nodes.note: Double bottom provides flotation even if the outer hull is punctured. Also allows water ballast without contaminating cargo. The kernel is that this doubles the weight and construction cost, but dramatically improves safety and cargo flexibility.

nodes.name: Dredger for channel deepening
nodes.kb: Boat with steam-driven pump or bucket dredge
nodes.note: Dredgers remove silt and mud from channels. Bucket dredge uses a belt-driven scoop; suction dredge uses a pump and pipeline. The kernel is that sediment is abrasive; pump impellers and bucket liners wear out quickly and require frequent replacement.

nodes.name: Dry dock facility
nodes.kb: Large dock that can be filled with water then drained
nodes.note: Dry dock allows hull repair below the waterline. Massive gates and pumping systems. The kernel is that the gates must seal perfectly; any leakage fills the dock and sinks the ship. Construction is expensive and takes years.

nodes.name: Edge rail in wrought iron
nodes.kb: Wrought iron rail with a thin raised edge for the wheel flange to run on
nodes.note: Wrought iron rail with vertical edge section for wheel flanges. Edge rail wears down from flange contact. Surveyors discovered that a thin raised iron edge on flat rail is better than thick cast iron rails; the wrought iron is softer and easier to shape, but wears faster.

nodes.name: Electric locomotive with trolley pole
nodes.kb: AC or DC electric motor drawing power from overhead or rail
nodes.note: Electric motors have better efficiency and control than steam. AC motors require substations; DC motors require heavy feeders from a central station. The kernel is that electric traction needs infrastructure investment in poles or conduits, but eliminates the boiler. Early systems used DC; AC came later with better transformers.

nodes.name: Fishplate for rail joining
nodes.kb: Wrought iron plate bolted over two rail ends to join them
nodes.note: Simple wrought iron plate on both sides of rail joint, bolted through. Prevents vertical deflection and twisting at the joint. The kernel is that bolted joints are maintenance-intensive because vibration loosens bolts; springs under bolt heads help, but regular tightening is essential.

nodes.name: Flanged cast iron wheel
nodes.kb: Cast iron wheel with projecting flange on one side
nodes.note: Flange on the wheel instead of groove in the rail lets wheels run on flat top rail. Requires casting tolerances within a few mm and case hardening to resist wear. The flange does slip sideways on curves if track is truly flat; banked curves help.

nodes.name: Flat bottom rail
nodes.kb: T-shaped rail resting on flat base seated directly on sleeper
nodes.note: Flat bottom rail sits directly on sleepers without chairs, saving weight and labour. Introduced after 1850 when rolling tolerances improved. The kernel is that the flat base distributes load better than a pointed foot, and eliminates the need for expensive cast iron chairs if sleepers can be accurately spaced.

nodes.name: Fore-and-aft rig
nodes.kb: Sails aligned with the ship length controlled by a boom
nodes.note: Fore-and-aft sails point along the ship length. A boom extends below the sail, controlled by rope blocks. This rig allows sailing close to the wind. The kernel is that controlling the boom requires skill and strength; an accidental jibe (boom swing) can decapitate a sailor. Modern fore-and-aft rigs use mechanical systems to prevent that.

nodes.name: Fore-and-aft rigging system
nodes.kb: Network of shrouds, stays, and halyards controlling sails
nodes.note: Fore-and-aft rigging has many lines: shrouds hold the mast, stays are forward-backward lines, halyards raise sails. Each line serves a specific purpose. The kernel is that a single failed line can drop the mast; rigging must be redundant and sailors must know which lines to splice.

nodes.name: Frame-first hull construction
nodes.kb: Building the skeleton frame first, then planking
nodes.note: Medieval ships built shell-first, laying planks then adding frames. Renaissance builders discovered frame-first: build the ribcage, then plank. Allows precise shape and stronger hulls. The kernel is that frame-first needs accurate geometry; shell-first is intuitive but shapes are imprecise and hulls weaker.

nodes.name: Grade crossing and safety gates
nodes.kb: Road crossing railroad at ground level with mechanical gates
nodes.note: Grade crossing gates lower mechanically when a train approaches; must be reliable or collisions occur. The kernel is that gate timing must be exact; gates must lower before the train reaches the crossing and raise after it clears.

nodes.name: Gyrocompass repeater
nodes.kb: Repeater display of gyro bearing fed electrically from master gyro
nodes.note: Gyrocompass master is large and fixed; repeaters on the bridge show bearing without leaving the compass. Multiple repeaters feed from one master. The kernel is that synchronizing repeaters with the master requires feedback mechanisms; errors accumulate if not corrected.

nodes.name: Hopper wagon for bulk minerals
nodes.kb: Open wagon with conical bottom and chutes for gravity unloading
nodes.note: Hopper wagons eliminate shoveling; load coal or ore, close the chute, and gravity empties it at the destination. Chutes must be wide enough that cargo bridges; a stuck chute is worthless. Hinged chutes that open suddenly can jam if a stone wedges in the opening.

nodes.name: Internal hull sheathing and ceiling
nodes.kb: Interior planking protecting cargo from bilge water and hull moisture
nodes.note: Hull ceiling is laid over the frames on the inside. Creates an air gap between cargo and hull structure. The kernel is that this requires careful carpentry to fit perfectly; gaps allow rot to spread.

nodes.name: Injector feedwater pump
nodes.kb: Steam jet drawing cold water into boiler against pressure
nodes.note: An injector uses a steam jet to entrain and accelerate cold water into the boiler against steam pressure. No moving parts; only valve adjustments. The kernel is that this is counterintuitive: steam at high pressure should push water out, not in. The trick is that the steam jet accelerates the water faster than the boiler pressure can push back.

nodes.name: Interlocking for signal control
nodes.kb: Mechanical or electrical locking preventing conflicting switch and signal combinations
nodes.note: Interlocking prevents a signalman from throwing a switch that would cause a train to derail or collide. Early systems were mechanical: levers moved in sequence, and a mistake locked the lever. Later systems use electrical logic through a relay bank. The kernel is that the logic must be physically embodied, not trusted to human memory.

nodes.name: Iron hull construction
nodes.kb: Wrought iron frames and plates riveted into a hull
nodes.note: Iron hulls are stronger than wooden hulls; iron does not rot. Riveted seams work but require enormous labor. The kernel is that iron hulls can be larger and thinner-walled than wooden hulls, and a shipyard can build multiple copies if frames are reused. Initial capital investment is high.

nodes.name: Jib triangular foresail
nodes.kb: Small triangular sail in front of the main mast
nodes.note: Jib hangs from a stay line forward of the mast. Small and easy to furl. The kernel is that removing the jib improves balance when the ship heels; jibs are the first sail doused in heavy weather.

nodes.name: Keelson internal keel
nodes.kb: Longitudinal timber glued to top of keel inside the hull
nodes.note: Keelson is sandwiched between the keel and the frames, glued and bolted. Reinforces longitudinal strength. The kernel is that hogging is prevented; without a keelson, large wooden ships flex and eventually break in half.

nodes.name: Automatic knuckle coupler
nodes.kb: Self-engaging hook-and-latch coupler closing on impact
nodes.note: Knuckle is a hinged hook; when two couplers touch, the spring-loaded knuckles close on each other. Eliminates the need for screwmen between wagons. The kernel is that the latching geometry must be precise enough that it does not pop open under oscillation, and hard enough to survive millions of couplings without rounding off.

nodes.name: Lateen sail
nodes.kb: Triangular sail with leading edge parallel to the wind
nodes.note: Lateen sail hangs from a yard at an angle; the luff (leading edge) can point higher into the wind than square sails. Allows sailing across wind and returning. The kernel is that this is geometry: a triangular sail pointing into wind generates lift just as an airfoil does. Medieval sailmakers did not understand the physics, but found that this sail works.

nodes.name: Leading truck for guiding
nodes.kb: Smaller four-wheel truck ahead of driving wheels for steering
nodes.note: Leading truck follows the curves because it leads; driving wheels follow the leading truck path. Without it, a long rigid wheelbase derails on curves. Much simpler than a bogie and works fine for short locomotives.

nodes.name: Lifeboat and davit system
nodes.kb: Small boat stowed on ship with crane for emergency evacuation
nodes.note: Lifeboats must be strong enough for occupants, yet light enough to hoist with hand-cranked davits. Canvas or cork flotation prevents swamping. The kernel is that early lifeboats were poorly designed; many people drowned in lifeboats that swamped. Modern designs have watertight compartments and proper freeboard.

nodes.name: Lighthouse and Fresnel lens
nodes.kb: Stepped glass lens concentrating light into a beam
nodes.note: Fresnel lens steps the surface instead of grinding a smooth lens; this reduces weight and glass volume. Efficiency is excellent, throwing light far out to sea. The kernel is that stepped surfaces are precise optical elements; the step geometry must be calculated carefully or the beam disperses.

nodes.name: Locomotive boiler with multitubular flues
nodes.kb: Horizontal cylindrical vessel with many small tubes for hot gases
nodes.note: Dozens of small tubes in a large pressure vessel for heat transfer. Tube failures rupture the boiler explosively; ferrule expansion is standard.

nodes.name: Log and sounding instruments
nodes.kb: Log line for speed, lead line with marks for depth
nodes.note: Log line is a rope with knots at regular intervals; tossed overboard, the knots passing a sailor's hand count the ship speed in knots. Sounding line is weighted and marked in fathoms. The kernel is that depth and speed are essential for navigation; old technology works reliably.

nodes.name: Marine chronometer for longitude
nodes.kb: Highly accurate clock keeping time during voyage for longitude calculation
nodes.note: Chronometers use a balance wheel and hairspring in a gimbal mount. Temperature compensation is critical; expansion changes spring rate and loses time. The kernel is that a simple spring-driven watch gains and loses seconds per day, but a chronometer must lose less than one second per month.

nodes.name: Marine diesel engine
nodes.kb: Diesel engine adapted for marine propulsion
nodes.note: Marine diesels are much larger and slower-running than automotive diesels. Direct drive to the propeller is possible. Efficiency is superior to steam turbines. The kernel is that marine diesel fuel (bunker oil) is heavy and requires heating before injection; fuel systems are complex.

nodes.name: Marine steam engine
nodes.kb: Compact steam engine adapted for continuous ship propulsion
nodes.note: Marine engines are much more compact than stationary engines and must run continuously at sea. Crankshaft is horizontal, connected directly to the propeller shaft. The kernel is that connecting a steam engine to a propeller requires a strong crankshaft on good bearings; vibration at full power tests the bearings.

nodes.name: Marine steam turbine
nodes.kb: Rotary turbine directly driven by steam pressure
nodes.note: Turbines operate at high speeds; rotor must be perfectly balanced. Requires reduction gearing to run propeller at usable speed.

nodes.name: Marshalling hump yard
nodes.kb: Hill over which wagons roll downslope into classification tracks
nodes.note: A train is uncoupled at the top, pushed over the hump by a small engine, wagons roll downslope and are switched into classification tracks by remote control. No manual switching needed. The kernel is calculating the gradient and friction so wagons roll at the right speed: too fast they collide, too slow they stop midway. Retarders (friction devices) on tracks control speed.

nodes.name: Mast stepping and rigging
nodes.kb: Method for setting masts and distributing load through ship structure
nodes.note: Masts are large wooden poles; stepping is the joint between mast and hull. Must be strong enough to carry both the sail load and bending moments. The kernel is that mast failure means loss of ship; stepped joint design evolved through centuries of trial and failure.

nodes.name: Paddle wheel for propulsion
nodes.kb: Large wheel with paddles pushing water astern
nodes.note: Paddle wheels are simple but inefficient; they throw water up as well as back. Efficiency is worse in rough seas where paddles lose water contact. The kernel is that paddle wheels project far above the deck, limiting gun ports and cargo space. Screw propellers fit inside the hull.

nodes.name: Pantograph current collector
nodes.kb: Articulated arm pressing a wheel or blade against overhead wire
nodes.note: Pantograph is a diamond-shaped linkage pushing a wheel up against the overhead wire. Spring pressure controls contact force. The kernel is that the wheel must not bounce off at speed, but excessive pressure increases wear and copper consumption. The contact strip is made from a copper alloy that conducts well but does not arc-weld itself to the catenary.

nodes.name: Periscope
nodes.kb: Optical tube with mirrors allowing viewing from submerged position
nodes.note: Periscope tube has lenses at top and bottom, mirror or prism in center. Light path bends 90 degrees at each end. The kernel is that mirror quality determines image brightness; tarnished mirrors make the image dim and hard to use in darkness.

nodes.name: Piston valve
nodes.kb: Cylindrical piston with ring ports moving inside a steam chest
nodes.note: A cylinder with ports in the side moves inside a steam chamber. Rings create sealing; ports on cylinder and chamber walls align to direct steam. Much lower friction than slide valve because only the seal rings contact the cylinder. Requires good machining and ring materials that do not gall.

nodes.name: Points and frog
nodes.kb: Movable rails and crossing point where two tracks meet
nodes.note: A frog is where two rails cross; a diamond-shaped casting with a gap in the middle. Points are two curved rails that slide together to guide wheels left or right. The kernel is that the frog must support wheels rolling through the gap at speed without bouncing; cast iron frogs crack unless cooled carefully. The angle between crossing rails is critical; too steep and wheels derail.

nodes.name: Standard rail gauge
nodes.kb: Standardized track width allowing interchange between railroads
nodes.note: Many early railroads used different gauges; passengers had to change trains. Standardization on 4ft 8.5in allowed through-travel. The kernel is that this was a political achievement, not a technical one; railroads had to agree to lose the monopoly on traffic.

nodes.name: Rail rolling in mill
nodes.kb: Passing heated bulk steel through rollers to form rail profile
nodes.note: Rolling mill produces consistent rail profile at tonnage scale. Early mills had to trial many roller shapes. The kernel is controlling the speed and temperature of the steel through multiple passes without cooling too much; too cold and the mill clogs, too hot and the steel deforms unevenly.

nodes.name: Rail welding
nodes.kb: Electric arc or gas flame welding of rail ends into continuous long rail
nodes.note: Welded rail eliminates joints, reducing noise and wheel impact loading. Thermal stress during cooling must be controlled or the weld cracks. The kernel is that you must preheat the rail before welding, weld under careful arc control, then cool slowly in a lagging blanket. Uncontrolled cooling fails within weeks.

nodes.name: Reduction gearing for propeller
nodes.kb: Gears reducing turbine speed to optimal propeller speed
nodes.note: Turbines spin 3000+ rpm; propellers need 100-300 rpm. Reduction gears convert speed and torque. The kernel is that gear teeth must be precisely machined and case-hardened; poor gearing efficiency losses appear as heat in the gear case.

nodes.name: Reefing sails
nodes.kb: Reducing sail area by rolling or folding part of the sail
nodes.note: Sailors work aloft on the yard rolling the sail and lashing it with reef points. Dangerous and slow. The kernel is that this is the only way to reduce sail in heavy weather without dropping it entirely; reef points must be strongly secured so the sail does not unfurl.

nodes.name: Refrigerated wagon
nodes.kb: Insulated wagon with ice chambers preserving perishable cargo
nodes.note: Insulation is cork, sawdust, or felt in the walls. Ice chambers are at roof corners, cold sinks to preserve cargo. Air circulation must be designed carefully: stagnant cold spoils, circulating cold prevents moisture. The kernel is that predictable ice consumption and maintenance of air exchange are essential; a poor design spoils cargo before it reaches market.

nodes.name: Block rigging and rope lashing
nodes.kb: Splicing and knotting techniques for rope connections
nodes.note: A badly spliced rope breaks under load; a properly spliced rope retains 80 percent of rope strength. The kernel is that this is craft knowledge passed sailmaker to sailmaker; a perfect splice is invisible and stronger than the line on either side.

nodes.name: Riveted hull plating
nodes.kb: Iron plate seams joined by driven rivets
nodes.note: Rivets are heated red-hot, inserted through holes in overlapping plates, then hammered cold on the far side. Requires enormous labor and skill. The kernel is that a poorly driven rivet pulls water in; a perfect rivet creates a watertight joint. Modern riveting uses pneumatic hammers, earlier work is all hand hammering and is exhausting.

nodes.name: Screw coupling
nodes.kb: Hand-screw coupling joining wagons by threaded hook
nodes.note: Two hooks with threaded rods; screwman walks between wagons turning the rod to couple them. Slow and dangerous. The kernel is that this requires discipline and exact position; if chains are too short, screwmen get crushed, if too long, wagons collide.

nodes.name: Screw propeller
nodes.kb: Archimedean screw submerged in water pushing ship forward
nodes.note: Screw propeller is more efficient than paddle wheel in rough seas, but requires shaft alignment that paddle wheels do not. The kernel is that any misalignment creates vibration that damages bearings. Modern propellers use bronze casting and careful balancing.

nodes.name: Semaphore signal
nodes.kb: Mechanical arm with positions indicating proceed, caution, or stop
nodes.note: Semaphore arm at different angles means go, stop, or caution. All-night operation required lamps. The kernel is that a driver must know the state from a distance. Early railroad signals were simply 'stop' or 'go'; caution required a second signal to warn that the next signal might be red.

nodes.name: Sextant for celestial navigation
nodes.kb: Double-mirror instrument measuring angles to celestial bodies
nodes.note: Sextant has two mirrors and a half-silvered beam-splitter. User sees the horizon and celestial body simultaneously, then measures the angle. The kernel is that accuracy depends on optical clarity and mechanical precision; a sextant made with care is accurate to 1 minute of arc.

nodes.name: Ship telegraph signal system
nodes.kb: Telegraph link from bridge to engine room for speed commands
nodes.note: Telegraph is a mechanical system using electromagnets; a bell rings in the engine room when the bridge operator moves a lever. Modern engine rooms are out of earshot; telegraph eliminated the need for runners. The kernel is that the bridge can command engine speed directly, improving maneuverability.

nodes.name: Sleeper and ballast foundation
nodes.kb: Timber sleepers on stone ballast distributing rail load
nodes.note: Sleepers must be set at precise spacing and depth for even rail height. Ballast size matters: too large and rails rock, too small and it settles too quickly. Track workers use a wooden gauge and a line to check alignment.

nodes.name: Sleeping car for passengers
nodes.kb: Passenger car with bunks for sleeping during overnight journey
nodes.note: Sleeping cars have bunk beds stacked vertically for economy, and superior suspension for ride comfort. The kernel is that passengers need privacy for sleeping; compartment design is essential. Early sleeping cars were dangerous if a coupling broke; springs and buffers improved safety.

nodes.name: Slide valve for steam distribution
nodes.kb: Flat plate sliding on ports to admit and exhaust steam in cylinders
nodes.note: Slide valve is a flat rectangular casting sliding back and forth on a flat plane. Ports in the plane align with slots in the valve to admit steam to cylinders and exhaust to atmosphere. The kernel is that it is simple and works, but creates a lot of friction because it is pressed hard onto the plane by steam pressure. Piston valves are an improvement.

nodes.name: Slipway for ship launch
nodes.kb: Inclined ramp for sliding finished ship into water
nodes.note: Ship slides down the slipway into water. Friction is controlled by grease and soap. The kernel is that the angle and friction must be calculated correctly; too steep and the ship accelerates uncontrollably, too shallow and it sticks halfway.

nodes.name: Smoke box and char arrester
nodes.kb: Chamber above boiler tubes collecting exhaust gases
nodes.note: Smoke box is a chamber where all tubes exit. Char arrester is a mesh inside; sparks are caught so they do not ignite lineside crops. The kernel is that locomotive operation without a spark arrester sets fires; railroads are liable for fire damage.

nodes.name: Sprung coupling buffer
nodes.kb: Spring-loaded buffer between coupled vehicles absorbing impact
nodes.note: Buffers are rubbing plates; springs inside the coupler absorb the impact of coupling. Without buffers, sudden jerks break couplings and cargo. The kernel is that springs must not be too stiff or they waste energy heating up, not too soft or the buffer compresses too far and gets stuck.

nodes.name: Square rig sails
nodes.kb: Sails perpendicular to mast running with wind from behind
nodes.note: Square sails are powerful with wind behind you, useless when sailing toward the wind. Multiple sails on multiple masts allow some directional control. The kernel is that larger sail area means better speed, so sailing ships carried many sails and took time to adjust them in changing wind.

nodes.name: Staysail
nodes.kb: Small triangular sail on a stay between masts
nodes.note: Staysails are rigged on the cable stays between masts. They fill the gap between main and jib. The kernel is that each small sail is easier to handle than one large sail, and distributes pressure to multiple parts of the rigging rather than concentrating loads on one sail.

nodes.name: Steel hull construction
nodes.kb: Bulk steel frames and plates for much stronger hulls
nodes.note: Steel is stronger than iron; hulls can be thinner and faster. Requires bulk steel production at scale. The kernel is that welded seams (instead of rivets) are superior, but welding came late; early steel hulls still used rivets. Transition from iron to steel hulls took decades.

nodes.name: Stephenson link motion
nodes.kb: Rocking link arm combining two eccentrics to control valve opening
nodes.note: A curved link arm rocks back and forth; two eccentrics (off-center cams) are attached at its ends. A rod from the link drives the valve. By moving the link up and down, you change which eccentric drives the valve, reversing the locomotive or adjusting cut-off. The kernel is that this is a pure mechanical function generator: no calculation needed, just mechanical linkage geometry that engineers discovered through trial.

nodes.name: Stern tube and stuffing box
nodes.kb: Bearing tube in hull supporting propeller shaft with watertight seal
nodes.note: Stern tube is a bronze or iron tube through the hull; the propeller shaft rotates inside. Stuffing box at the hull side has packing that compresses to seal water out. The kernel is that the seal must allow the shaft to rotate freely, yet not leak; packing material (cotton or asbestos impregnated) is compressed progressively.

nodes.name: Sternpost rudder
nodes.kb: Flat rudder hinged on the sternpost, directly below the helm wheel
nodes.note: Rudder is a flat board pivoting on iron gudgeons. Tiller arm connected to wheel sheaves and rope. The kernel is that medieval steering oars were inefficient; a post-mounted rudder has much better control. Larger rudders are essential at speed.

nodes.name: Stockless anchor
nodes.kb: Anchor with hinged flukes no rigid stock bar
nodes.note: Flukes rotate on a pin, so anchor stows flat on deck. Older anchors had a rigid stock bar perpendicular to flukes; that required complex rigging to haul and stow. The kernel is that hinged flukes must seat reliably into the seabed; geometry must be exact or the anchor does not set.

nodes.name: Submarine pressure hull
nodes.kb: Strong cylindrical hull withstanding deep water pressure
nodes.note: Submarine hulls must be round to distribute pressure evenly; any flat section risks catastrophic collapse. Riveting was unreliable at deep pressure; early submarines were limited to shallow depth. The kernel is that this requires bulk steel, perfect riveting or welding, and careful design of openings.

nodes.name: Superheater
nodes.kb: Additional tubes carrying steam through the hot gas stream
nodes.note: Superheater tubes run through the furnace smoke box; steam passing through is heated above saturation temperature. Dry steam has much better expansion efficiency and does not condense in the cylinders. The kernel is that if steam reaches saturation again in the cylinders from pressure drop, water slugs damage the valves and pistons; superheat prevents this.

nodes.name: Tank wagon for liquids
nodes.kb: Cylindrical pressure vessel on wagon chassis
nodes.note: Tank wagons must be strong enough to support their own weight plus contents at speed over rough track. Seams must not leak; early tanks used hand-riveted seams prone to failure. The kernel is that a full tank at 60 tonnes bounces on rough track; suspension must be robust or the tank bends and ruptures.

nodes.name: Third rail power conductor
nodes.kb: Copper or steel rail beside tracks conducting power
nodes.note: Third rail is at ground or low height beside the track. A shoe on the vehicle contacts it for power. Simpler than overhead catenary, but third rail gets dirty and the shoe wears. The kernel is that contact pressure and shoe material determine the electrical connection quality; insufficient pressure or worn shoes arc and cause voltage drop.

nodes.name: Track circuit for detection
nodes.kb: Electrical circuit through the rails detecting presence of train
nodes.note: A low voltage circuit is sent down one rail through a relay to the other rail. Train wheels and axles short the circuit, stopping relay current. The relay releases, changing the signal. The kernel is that this is fail-safe: if a wheel falls off, or a rail breaks, the circuit opens and the signal shows stop. No human can override it.

nodes.name: Triple expansion marine engine
nodes.kb: Three cylinders: high, intermediate, and low pressure
nodes.note: Three stages of expansion extract more work from steam. Complex coordination of cylinders; triple expansion engines were the workhorse of ocean freight.

nodes.name: Tug boat for towing
nodes.kb: Small powerful boat for towing large cargo vessels
nodes.note: Tugs are high-powered relative to size; maneuverability is essential for harbor work. Engine and boiler dominate the design; cargo space is minimal. The kernel is that tugs must generate high torque at low speed to pull; reduction gearing or direct-drive low-speed engines are used.

nodes.name: Locomotive turntable
nodes.kb: Rotating platform on central pivot for turning locomotives end-for-end
nodes.note: Central pivot must support a locomotive and distribute its weight through ball or roller races. The kernel is that a flat bearing surface with rolling elements is essential; a simple pivot fails under the oscillation of a heavy moving locomotive. Early turntables had crude bearings that required frequent greasing and re-packing.

nodes.name: Vacuum brake
nodes.kb: Partial vacuum in pipe pulls piston in brake cylinder applying all brakes
nodes.note: Brake pipe runs the length of the train; a pump on the locomotive creates vacuum. If any coupling breaks, air leaks in and brakes lock on all wagons instantly. The kernel is that vacuum is unreliable; brake cylinders weep, couplings leak, and the vacuum pump must run continuously. Westinghouse air brake is more reliable.

nodes.name: Variable pitch propeller
nodes.kb: Propeller blades rotating on boss to change pitch angle
nodes.note: Variable pitch blades allow reversing without reversing engine rotation. Requires oil pressure or mechanical linkage to operate. The kernel is that this is complex and reliable operation needs careful maintenance; fixed-pitch propellers are simpler and still common.

nodes.name: Walschaerts valve gear
nodes.kb: Eccentric and crosshead combination for precise valve timing
nodes.note: Walschaerts uses the main piston rod as input to a linkage that drives the valve. The motion is more nearly sinusoidal than Stephenson, and the geometry allows rapid cut-off. Later discovered to be better than Stephenson. The kernel is that taking valve motion from the main piston rod instead of a separate eccentric is mechanically elegant and gives better speed control.

nodes.name: Water tube boiler
nodes.kb: Tubes carrying water surrounded by hot gases
nodes.note: Water tube boilers have tubes in a furnace, opposite of locomotive boilers. More efficient steam generation than fire-tube boilers.

nodes.name: Watertight bulkhead
nodes.kb: Internal wall extending from keel to deck sealing compartments
nodes.note: Bulkheads divide the hull into compartments; if one leaks, the ship does not sink immediately. Requires bulkheads to be truly watertight; any opening (door, pipe) must have a tight closure. The kernel is that a single leak in the lowest compartment sinks a ship; bulkheads buy time for repairs or evacuation.

nodes.name: Welded hull seams
nodes.kb: Electric arc welding of hull plate seams
nodes.note: Welded seams are stronger than riveted and save labor. Early welded hulls had fatigue cracks in service; design must avoid stress concentrations. The kernel is that riveted seams leak gradually, welded seams either work or fail suddenly. Transition from rivets to welds required understanding fatigue.

nodes.name: Westinghouse air brake
nodes.kb: Compressed air in pipe applies brakes; loss of air releases brakes
nodes.note: Westinghouse added a triple-valve: a mechanism that automatically applies brakes on each wagon when line pressure drops. No vacuum pump needed, just a compressor on the locomotive. The kernel is the triple-valve; loss of pressure in the main line triggers individual car brake application through the auxiliary reservoir on each wagon. This was revolutionary.

nodes.name: Windlass for anchor hauling
nodes.kb: Horizontal rotating drum hauling anchor cable
nodes.note: Windlass has gears reducing speed and increasing torque. Necessary for hauling heavy anchors against water pressure. The kernel is that gear reduction is essential: without it, even muscle power cannot raise an anchor in deep water. Early windlasses were hand-crank; later versions used steam power.

nodes.name: Wooden waggonway
nodes.kb: Wooden or cast iron rails in a groove for wheels
nodes.note: Wheels with flanges to stay on track are less efficient than flanged rails with flat wheels. Medieval coal mines used L-shaped cast iron rails; wheels rode on top. The innovation is that grooved track keeps wheels from falling off without a separate flange.

nodes.name: Acrylic: polyacrylonitrile fibres
nodes.note: Acrylonitrile-based polymerisation, wool-like properties, developed in 1940s, emerges as major fibre by late 1940s

nodes.name: Alum tanning: mineral salt curing
nodes.note: Alum and salt pickle hides, faster than vegetable tanning, less durable, primarily for light leather goods

nodes.name: Asbestos cloth: fire-resistant fabric
nodes.note: Woven asbestos fibres, extreme heat resistance to 1100C plus, essential for protective wear and insulation, long-term health consequences unknown

nodes.name: Automatic bobbin changer: weft supply
nodes.note: Automatic supply of full bobbins when current runs out, eliminates manual bobbin replenishment, essential for unattended running

nodes.name: Automatic loom: self-threading shuttle
nodes.note: Empty shuttle automatically ejected and threaded shuttle inserted, eliminates hand threading, increases speed and reduces downtimes

nodes.name: Ballpoint pen: ball-point writing
nodes.note: Small steel ball in socket, ink flows as ball rotates, Hungarian invention 1938, mass production challenges overcome by 1950s

nodes.name: Band knife: reciprocating cloth cutter
nodes.note: Motor-driven reciprocating blade cuts through stacked cloth, pattern template guides cutting, eliminates hand scissors

nodes.name: Beam: warp holder and tension
nodes.note: Heavy wooden roller wound with warp, large diameter maintains even tension, critical support structure

nodes.name: Bicycle: mass-produced consumer good
nodes.note: Chain drive and pneumatic tyres, mass production enables affordability, transforms personal transport from 1890s

nodes.name: Bleaching by chlorine: rapid whitening
nodes.note: Chlorine water or bleach powder oxidises colour bodies, fastest industrial method, some fibre damage especially to cotton

nodes.name: Bleaching by hydrogen peroxide: mild oxidation
nodes.note: Milder than chlorine, leaves no toxic residue, gentler on fibres, requires careful pH control, becomes preferred method by 1920s

nodes.name: Bleaching by sunlight: oxidative whitening
nodes.note: Laid on grass, UV radiation breaks colour bodies, slowest method but gentlest on fibres, traditional for linen

nodes.name: Board game: printed game on board
nodes.note: Printed game board with rules and pieces, mass production of family entertainment, 19th century emergence

nodes.name: Bobbin and flyer assembly: early spinning
nodes.note: Bobbin holds spun yarn, flyer guides it at controlled rate, differential speed creates twist, foundation spinning geometry before ring frame

nodes.name: Bottle: glass container
nodes.note: Hand-blown or later molded glass, seals and preserves liquids, mass production by 1870s

nodes.name: Brassiere: supportive undergarment
nodes.note: Elastic-based support without rigid boning, emerges in 1910s-1920s as alternative to corset, major innovation in women's comfort

nodes.name: Button: bone material
nodes.note: Carved bone disc, fine quality and good durability, medieval production standard

nodes.name: Button: horn material
nodes.note: Shaped horn disc, drilled and edges finished, traditional high-quality material, medieval production

nodes.name: Button: celluloid plastic material
nodes.note: Molded celluloid sheets stamped into buttons, cheaper and easier than natural materials, emerges in 1870s

nodes.name: Button: shell material
nodes.note: Mother-of-pearl and other shells cut into discs, lustrous appearance, waterborne trade commodity

nodes.name: Buttonhole machine: eyelet cutting and binding
nodes.note: Cuts buttonhole and simultaneously binds edge with thread, replaces hand work, enables mass production of shirts

nodes.name: Calendering: surface pressing
nodes.note: Heated rollers under controlled pressure compact surface, produces sheen and smoothness, essential for cotton satins

nodes.name: Camera: mass-produced photographic device
nodes.note: Fixed-focus simple lens, roll film, Kodak Brownie 1900 makes photography accessible to masses

nodes.name: Cap frame spinning
nodes.note: Wooden spindle with metal cap, flyer rotates with spindle, early frame for coarser counts, easier to wind than flyer and bobbin

nodes.name: Capability: reliable electric motor
nodes.note: Prerequisite placeholder for electric motor power availability in textile machinery

nodes.name: Cardboard box: folded laminate container
nodes.note: Laminated paper sheets glued and folded, replaces wooden crates for many applications, mass production by 1870s

nodes.name: Carding: opening and aligning fibres
nodes.note: Hand cards with bent wire teeth tease fibres, two cards with offset teeth align them parallel and remove neps, foundation of modern spinning

nodes.name: Cashmere: goat undercoat fibre
nodes.note: Mongolian and Himalayan goat undercoat, extremely fine and soft, luxury fibre, Kashmir region centres of trade

nodes.name: Chain stitch: thread-only interlocking
nodes.note: Single needle thread creates loops, used in early machines and special applications, less strong than lockstitch

nodes.name: Chrome tanning: chromium salt curing
nodes.note: Chromium sulfate rapidly tans hides, produces softer leather than vegetable tanning, faster but requires chemical control

nodes.name: Circular knitting machine: tubular production
nodes.note: Rotating bed of needles forms tube, true circular motion, enables continuous production, coarse and fine gauges

nodes.name: Clockwork toy: spring-driven mechanism
nodes.note: Spring-wound mechanism drives gears and linkages, walking or mechanical action, premium toy for wealthy children

nodes.name: Comb: hair grooming tool
nodes.note: Horn or bone cut into teeth, traditional technology, mass production emerges in 1800s with celluloid versions

nodes.name: Combing: alignment of long fibres
nodes.note: Combs of progressive fineness remove short fibres and neps, produces smoother yarn than carding, only for long-staple fibres like flax and worsted

nodes.name: Cordage for paperboard production
nodes.note: Paper pulp twisted into cord, intermediate product for paperboard and containers

nodes.name: Corrugated box: fluted paper structure
nodes.note: Wavy paper core between flat faces, light and strong, enables efficient shipping, emerges in 1890s

nodes.name: Corset: rigid body support garment
nodes.note: Boned structure shapes silhouette, whalebone and metal stays, essential women's garment from medieval through 20th century

nodes.name: Cotton gin: separation of seed from fibre
nodes.note: Wire hooks on rotating cylinder brush cotton past fixed blade, seeds fall away, reduces hand ginning labour by factor of fifty

nodes.name: Yarn count standardisation
nodes.note: Count is length per weight unit, English Cotton Count is 840 yards per pound, essential for yarn specification and trade

nodes.name: Cropping: nap trimming
nodes.note: Rotating cylinders with sharp blades trim raised nap to uniform height, creates smooth surface, high speed continuous operation

nodes.name: Crown cork: crimped bottle seal
nodes.note: Crimped tin cap with cork liner, seals carbonated beverages, bottling machine applies caps, invented 1891

nodes.name: Currying: leather finish dressing
nodes.note: Oil dressing and working of leather after tanning, imparts finish and handling, essential finishing step

nodes.name: Cutting table: stacked cloth cutting
nodes.note: Large flat table with edge, cloth stacked and cut to pattern, enables multiple pieces from single cutting

nodes.name: Desizing: size removal
nodes.note: Enzymatic or chemical removal of starch sizing applied to warp, must precede dyeing and finishing

nodes.name: Discharge printing: dye removal
nodes.note: Bleaching agent printed onto dyed cloth removes colour, creates light patterns on dark background, requires proper discharge agents [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Dobby head: mechanical shed control
nodes.note: Pegged barrel or chain cam controls shaft raising, each peg or link controls one pick, allows complex patterns without Jacquard cost

nodes.name: Doll: articulated child plaything
nodes.note: Articulated limbs and face, wood or cloth construction, mass production with porcelain heads emerges in 19th century

nodes.name: Doubling frame: twisting multiple yarns
nodes.note: Two or more bobbins feed into single twist spindle, creates plied yarn for strength and appearance, essential for warp threads

nodes.name: Drawing: fibre blending and extension
nodes.note: Two and more rovings drawn together and doubled, evens out slubs, allows fibre blending and increases draft

nodes.name: Drawing pin: short fastening point
nodes.note: Short point with wide head, brass or steel, holds paper to boards without permanent damage

nodes.name: Dyeing in fibre: pre-spin colouration
nodes.note: Loose fibres or cards dipped in dye bath, blends different coloured fibres before spinning, essential for heathers and mixtures

nodes.name: Dyeing in garment: finished good colouration
nodes.note: Finished garment dipped in vat, enables custom colouration, risk of shrinkage, labour-intensive due to garment complexity

nodes.name: Dyeing in piece: woven cloth colouration
nodes.note: Folded cloth in dye bath, most efficient use of dye, requires careful handling to avoid creases, standard for finished fabric

nodes.name: Dyeing in yarn: skein colouration
nodes.note: Skeins hung in dye bath, requires even access to liquor, risk of uneven colour, essential for solid-colour fabrics

nodes.name: Elastic: rubber thread
nodes.note: Rubber covered thread or cord, recoverable stretch, essential for undergarments and sportswear, emerging in early 20th century

nodes.name: Embossing: surface pattern pressing
nodes.note: Hot press with pattern die creates surface texture, replicates grain or adds decoration, mechanical equipment by 1890s

nodes.name: Gummed envelope flap: adhesive sealing
nodes.note: Starch-based adhesive applied to flap, dries to enable moistening, improvement over wax seals and tape

nodes.name: Envelope: paper folded container
nodes.note: Paper folded and gummed, gummed flap seals contents, mass production by 1850s transforms postal efficiency

nodes.name: Eraser: rubber pencil mark removal
nodes.note: Rubber abrasion removes graphite, cap-mounted or pencil-top versions, mass production emerges in late 1800s

nodes.name: Eye-pointed needle: self-threading sewing
nodes.note: Needle with eye at point, thread slides in from end during forward motion, essential for mechanical sewing machines

nodes.name: Flameproofing: combustion resistance
